You know, the courts, the legislatures, the president. But in the international law, it's about which principle is supreme. Generally speaking, in international law, state sovereignty is the highest principle. It's higher than human rights, actually, generally speaking. So that's international relations. We then have political economy, which I've mentioned about. This is the intersection between political and economic institutions, analyzing how political institutions affect the economy.
1.59: So one famous book talks about how, if you have very authoritarian government, then you tend to get corruption. You don't tend to get a lot of trust. Property rights are not very secure, and therefore it's very hard for the economy to grow. So if you have a sort of authoritarian or an anarchic political system, then that's going to have a very negative impact on the economics. It's going to be very hard to get particularly a free market emerging where people have secure property rights, where if someone cheats you, you can go to the courts. All of that is very difficult when you don't have the right political institutions in place. So this is really exploring the connection between political institutions and the economy.
1.60: Another subfield is public policy, which is, the question is, how is policy influenced? Who sets the direction of economic policy in a country? Is it lobby groups? Is it the bureaucrats in the civil service? What is the role of executives, et cetera, the media? So there are all these different forces that would affect policy and whether certain policies are enacted. It could well be that the population as a whole wants a certain policy. Maybe they want more spending on the health service; maybe they want lower taxes. But that's not what comes out formally because there are different interests.
1.61: Maybe lobby groups perhaps have more power than the average citizen, and so what turns out in the end. Or maybe the civil service or the bureaucracy, actually, is able to frustrate certain policies and is able to have influence in shaping the direction of policy. So there are all these different actors. It's not just the people having their preferences enacted. There are actors within the system at the elite level, also at the bureaucratic level, that might be able to steer policies in a certain way, which may systematically be different from what the population wants. And so then you get discontent rising in the system.
1.62: One of the reasons for populism might be, so, for example, in Western countries, one argument is that immigration is higher than what most citizens want for a whole bunch of reasons to do with lobby groups within the system, the preferences of certain elites within the system. And therefore there is a sort of dissonance between what the population wants and what the government is delivering, and that's creating discontent within the system that leads to more populism. That's one argument.
1.63: And then finally we come to, research methods isn't really a proper field of politics. It's more just a way of how do you study, how would you study the political? There are many different methods. There's case study methods where you look at different countries, let's say, or business, where you look at a company. That's more like a case study approach, business studies. Whereas, a lot of comparative politics now would tend to use large-scale quantitative data sets. So, 200 countries over 50 years, along, you know, 10 different characteristics, like rich or poor, are they a democracy or not, how big is their population, were they colonized, how many ethnic groups in the country. All of these things are thrown into the model and you see which are the, which are the factors that predict a country going to civil war or becoming a democracy.
1.64: And that, that's sort of a quantitative modeling approach, which is probably, at least in the top journals in political science, that tends to be the approach. Now if you're doing political philosophy or international, not international, but political philosophy to a large extent, then you would not use quantitative methods because it's all about the "ought." So you're engaging in philosophical reasoning and arguing about pros and cons, first principles, premises, and so forth.
1.65: So just to conclude then, I've tried to give you a very, very broad overview of what is politics. We've talked about politics as institutions of government and politics as power, the processes and functions of the power flowing through the institutions. We then turned to look a little bit at models and different subfields within politics, such as, I talked about comparative politics, international relations, and political theory or political philosophy. Those are the three big branches of political science. And again, just to sort of reiterate, there is this distinction between the "is", the empirical, the study of political behavior and institutions—that very scientific approach, which you can do through different methodologies.
1.66: You can use case studies, you can use large-scale quantitative modeling, or that's the "is" part, which is most of political science. But then we have the "ought", you know, how ought we to design society and politics? And that's more the political theory. Again, those are sort of two separate foci. And again, to reiterate, there's also that difference between power, power as process and government as institutions. So between those two, that kind of gives you a very sort of quick, high-level view of the field. And there are different theories and subfields that would tend to focus on different combinations of those two processes. Lecture 2: Comparative Political Institutions At a glance — Comparative political institutions.
2.1: Welcome back. I'm going to be talking next about comparative political institutions . This is a topic, this is a basic intro to politics topic that falls within the study of government and institutions. That's the empirical part of political science. That is, we're trying to explain how things work, and we're looking very much, classically, at governing institutions. I'll particularly be comparing the governing institutions of the US and Britain, but also to some degree, France and other countries as well. I just want to take you through some of the basics in institutions when we're studying government institutions.
2.2: The first is that we can divide the institutions of government into three general branches. That is the legislatures, the executives, and the judiciaries. The legislatures make law and enact legislation. So a bill will be proposed in the House of Representatives or in Parliament, for example . So the legislatures draft and make the laws. The executives , think president, prime minister, their cabinet . That's the executive. The executive implements the law and executes the law. And the judiciary, the Supreme Court of the United States, for example, interprets the law and adjudicates on the meaning of the law. The judges will have to think, what were the legislators thinking when they drafted a law? What was the actual intent behind the law?
2.3: That will be important for the judges when they are deciding in a case as to whether, for example, whether you can have quotas for different racial groups in university admittance or for government contracting. That would be an example where the judiciary would render a decision as to know that is either consistent with or inconsistent with the meaning of the civil rights laws that were drafted in 1965. So they have to get into the heads, in a way, of the legislators. At least in theory, that is how they should interpret the meaning of the law. So we have legislatures, executives, and judiciaries.
2.4: You also have a constitution. A constitution would tend to set out who has power and when. So you might say, well, the president can veto legislation from Congress, but Congress, in a two-thirds vote, can override the presidential veto. The Supreme Court can strike down a law. All of those things are specified in the constitution document, which would tell you who has power and where. It's all about the distribution and structure of power in a particular polity. These are the three branches of government.
2.5: The way in which they have power over each other is sometimes referred to as checks and balances , the ways in which you don't allow the executive, the president, to just do whatever he wants without regard to any of the other branches of government. They're checked and constrained by the other branches of government. The constitution then specifies the rules as to where power is distributed, who has power over whom. Again, we can contrast that democratic, the democratic constitutions, which are about these checks and balances, the liberal democratic constitutions, with autocratic systems that might say the king or the president has absolute power to dissolve the legislature, to get rid of the judiciary, pack it with his own cronies. That is an autocratic system as compared to a democratic system .
2.6: Sometimes in autocratic systems, you will have a parliament and you will have even a supreme court, but those will be toothless and just symbolic and will have no real power. There's a distinction between the symbol of having, calling yourself the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, using the term democratic, but actually no one would claim North Korea as a democracy. So there's a distinction between the symbol and the reality of power.
2.7: OK, so that's the three branches of government. What I want to do next is compare within democratic. Again, I'm excluding the autocracies, which are, of course, very important in the world, and we will be talking about them as well. But I'm excluding the autocracies to focus on the democracies. But within the democracies, we have a couple of different designs. It's about, how do you design the system to achieve the best result? There's not a single blueprint for how you design a political system. But there are a few blueprints, not 100 on the menu. There's probably two or three on the menu. The two most common ones, obviously, are presidential versus parliamentary systems.
2.8: To some degree, these are connected to the history of different societies. So where you had a revolution, overthrowing the aristocracy, like in France, the French Revolution, or the United States, breaking away from the British Empire, Britain. Then you have the parliamentary systems, which are more common in, where the monarchy survived, and there was a reform of the society like Britain, where the power of the king was gradually moderated and more power flowed to parliament, but you don't get rid of the monarch. There remains a constitutional monarch. That's true in some of the Nordic countries as well . So you're more likely to get a parliamentary system.
2.9: And then, of course, if Britain then has colonies, they will tend to copy the metropole , and then you get the spread of that parliamentary system. So that is presidential versus parliamentary. These are the systems that have emerged in the world. And then in other cases, you have a country like Japan, picking and mixing from the different systems to design their own. So we're comparing then democratic political systems. There's presidential and parliamentary. There's a question here about the structure of government, how power is distributed amongst the different branches, which differs, to some degree, between the presidential and the parliamentary system. We want to consider the role of the executive president, prime minister, and their cabinets. In which system is the executive more powerful?
2.10: So I have a chart here that just shows you the presidential democracy versus the parliamentary democracy. So in a presidential system, people vote not just for, they don't just vote once for a particular entity. They vote for the President, and they vote also for their local representative. So in the US system, for example, you would have down ballot voting for representatives in Congress, Senator, and your representative. You would have separate votes, which means that you could vote Republican for President and Democratic in the Congressional elections for your senator and for your congressman. So you would tend to get, therefore—you could get different parties being represented in the legislature and in the executive.
2.11: Whereas in a parliamentary democracy, it's the vote just for the legislature. Now, yes, there is a prime minister, but you don't vote separately for the prime minister and for your member of parliament. You vote only one ticket, and the prime minister has a seat as an MP, but you're only really voting once. So the power comes from the citizens through to the legislature. The legislature then, in a way, appoints the executive, the Prime Minister, because the party chooses the Prime Minister; the Prime Minister chooses their cabinet. But they are elected by the people. Whereas in the presidential case, the President is directly elected by the people, and the legislature is also directly elected by the people, and people may decide to split.
2.12: So in the '80s and '90s, there was something called gridlock, which happened a lot in the US, where people might vote for Bill Clinton, the Democrat, as the President, but they might vote Republican for their local member of Congress or their Senator. So you would tend to get a split, where maybe Congress would be controlled by one party, President by another party. That leads to, they have to compromise if anything is to get done or else you get nothing done, which unfortunately is, to some degree, one of the issues in US politics. So presidential versus parliamentary, those are some differences.
2.13: In terms of the legislative process, how a bill becomes law, we want to understand how that process works in a parliamentary system and in a presidential system as well. There are some differences which we can talk about. Clearly, in the case of the parliamentary system, like Britain, bills are proposed in the House of Commons. Yes , they are scrutinized by the Lords, but generally, the House of Commons has the power. The Lords really has limited power. Whereas you would never say in the American system that the Congress has limited power or that the Senate has very little power. They all have quite a bit of power.
2.14: That's one important difference legislatively, that in the parliamentary system , the party that essentially controls parliament has a lot of power to enact legislation, whereas in the presidential system, particularly when you have different parties that are running different branches of government, the power of, let's say, the president is much more limited. But in other cases, if they have the same party, if the Republicans are dominant in the Senate, the House, and the presidency, then actually they may, to some extent, have more power even than in a parliamentary system.
2.15: We want to look at the process of legislation. We also want to look at public participation and accountability. How are leaders held accountable by the public , and the implications of these for how successful a particular political system is for delivering on accountable government, good government, and representativeness. We'll be looking at those dimensions of political system performance , comparing the two major liberal democratic political systems . And in this map, this shows you which parts of the world have a presidential system, which parts of the world have a parliamentary system. You can see that the United States and most of Latin America has a presidential system. Again, the legacy of revolution. France also, it's mixed , but clearly it does have a president. The French Revolution partly explains why that is the case.
2.16: You have dictatorship or autocracy in many parts of the world. Russia, China, Vietnam, North Korea. These are examples. Much of sub-Saharan Africa as well is falling into this non-democratic form of government where power is largely in the hands of an autocratic leader , whether that is the President or the king or the monarch. That is really where power lies in a dictatorship. However, in this map, what we see is, even though a lot of the countries I just mentioned in sub-Saharan Africa, China, Russia, et cetera, are de facto autocracies, where the leader has pretty much absolute power, there are symbolically the system that they choose to adopt actually does make room for a legislature and a court. It's just that those are toothless.
2.17: So formally, they might be parliamentary or presidential in their design , but practically, they are autocracies. It's only in places that are democracies that you actually have power flowing to the legislature and the courts, for example. You can also see that some of the countries that were part of the British Empire, Australia, Canada, for example, are more likely to have a parliamentary system rather than a presidential one.
2.18: OK, so just to talk then about the features of these systems, what is a presidential system? The President is the elected head of state in a particular nation , head of the government, chief executive officer of the nation. In a presidential system, we have a separation of powers because people are voting directly for the President, but they are also voting directly for their representative in the legislature, like their member of Congress. There's also courts as well, acting as another power center. The system posits the President and the legislature as co-equal, each having similar levels of power. The President is not a member of the legislature. That's different from the Prime Minister, who is a member of the legislature, is elected as an MP. The President is not elected as a member of Congress . So that's one difference.
2.19: Now, whether that matters in terms of—the President of the US is not accountable locally to a particular constituency, the way the Prime Minister, for example, does have a constituency that they have some accountability to as well. So what is a presidential system? And we've got a picture of the Mexican Assembly here, which is, again, part of that presidential system. We have the direct election of the President by the people. That is separate from the assembly, which is directly elected. You have a vote for members of Congress, a vote for the President. Fixed terms of office, very neatly delineated. It's not to say that there are no fixed terms in parliamentary systems. They can also sometimes have terms. They are, as in Britain, more fluid to some degree, not four years fixed, although there are conventions that delimit how long a term of office is, even in a parliamentary system.
2.20: The President has a lot of power in foreign policy and foreign affairs. They can make a decision, for example, to go to war in a presidential system, whereas in a parliamentary system, actually, the Prime Minister actually has to bring that before Parliament. So they can't just unilaterally make these foreign policy decisions. Now, even though the President, in the US case, can declare war and can act, has a certain amount of power independent of Congress, to some degree, the President in foreign policy is more powerful than the Prime Minister. In a presidential system as well, the President can veto legislation coming from Congress, from the legislature . So you have a presidential veto. That doesn't exist clearly in the parliamentary system . The Prime Minister cannot veto legislation. Of course, he or she wouldn't necessarily do that, but they can't veto legislation coming out of parliament. So that's another important distinction .
2.21: So the presidential system has a lot of these formalized checks and balances that delimit who has power when. It's designed so that each part of the system checks the power of the other part of the system. To some degree in the parliamentary system, power is a little bit more concentrated in the legislature, which is—Parliament in Britain, for example, is supreme , supreme over the courts, for example, in a way that is not as true, really not true in the presidential system, where the court can strike down legislation. Legislatures in a presidential system, they can vote to impeach. They can impeach a president. We saw some of that clearly with talk of impeachment of President Trump. We have this power to impeach, but it's very difficult to get the votes necessary to impeach.
2.22: In a parliamentary system, there isn't impeachment, but you can have a vote of no confidence in the Prime Minister, and that's one way in which the legislature checks the power of the executive in the parliamentary system. The parliamentary system of government, which, by the way, is more common than the presidential, arguably, globally, although it's a toss-up to some degree, depends on definitions . But the parliamentary system, you have people voting in the assembly, i .e., parliament, and the Prime Minister is the leader of the largest party in the assembly. Sometimes there are coalitions. In Britain, this country, we saw a coalition between the Conservatives and liberal Democrats as well to make up the numbers so that they are large enough to control a plurality of power in the system.
2.23: Presidential system works, again, more on these formal checks and balances, the electorate voting separately for, as I mentioned, separately for the assembly. So you vote for your member of Congress, you vote for the president separately , and they each check each other. It's worth saying that, going back to this term liberal democracy, democracy really is about the majority ruling, not the aristocracy or the king. So it's power to the people, popular sovereignty, and the idea that the people have power, not the monarch or the king or even the president. That's the notion of popular sovereignty.
2.24: But there's also liberalism. That's democracy, but liberalism is about the rights of the individual, the rights of the individual against the state, but even sometimes the rights of the individual against the tyranny of the majority . That's part of, that you have your rights that can't be trampled on, even if there is majority sentiment to deny you rights, let's say, as a Catholic in Britain. The courts are in some ways the guarantor of liberal, the liberal part of liberal democracy. The courts defend your rights as an individual in the system.
2.25: They are perhaps less important to the democratic side, the idea of majority rule, popular sovereignty. That's more the legislature, and to some extent, the executive. The judiciary is about the liberal side, the defense of liberalism. So one of the terms you may have heard or may not have heard is the term illiberal democracy. Illiberal democracy. So you will have elections in different countries. Singapore, for example. You might have elections in Ivory Coast, in a number of different countries. But on the other hand, and so you have democracy in a way. You have elections, you may have the transfer of power from one party to another, but you have very weak protection of your rights. If somebody who's well connected to the ruling elite takes something of yours, cheats you in a business dealing, and they are well connected, they can work the system. So your rights are not properly protected, or you can be thrown in jail, again, without a lot of protection for your rights.
2.26: That shows you the weakness of the judiciary and the legal system in protecting your constitutional rights . So just to say that liberal democracies are really mixing together two things, which is protection of your individual rights, the liberalism, and the democracy side, which is popular sovereignty that the majority rules, not a small elite. Those two elements can be in tension . There can a tension between liberalism and democracy. To some extent, one way we can—well, we could understand some aspects of populism as a tension between what populism is sort of about is the majoritarian, the desire of the people being frustrated. To some degree, that might be because of the power of the judiciary and its emphasis on constitutional liberties as against majority rules. You can have tension between the liberalism and the democracy.
2.27: Just continuing on with presidential systems, what we have is the judiciary , which is the protector of individual rights, but also the meaning of legislation and interpreting the legislation. Then you have the executive and the assembly, each given certain powers. There are certain rules for how disputes between these are resolved. I mentioned presidential vetoes . In the US system, the president can veto legislation, but that then can be overridden by a two-thirds majority in Congress. So in the US system, the President is the formal head of state. There's a formal role, which is that you represent the country, US, France, et cetera, but also a more legislative role and a power role. In other countries, constitutional monarchies like Britain, the formal head of state is the king or queen, the monarch. So the Prime Minister is not the formal head of state, but the Prime Minister is the de facto leader of the executive.
2.28: Prime ministers, as distinct from presidents. The parliamentary system has a couple of features that are distinct from the presidential system. I mentioned that formal head of state, the monarch—that's not there in a presidential system. And that, again, reflects the history of presidential republics that overthrew monarchs. Whereas in a parliamentary system, particularly a constitutional monarchy, the monarch would be the formal representative of the state and the incarnation of the state. Also, the legislature in a parliamentary system, like Britain's , the House of Commons, the leader is drawn from the House of Commons. It's an MP that becomes Prime Minister. That's another difference.
2.29: The other aspect that is important is how you remove. In a parliamentary system, and a good example is what's happened in Britain over the last few years, there have been a succession of different prime ministers. You started out with Boris Johnson in 2019, and then Liz Truss came in, and then Liz Truss was removed. Rishi Sunak came in, and maybe now Rishi Sunak is going to be removed. So that would never happen in the US case. No matter how discontented people were with Joe Biden, he wouldn't be removed and replaced with somebody else. They can't do that. That is not part of the American constitutional set-up. So that's a distinctive element of the parliamentary system. You could say that that's a good thing, perhaps, in that it allows for more responsiveness. So maybe if Johnson is really unpopular, you can remove him and get somebody else. And that's maybe responding to the public mood. Maybe that's a good thing. It's more flexible. Maybe it's not a good thing because it creates chaos. But there's a debate to be had there.
2.30: It's worth saying, by the way, the President, yes, can be impeached, but the bar for that is much higher than in the parliamentary case. So it's not the same process. Generally, you might say that the President has more power in the sense that it's harder to get rid of him or her than in a parliamentary system. The Prime Minister is always, to some degree, beholden to the good graces of his or her party.
2.31: Where does prime ministerial power come from then if prime ministers are not directly elected? I mean, it's quite interesting because there's a whole debate about, is Rishi Sunak legitimate or Liz Truss legitimate because they weren't elected by the people to lead the government? So there's this whole question of legitimacy. But in general, you would never question the president's legitimacy because the president has been directly elected by the population. Even if the population comes to not like the President, but they did elect him or her . So that is their choice, and it has that legitimacy. So the prime ministerial power then derives instead from a number of different sources. One is their patronage, their ability to place people in relatively good positions within the government.
2.32: There are certain government positions which are more highly valued than others, which have greater prestige than others, and which also may lead to an individual who has performed particular roles like Chancellor of the Exchequer, becoming Prime Minister later. Whereas if you are, I don't know, doing culture and media, that might be less prestigious, and that's not necessarily a stepping stone to becoming a Prime Ministerial candidate . So level and range of patronage, control of appointments to cabinet , which is, again, the cabinet around the table is what —these are the top positions within government which actually set policy direction.
2.33: So prime ministers can appoint people to cabinet. They can also have reshuffles where they drop a number of people from the cabinet and put other MPs in as members of the cabinet. They have a certain amount of power over MPs who would desire to get closer to the levers of power. They also have position as head of the civil service. In theory, the civil service is supposed to carry out the wishes of the prime minister. Now, there's a whole debate over, does the civil service actually, in practice, have its own agenda, have independent power from the Prime Minister? Is that a good thing or a bad thing?
2.34: Same in the presidential system. Is it a good thing that the federal government bureaucracy didn't do what Trump wanted it to do? Is it a bad thing? There are different debates over this. One view is that people don't elect bureaucrats , therefore bureaucrats should not, they should simply be carrying out the wishes of the executive. Another view is, well , there's a certain degree to which the bureaucracy and the executive know how things work and perhaps can gauge the public mood or should have some discretion or some impact on policy. That's a debate.
2.35: Finally, and this is true of presidents as well, the ability to use the media, for example, if there is a backbench rebellion in Parliament, and Sunak goes on the media and is able to portray the backbenchers as fomenting disunity and causing the party to have trouble in the next election, then maybe Sunak is able to quell and to draw the sting from that backbench rebellion. So use of the media is also an important aspect of power for prime ministers. It's very important aspect, by the way, for presidents, too. If Congress is not enacting legislation that the President wants to get enacted and the President goes on the media and tries to essentially attack those people who are stymieing the legislation as impeding the will of the people, maybe the President can generate enough pressure in the media to force Congress to back down in a certain way. So it's all, use of the media is part of the tools of power that both prime ministers and presidents can wield.
2.36: OK, so when I talk about the executive, that's not just the president or prime minister, but also the cabinet. So virtually all political executives feature a cabinet . Here there's some quite interesting differences between presidential and parliamentary systems . What cabinets do is that they are a way of coordinating the policy agenda of the executive, and that's typically the party that controls government. So the parliamentary cabinet in the British system would all be drawn from the conservative government because that's who's been elected. It's worth saying that, in a system that involves power-sharing, you would tend to have members of the cabinet from different parties. In Lebanon, in Northern Ireland, you would tend to have a cabinet made up of members of different parties, representing the entire legislature, not just the winning party . Whereas in a first-past-the-post or winner-take-all system like the US and Britain, the cabinet would be only made up of members of the winning party.
2.37: In the British system, the cabinet is appointed by the Prime Minister from MPs who've won their seats, who sit in Parliament in the legislature. So the Prime Minister is selecting people who've won office. In the US case, the President's cabinet, there's nobody in the President's cabinet that is a member of Congress. So in the British system, the Prime Minister appoints members of the cabinet from Parliament who are members of the legislature. In the US case, the President appoints people who are not members of the legislature, and so they have no divided loyalty to their congressional electors. They've got only loyalty to the President. So the US cabinet includes Secretary of State, Secretary of the Treasury, Secretary of Defense. These are all people that are appointed directly by President, in this case, President Biden.
2.38: And that's a difference, again, between the parliamentary system. So there's an independent power center there, totally independent from the legislature, whereas in the British system, there's an interpenetration. These members of the cabinet are from the legislature. Even if they are ejected from the cabinet, they still have their seat and they still have a voice. Whereas if you are in the American cabinet and you are ejected, you have nothing, no power left. There are a number of differences that way.
2.39: We have then the legislature. We can talk about the legislature and its relationship to the executive and the power of the legislature vis-a-vis the executive. We can also see some distinctions here between the presidential and parliamentary system . It's worth saying that, in terms of the legislatures or assemblies, they have a number of different functions. One is to propose and scrutinize legislation. Laws are proposed in the Senate or the House of Representatives or the House of Commons. They make their way through a number of different readings. Now, in the British system, they then go to the Lords. They are also, by the way, scrutinized in committees which are formed to actually go line by line through legislation and improve them. So part of what the assemblies are doing is they are scrutinizing legislation, refining and making it better.
2.40: There are, again, important differences. In Britain, the House of Lords, yes, they can scrutinize legislation. Yes, they can propose amendments, but ultimately power lies with the House of Commons, and the House of Lords doesn't have a lot of power. Whereas in the American system or the presidential system, a bill can be proposed in the—typically, what will happen is a bill will be proposed in the House and in the Senate at the same time, but the bill has to pass through both houses in order to go through, and it's not automatic that it will necessarily pass both houses. So the Senate is a much more powerful body than the House of Lords, for example.
2.41: Assemblies also decide on appropriations of money. They have a budget, for example. They have to authorize the use of funds. So the American President can declare war, but if the President wants to continue that war, they need to get authorization from Congress. Assemblies are also important, generally, for recruiting people into politics. Parties tend to recruit people into politics. Those parties are linked very much to the legislature. And then lastly , legitimacy. The assembly is seen as a representative of the people. So the people vote for their local MP or member of Congress. They see that person there. They see that they're being represented properly by the system.
2.42: That's important for system legitimacy, and when we get into a situation where people think , "Oh, the assembly doesn't represent me." I talked about Northern Ireland for a long time. In Northern Ireland, the party associated with the Protestant voters won every election for 50 years. So the Catholic third of the population felt like, "We aren't being represented here." Yes, it's a one-person, one-vote system, but on a one-person, one-vote system with everyone voting for an ethnic party or for a religious party , that resulted in a victory for one side every time for 50 years. You can see where perhaps one section of the community would feel that they weren't represented. So representation is important in an assembly.
2.43: Now, there is a question of who needs to be represented. We talked about Protestant and Catholic in Northern Ireland or in Lebanon, it might be Christian, Shia, and Sunni Muslim, seeing themselves represented in government. If they're not represented, that could lead to discontent, which could lead to violence. But then there are other kinds of characteristics. Does the assembly need to be 50% male, 50% female? For example, is it important to have the working class be represented? There are almost no members of parliament or Congress who don't have a university degree, who are from working- class backgrounds. Is that a problem? If people who come from those backgrounds feel that they are not represented, does that lead to populism and discontent within the system?
2.44: So assemblies also have to represent, to some degree, the populations that they govern, but they don't necessarily have to represent every dimension and every group identity in a perfect mirror image of the population so that there are X number of left- handed people. That's a bit ridiculous. The question is, and there's a whole debate over how much do the assemblies have to represent the characteristics of their populations or not.
2.45: So just to look at a couple, a few case studies, we have the US as a presidential system, Britain as a parliamentary system, and France, which is actually a bit of a mixed system. It has a president and a prime minister. In the US case, then, we have a classic presidential system where the executive is separately elected from the legislature, and there is a formalized separation of powers. Britain, a classic parliamentary system, fusion of the executive and legislative branches in the person of the Prime Minister, who is the leader the executive and also elected to the legislature. Then France, with a unique system that has got both an elected President and an elected legislature.
2.46: Just in terms of the mechanics of power in the American system, laws are drafted in Congress. That is, a House bill and a Senate bill are both tabled. They then go to the President. If they've been passed by Congress, they then go to the President to sign the bill. The President can say no and veto, but Congress can override that veto with a two- thirds vote. One example of that is Ronald Reagan wanted to see affirmative action removed in the US case, and that was overridden by Congress. So Congress has power; with enough support, it can override presidential legislation .
2.47: President can also issue what are called executive orders, which do not require legislation . There are certain areas in which President has power to issue an executive order. Maybe the executive order might be around government contracting. If I use the affirmative action case, there can be an executive order mandating some sort of affirmative action quota, say, X proportion of government contracts going to African- American-led firms. Now, that executive order, if another party comes in, they can rescind that executive order. None of that involves tabling legislation. That is an area where the president has a certain sphere of power to pursue a policy agenda independently of the legislature. But the legislature can, however, legislate and make it explicit. In that sense, ultimately, they can override the power of the President in that sense.
2.48: I mentioned already about presidents can make war, but Congress has to approve the funds. Ultimately, once again, the President has only limited, particularly over the longer term, only has limited power and cannot simply steamroll the legislature. The Supreme Court, however, can declare certain laws unconstitutional. However, the President can appoint members of the nine members of the Supreme Court. If a member of the Supreme Court dies, then there's an opportunity to appoint a member of the court. To that extent, the executive has power over the judiciary and the content, the composition of the judiciary, is controlled to some degree by the President.
2.49: But of course, those nine justices have long terms because they have those terms for life . In other systems, they don't have such long terms, which would then grant more power to the executive over the judiciary. It's also worth saying that the Senate has to confirm the President's judicial appointments, so that gives some voice from the legislature into the judicial appointments process. It's also worth saying that there have been different eras in American history where the power of the President has waxed and waned. Teddy Roosevelt in the early 20th century, seen as an American President that actually presided over the rise, the growth of power to the President , where there are other presidents who are more acquiescent to the legislature. So there's a certain degree to which the power of the presidency waxes and wanes over time .
2.50: In the United Kingdom, I mentioned that the parliament can, through a vote of no confidence, remove a prime minister, and we've seen that in Britain in recent years. And so that is a check on the power of the executive. The legislature can end the term of the leader of the executive. So that's an important check on the power of the executive in the British system. There is this term bicameral, which means two chamber. And so House of Representatives, Senate. House of Commons, House of Lords. Upper house. These upper houses or second chambers have different degrees of power in different societies. Even in the Soviet Union, you had an upper house. Actually, the upper house may have different principles, which constituted. Even in the Soviet Union, you had the Duma, the Parliament, and you had the Congress of People's Deputies, which was really about representing all the different republics within the Soviet Union system.
2.51: In a way, the Senate is like that, too. The Senate in the US, it's two senators for each state. Whether you have 40 million people like California or 250,000 like Alaska, you get two senators. It's not on a representation by population basis , whereas the House of Representatives is on a representation by population basis. So there will be a lot more members of Congress from California than from Alaska. But in the Senate, they will have the same number of representatives. The reason for that is, the building block for the Senate is the state. The view is that people have an identification with their state. I am a Virginian, I am an Alaskan, which is important. If you had election after election after election, and Alaskans were never in the winning party, it's a bit like Northern Ireland, the Catholics never being in the winning party . You could get discontent forming.
2.52: The federal principle is to say, well, we have to recognize society is made up, yes, of individuals who expect equal representation, but it's also made up of groups which are important in this society, whether it's Protestant Catholic, whether it's being a Virginian or a Massachusettsan or a New Yorker. Those are important group identities, and we have to account for them. The upper house, sometimes, and I mentioned the Soviet Union as well, even though, of course, the Soviet Union was not a democracy. But it's just interesting that the principle they adopted was that they want to represent the republics in that upper house.
2.53: The upper house then scrutinizes legislation from the Parliament. The upper houses have different levels of power. Britain, the upper house is much weaker than the US, where the Senate is much stronger. Those are all what are called two-chamber or bicameral systems. There's also a relationship between the legislature and the Supreme Court or the high court in Britain. In Britain, the legislature is supreme. It's recognized in the British Constitution that the legislature, parliament is supreme, parliamentary sovereignty, whereas that's not necessarily the case in the American system , where the Supreme Court can veto, strike down legislation.
2.54: What about France? This is a mixed system, a semi-presidential, where you have an elected president, but you also have an elected legislature with a prime minister. Now, France is an interesting melding of these two systems. So the president can appoint the prime minister. As in a classic presidential system, the President has power over foreign policy . But in terms of the legislative agenda, the Prime Minister has the power. Now, notice in the British system, which is purely parliamentary, the Prime Minister is important in driving legislative agenda, as well as having power over, for example, foreign policy.
2.55: You can have a situation in France where different parties—so the presidency can be Emmanuel Macron and the legislature can be the Socialist. You can have this situation where you can have different parties in control, and there you get something like the American gridlock, where you get—it's very difficult to get legislation passed, and particularly the President's legislative agenda through. That's tougher when the legislature is controlled by another party. You get these complicated arrangements. The President can dissolve Parliament , actually, in the French system. Then you would say, well, the executive has power over the legislature, but on the other hand , parliament can remove the president through a vote of no confidence. So that's the legislature having power over the president. So you have this very fluid system of checks and balances.
2.56: The high court, or Supreme Court in France, is largely appointed independently of the President and, to some extent, the legislature. So that's a separate power center , but on the other hand, it doesn't seem to have the same powers in the American system. The next question we might ask is, OK, so let's deal with the executive for a second and ask, what are the powers of the executive in the presidential and parliamentary system?
2.57: So, one is that the Prime Minister or the President is a representative of the country, symbolically to the world. The face of Britain to the world is the Prime Minister. The face of the United States to the world is the President. They're symbolizing the larger society in its unity and its national identity in a way, a formal relationship. They also have a policy-making leadership role , which is that they want to drive a particular legislative agenda, which is typically the agenda that they ran on in the elections. That's another function of the executive, is to actually drive forth a particular legislative agenda. Maybe it's fighting inflation , it's cutting hospital waiting times, it's reducing migration levels, it's increasing trade. Whatever it is, that is what the executive is partly about, delivering that particular policy agenda.
2.58: The executive is expected then to, in a way, govern in the interests of those who brought it to power, but also broadly in the interests of the country as a whole. Of course, it's complicated because, in some cases, parties really represent a narrow group and are really judged only on how they perform to the people who elected them. This is particularly in societies, and there are quite a few societies in the world, where people vote for ethnic parties, and you're assessed as a leader as to how well you deliver for your ethnic constituency, not for the country as a whole. One of the arguments, again, to return to Lebanon or Northern Ireland, if you are in the Democratic Unionist Party or in Sinn Féin in Northern Ireland, you will be assessed on how well you delivered for your people in a way. Unionist for the Protestant people . Sinn Féin, how well did you deliver for the Catholic population , not only for Northern Ireland as a whole.
2.59: In terms of getting back to the functions of political executives , we mentioned driving forth a policy agenda symbolizing the nation. There's also this idea of representation so that people feel that they're being listened to, being represented by the people that they put into government. That's important for the legitimacy of the system, trust in the system. Political executives also have to steer the bureaucracy of state, and sometimes known as the "blob" in Britain or the "deep state" in the US. Those are a bit conspiratorial, but the idea is that you have to actually get the bureaucracy to do what you want it to do, to carry out the functions, whether it be an education, whether it be in the military.
2.60: Sometimes that's been satirized with shows like Yes Minister, where this idea is that the civil service, because the bureaucracy is there through multiple prime ministers or presidents, they will outlast them all, and they're able, therefore, to deflect some of the policy initiatives of the executive . Then finally, crisis leadership in a wartime situation. There's talk of the wartime leader. Who's a good wartime leader? Maybe Winston Churchill, a very good wartime leader, maybe not as good in peace time, was voted out of office fairly quickly after World War II. It's also worth saying, by the way, that in a crisis like a war, sometimes the adversarial nature of politics, particularly in a system like, and we'll talk about this next lecture, what's called a first-past-the-post or adversarial system where it's winner take all, which is different from a consensual system where all the parties cooperate .
2.61: Northern Ireland is one, Lebanon is another, where, at least in theory, the parties are supposed to be cooperating . In a war, you will get sometimes a government of national unity where it's all the parties no longer competing with each other, but in some ways cooperating with each other. And that is more of a consensual form of government and less of a competitive form of government. Whereas in the first-past-the-post system, it's usually, if you think about House of Commons debates, it's one side and the other side jeering. It's a battle, not people more or less consensually agreeing to things and not wanting anyone to feel left out, which is more that consensual style. And that consensual style can emerge in a war where everybody's united completely. Then you'll get a more consensual style of government. But it's also worth saying that that consensual style of government is constitutionally mandated in constitutions in divided societies like Northern Ireland, where it's very important that no one feel left out.
2.62: In terms of where the power lies in the executive, we have a number of different dimensions of power that determine the influence of presidents and prime ministers. There's the formal constitutional role that is given to a president or a prime minister in the system, but that may not actually necessarily translate into the reality. There are also informal conventions that also interpret the formal constitutional dimensions, and those informal dimensions can also matter. In terms of informal dimensions of power, the personality of the leader is important. Are they charismatic or not? Can they win the media to their side and therefore win? If they got the media behind them and they're charismatic, they're more likely to be able to persuade legislators of their agenda .
2.63: Then there's the external context, which is broader pressures that bear on the executive branch outside. So it might be international alliances. Perhaps the US is pressuring Britain to join a war in Iraq or whatever. So you can have these external forces that also affect the power of a particular leader. Now, in terms of the relationship between the executive and the legislature, it's often the case. I mentioned that presidents can have more power than prime ministers over the policy agenda, but not always. Because it's partly about, at what point can prime ministers be removed by a vote of non-confidence, or at what point can presidents be impeached? We've mentioned that, on that dimension, presidents have more power because it's harder to impeach a president than to remove a prime minister.
2.64: The role of the courts, again, that's the defender of individual liberties, and it's also the interpreter of legislation. Those courts have more influence in the American case than in France or Britain. As I mentioned in the British case, Parliament is sovereign and has ultimate decision-making power over the courts in a way that's not true in the American presidential system . Just looking then at the performance of these two liberal democratic political designs, we have the parliamentary system and the presidential system. The benefit of the American presidential system is a very clearly specified separation of powers between the executive, the legislature, and the judiciary. That enacts formal checks and balances on , let's say, the power of the president.
2.65: This debate came up with President Trump. To what extent can Trump just do what he likes, or is he actually very much limited in what he can do because of the power of the legislature and the judiciary? Stability. You have that fixed four-year term, let's say, where you're not going to get a succession of leaders the way you have, let's say, in Britain in the last few years, which can create a certain amount of instability. So stability is a benefit of the US system. Because the President has a certain amount of independence to, let's say, make war or issue executive orders, there is a certain degree to which the President is independent of the legislature in the American system, which is not true in the British system.
2.66: The Prime Minister cannot just pursue a policy direction without buy-in from his or her party in the House of Commons. The Prime Minister is constrained. They have to win backing from the legislature, or at least the majority or the largest party in the legislature. They can't just more or less go it alone in the way that the US President can. Having said that, of course, as I mentioned, when it comes to appropriations of monies from the budget, the President is still dependent on Congress. So it doesn't have total power, but at least in a short-term window, they do have a certain degree of freedom.
2.67: Then finally, in the US system, there is a certain amount of power that derives from locality. As a member of Congress , you are elected—you're up for election every two years. You're up for election every two years. You're campaigning almost all the time. You have to please your constituents because they're the people you're ultimately beholden to, because they can remove you from office at any time. You have to be very tuned into your local constituents as a member of the House. Senate, OK, that's the state level. You don't have the same district-level representation as a member of the House. And you're only elected—the Senate only changes over every six years. So you're only up for election every six rather than every two years. It's perhaps not the same relationship.
2.68: But still, if we think about the House of Representatives, that power of the local is very important. So you would think, therefore, that this system is going to be more responsive to local concerns than a parliamentary system, where, yes, you are an MP for a particular constituency . Yes, they can remove you, but you're not up for election every two years, for example. Perhaps the electoral cycle is on a longer basis. What are the drawbacks of the American presidential system? Well, on the one hand, the dark side of stability is rigidity. If you have a president who is deeply unpopular, you can't remove them. If you have a prime minister who's deeply unpopular, you can remove them. That rigidity is arguably a downside.
2.69: You have this potential for gridlock. You would rarely get a situation in the House of Commons where the prime minister wants to pursue a particular policy, and his or her party blocks the prime minister's agenda. Because if that were the case, the Prime Minister, as I mentioned, has the power to appoint people to cabinet, better or worse jobs . The Prime Minister can really drive the legislative agenda, and so you don't tend to get this gridlock. Now, you will, of course, get backbench rebellions, and we've seen this. We're seeing this now in the British system, where you can have factions within the Conservative Party, for example, which are not happy with particular legislative directions and might stage a revolt and might vote with the opposition. There is a certain potential for the legislature blocking the Prime Minister's agenda, but generally, the Prime Minister's agenda gets passed, and votes go down on party lines, usually, without too much rebellion or people crossing to vote with the other party.
2.70: Whereas, at least in theory, in the US system, although this was more true in the '80s and '90s for reasons that we'll talk about later, you could have this potential for gridlock, where people have voted for the Republicans as President and the Democrats in the House, and therefore, it's very difficult to do anything. One of the arguments for why the Supreme Court has become more important in the US is because, with this gridlock, it's very difficult to pass legislation in the American system. And because of that, the courts are having to make more decisions, because the legislature is not able to be decisive. Whereas in the British system, that's not a problem. The legislature can, very much , the Prime Minister can get his or her agenda passed pretty well untrammeled by resistance from the legislature. So that's gridlock.
2.71: We've then got concentration of power in the US system. I mean, that's a debatable one . Yes, the President has a certain amount of short-term executive power, but as we've seen, there's a lot of checks, and it's not clear the President actually has that much power, particularly over the long term . Then finally, one of the issues, particularly in the US case, is this indirect election argument, which is that, when you vote, say, in a presidential election, you vote for the President, you're actually technically voting for members of something called the Electoral College within a state. That's based on winner-take-all. So whichever party in Montana, if there are— it can be 51, 49. And so all the delegates go. If the Republicans are at 51, the Democrats at 49, Republicans take all of the representatives for Montana.
2.72: Because of that winner-take-all at every state level, it can be the case, depending on the distribution of votes, if you're a party—What you ultimately want is your votes to be nicely spread so that you can win every contest by just a little bit, and then in certain states, OK, fine, you'll take a big loss. But if you can actually just beat the other party by a few points in the other areas more broadly across the country, you can have a more efficient distribution of the vote. What that then might mean is, as in the US in 2016, the majority of the vote went to the Democrats, but the majority of the Electoral College delegates went to the Republicans, and so the Republican President was elected.
2.73: Now, usually the proportion of the vote in terms of raw popular vote approximates, roughly, to who gets into power. But in a very finely balanced system where the parties are very similar in strength like the US, the result can sometimes go to the party that actually has a lower share of the popular vote. Now, it's worth saying that can also happen in a parliamentary system. In Canada, for example, the Liberal party of Justin Trudeau has a vastly larger parliamentary representation, or a considerably larger representation, than its proportion of the popular vote. So it has a more efficient distribution of vote than the Conservative Party. So this can also happen in a parliamentary system as well.
2.74: So then what are the benefits of the British parliamentary system? And I mentioned that the Prime Minister can really enact their agenda without much resistance from the legislature, partly because they got a majority or a plurality of votes, and therefore, that's how they came into power . And so there's a more efficient lawmaking process. The Prime Minister can really drive the policy agenda. Flexibility. This is the downside of —the British system is more flexible, but for that reason, a bit more unstable. So we can remove , if the popular mood turns against a prime minister, they can be removed, but then that can create instability and perhaps a lack of consistent policy direction over time.
2.75: You have also a benefit in terms of the collective responsibility. So the cabinet , it's all made up of MPs. It's responsible to Parliament in a way, and that ensures greater accountability of the Prime Minister to the House of Commons, the legislature. The last point to note is that there have been some attempts to study, globally, whether presidential systems or parliamentary systems have better results. And there is some evidence, it's not conclusive, to suggest that parliamentary systems have been less conflict-ridden than presidential systems . So the jury is not fully out on this, but one of the arguments is that parliamentary systems may be a better fit, certainly too much of the developing world, for example, or places where there's a different mix of different interests, and particularly where you have ethnic voting and ethnic parties, which we'll talk about more later in the next lecture.
2.76: In terms of drawbacks of parliamentary systems, one of the drawbacks is, again, the flip side of the fact that it's very efficient and effective in delivering the policy agenda that it was elected on. The flip side of that is you might get a so-called elective dictatorship. So there's no one to check the party in office and the prime minister that is running that party. And so if people get really dissatisfied with the direction that a prime minister is taking, you can't remove them from office and you can't change the policy direction. Whereas maybe in a presidential system where the legislature has independence, they can check a president and their agenda. In the British system, there's no real ability, in the short-term anyway, to change direction.
2.77: There's this elective dictatorship problem in the British system. There's an instability problem, which is, again , you can have a succession of leaders. I mentioned Johnson, Truss, Sunak, maybe another. That instability. Then there tends to be this party dominance where there's very little ability necessarily for individual legislators to vote against their party because the party more or less whips the MPs to vote for the party's legislation. Whereas maybe in, at least it used to be the case in the American system, there was much more crossing of the aisle, where people would vote the interests of their local constituents or vote for their conscience, rather than for the party line. Whereas maybe in the British system, there's more pressure to take the party line, because if you don't vote the party line, you'll be seen as disloyal, be much less likely to be selected for nice positions in the cabinet that might be a stepping stone to being Prime Minister. So the party of government tends to be very dominant with less room for other countervailing interests to be expressed.
2.78: We can also look at the French semi-presidential system just briefly, and does it combine the best or the worst of the US and British systems? And one of the benefits is you have a balance of power between the legislature and the executive between the President and the legislature as led by a Prime Minister. So the Prime Minister has some power and the president has some power, and they can check each other to some degree. That's arguably a benefit. You can see that, in a lot of these assessments , there's a tension between the efficiency and effectiveness of a system in delivering a legislative agenda and checks against authority and defenses against executive power. And that's to some degree a trade-off. Are you more worried about the executive getting out of control and becoming authoritarian, or are you more worried about the system bogging down because of too many checks and balances and not getting anything done? That is to some degree a tension that one has to manage. You can't have it both ways.
2.79: So in the French system, which seems to be very focused on checks and balances, President, Prime Minister , etc., clearly the benefit is that that can guard against authoritarianism , but the negative of that would tend to be that it's less efficient in getting things done. Also in the French system, because of the complexity of the elected legislature with its Prime Minister, this relationship between the two, that you can have these power struggles, especially where the legislature is of a different party from the President, and that can make it very difficult to know who has got responsibility in a particular area.
2.80: This gets back to what I just mentioned, which is this tension between checks and balances , guarding against an untrammeled executive power versus efficiency in delivering a legislative agenda, that there's a tension between those two in the design of any system . Maybe the British system is more effective for delivering a legislative agenda, but in a way doesn't provide as many checks on the power of a so-called elective dictatorship. So if a prime minister is really running the country into the ground, now you could say, well, then the party can remove the prime minister, and that's true . But if the party is behind the prime minister, actually, then there's not much that can stop that prime minister from doing a lot of damage. Whereas in these more mixed systems, there's much more of a check from the legislature onto the president.
2.81: So, just to conclude, we've done a grand tour of comparative political institutions, largely focusing on comparing the presidential and the parliamentary system , and focusing especially on the American presidential system and the British parliamentary system. We looked a little bit, perhaps, at the mixed French system. We looked at where power lay in each system in terms of the three main branches of government— the executive, the legislature, and the judiciary. We examined the different functions of the executive's legislatures and the courts in each system, the differences, the power of the prime minister versus the power of the president, which system is better for delivering a legislative agenda, and which system is better for checks and balances on authoritarianism.
2.82: And all of these things are important because it may be that we would say, OK, well, the power —there's not much of a risk of a prime minister or a president becoming a military dictator and taking absolute power. We don't worry about that too much in Britain. I know these debates have occurred in the US more, but still, maybe that's not the main consideration. Maybe what people are more worried about is the fact that these legislatures can't get things done in terms of policy.
2.83: But in many, particularly developing countries, the worry is more about a lapse into authoritarianism. Maybe people would say, well, I'm willing to sacrifice some policy effectiveness to get more checks and balances against the potential of authoritarianism. And so, maybe the decision as to which system to adopt in, it depends partly on how mature the democracy is. How long has a country been a democracy? What is the likelihood of it lapsing into some kind of an authoritarian system. That might concentrate minds in a different direction. Lecture 3: Political Parties At a glance — Political parties.
3.1: The next topic that I'm going to be addressing is electoral systems and parties. This is another absolute necessity when we're talking about introduction to politics . It's one of those classic topics alongside comparing presidential and parliamentary systems. We're going to be now looking at different electoral and party systems, which is not the same thing as comparing political institutions and presidential and parliamentary systems. And so the US is a presidential system, the UK is a parliamentary system. They are both what's called first-past-the-post , majoritarian electoral democracies. Even though one is a presidential and one is a parliamentary, they have the same type of electoral system, which is called first-past-the-post , which is a version of majoritarian electoral systems.
3.2: And what that basically means is, the largest party wins. It doesn't even have to represent the majority of voters. It just has to represent the plurality. It has to be the largest party. It could have 35% of the vote. It doesn't have to have 51% of the vote. Against that, we have more consensual and proportional types of electoral system, of which the most well-known one is proportional representation. The emphasis then in the first-past-the-post system is not on representing everybody because only the winning party forms the government, forms the cabinet, et cetera.
3.3: The consensual system, though, is more about representing everybody. And just crudely speaking, in proportional representation, if you win 20% of the vote, 10% of the vote , if you win 10% of the vote, you get 10% of the seats. Whereas in a first-past-the- post system, you can be the UK Independence Party winning 13% of the votes, and you can have no representation. Or maybe they had one seat, sorry, one seat. But basically, you can win a significant chunk of the vote and have no representation in the House of Commons. So it isn't very representative to have a first-past-the-post system.
3.4: And it's also the case, by the way, that the first-past-the-post system tends to discriminate against third parties or small parties because they're not viable. They have no chance of winning, and therefore, you tend to move towards either two large parties, occasionally two large parties , and reasonable-sized third parties. But generally, it militates against having lots of parties. Whereas the proportional representation system, you may get 20 parties, each with, maybe not 20, because there's usually a threshold, but you may get a large number of parties.
3.5: You could say that's better because most people feel represented. I'm a Green, and there's my Green party representatives in proportion to the Green vote, or I'm a UKIP voter , and there's my 13% of the seats in the legislature. Whereas if I'm a UKIP voter and I've got one seat, then maybe you'd say, "Well, I'm not being represented." So this is the difference between the majoritarian and the more representational and consensual electoral systems .
3.6: Now, at the very extreme, a PR, a proportional representation, system , can also be part of a power-sharing political system in which not only are parties represented in the legislature in proportion to the popular vote, but they are also represented in cabinet, at the cabinet table, in proportion to their vote , or at least in having some representation in the executive. That's typically in deeply divided societies, Lebanon, Northern Ireland, where group identity matters a lot to people, and therefore, you can't exclude groups.
3.7: It's viewed that if you exclude groups from the governing coalition, you might be risking civil war or violence. That's a different theory of government, based on a consensus between parties before moving forward, everyone feeling represented before moving forward, because there's a risk of, if people are outside the tent, then they might be incentivized to engage in insurrection or civil war, separatism and so on.
3.8: It's very much worth, when we're thinking about electoral systems, thinking about the idea of representation. This is a picture of two maps of the US, one that is just red and blue, blue for the Democrats, red for the Republicans. In 2016, most of the map is red, and Republicans win election. Now, you can look at that. It's very stark. You're either blue or you're red. But of course, in reality, the vote in most of these constituencies is oscillating in a band between 55, 45, and 45, 55. And you have a lot of these purple, a lot of these purple districts. And the fact that they have to—whichever party got slightly more wins. So it's winner-take-all. And so, you could say this is very binary , and it doesn't really represent the nuances of opinion in the country .
3.9: So one of the questions is whether a first-past-the-post system really does a good job of representing the nuances amongst voters, or does it totalize and homogenize the vote into this binary , which can leave people feeling they haven't been represented, especially if you are on the losing end in successive elections? I'm drawing some of this from Andrew Heywood's book on politics, chapters 10 and 11, where we talk about the relationship between electoral systems and politics and party systems, because there is a relationship, as I mentioned, where in a first-past-the-post electoral system , your party system tends to involve large parties.
3.10: I want to talk about elections first, in part one, and then in part two, I'm going to talk a bit about parties and party systems. One of the questions is, what is the function of an election? One of the key definitions of democracy is that power must be transferred, and also that different groups are free to organize as parties and not thrown in jail if they oppose the government. Elections are central to the meaning of democracy. However, there are many questions around elections and how to design electoral systems . So which posts are appointed versus elected? Who's entitled to vote within the population? What's the voting age? Who's not allowed to vote? Are prisoners allowed to vote, et cetera? Sometimes they are, sometimes they aren't. And to what extent is there an adversarial versus a consensual system?
3.11: So first-past-the-post is very adversarial. You just have to look at the House of Commons to see the competition that the two parties are competing. Now, a virtue of that is, at least in theory , people will have a clear choice and they can see the differences between parties. Whereas in a more consensual, proportional representation type of system, where everyone's supposedly cooperating , you could argue there's deals that are stitched up in backrooms and maybe people don't really see what they're voting for and what the differences between the parties are. So there are pluses and minuses both to the first-past-the-post system and to the proportional representation system.
3.12: Just sticking with elections for the minute. Elections have a number of functions. As I mentioned, they're central to the legitimacy of democracy because the fact that people are willingly leaving office and conceding is very important to the democratic norm that says that you don't have absolute power, you can't be president for life, you've got to give up the reins of power when you lose an election. One of the reasons there's been so much controversy over some of Donald Trump's statements is the sense that this is infringing on this norm of the peaceable transfer, willingness to transfer power and concede when you lose an election.
3.13: What are the functions of elections? Well, one is the recruitment of politicians, training people for office, bringing them into parties, bringing segments of the electorate into politics. That's one function of elections, clearly providing representation . And that's an important distinction is the function of representing the people, where you might say, well, obviously, you have to have PR because proportional representation is a better mirror of the voters and their preferences, where the percentage of the vote translates directly into percentage of seats. That's better for representation than first- past-the-post, where percentage of vote may not translate, as I mentioned with UKIP, 13% of the vote, but less than 1% of the seats. So it's not very good in terms of representation.
3.14: But that is at least one function of elections, is to make people feel like they're being represented. There's also the election process in which voters are drawn into politics. If all they care about is their hobbies and their family, well, at least once every four or five years, or perhaps more frequently in countries where you have more frequent elections, they are drawn into politics, have to think about politics. That's maybe another function of elections is participating in the political process. That also is important for building up the legitimacy of the political system and the democracy, that elections help people feel like, OK, the system is responding to our preferences, and therefore it's legitimate, and so we're not going to conduct an insurrection and try and overthrow the system. We're not going to conduct a coup.
3.15: And that's very important, the legitimacy of a democracy. And of course, this is very much a live issue in debates over democratization in the world. What percentage of the world's countries are democratic? There was a big increase in the period from the 1960s to the 1980s. We saw a big increase in the number of democracies, at least in terms of holding elections and having at least one transfer of power. There was this what was called the third wave of democratization in the period between the '60s and the '80s, maybe into the '90s. But there's been a debate over to what extent are some of these democracies backsliding into autocracies and no longer being democracies, leaving aside whether they're liberal or illiberal democracies.
3.16: To what extent is there then a backsliding? And to what extent is that because the legitimacy of the political class and of the democracy and the democratic institutions has weakened within the population? Now, that may not be the reason why there's backsliding. There are other reasons. There could be insurrectionary activity and various other reasons. But perhaps one reason could be that the legitimacy, the perceived legitimacy, of the government is low or falls in the eyes of the voters , and that can lead to backsliding. So we need to have legitimate government.
3.17: In terms of electoral systems, I mentioned the majoritarian and the more consensual and representative systems. But even within that, we can have different mixes of representation and majoritarianism within different electoral systems. What I want to do next is just walk through a number of the alternative electoral systems in slightly more detail. You can see how the mix of representativeness versus majoritarianism. Again, the majoritarianism is linked to effectiveness, because if you've got to manage a coalition of four, five, six parties towards some policy end, that's trickier. You clearly have to get buy-in from all of the different elements in your coalition.
3.18: Just to take a UK example, which is not a proportional representation system, but there was a coalition between the Conservatives and the Liberal Democrats, David Cameron and Nick Clegg leading those parties. They had to agree on legislation, and it's trickier . It's more consensual in that there's more sharing of power between different parts of the electorate, but maybe it's less efficient.
