Maybe, again, as with the presidential and parliamentary system, where the parliamentary system allows for, to some degree, the Prime Minister to drive a particular legislative agenda without obstruction, and so is more efficient in some ways. So, too, the majoritarian electoral system is in some ways more efficient as well for getting things done. So it's that same trade-off between the getting things done and the representing.
3.19: So there are a number of different subtypes within these electoral systems. So voters can be asked to choose, first of all, between parties. So pick a party. Who do you want to vote for? The Conservatives or Labor or Republicans or Christian Democrats and Social Democrats. You choose a party, or sometimes you just choose between candidates, individuals, Donald Trump, Joe Biden, whatever. Voters can also sometimes select just one candidate. So in the first-past-the-post system, you just choose one candidate. In some of these other systems, you have a rank ordering of candidates, and that rank ordering then informs who ultimately becomes the winner.
3.20: The electorate may or may not be grouped into constituencies, and that can be an issue because if you have, say, a proportional representation system where it's whatever the percent vote for the Greens is what they get in the legislature, we don't really care if there's big variation from constituency to constituency. It's just going to be purely based on national-level proportion of the vote. But that means that you don't have a local MP, a local member of Congress that you can go to with your problems. It's not as locally representative. So that is another trade-off then . Do you have constituencies or do you just have a national level list? That's an important difference.
3.21: And some constituencies can have multiple members in some of these PR systems. So it's actually the case that, in the proportional representation system, you can get constituencies , and they can have different numbers of members depending on their population level, but that each of those constituencies mirrors the national picture in a way. So you don't have a conservative area and a liberal area. You just have each area as a mirror of the national, but you do have some kinds of constituencies. And in terms of forming a government, the level required is sometimes, as I mentioned, just having the largest number of votes of any party. But in other cases, you have to have a majority of 50.1 or more to form a government.
3.22: That's, of course, going to mean the more the requirement is that you have to have 50% plus, the more you're going to actually have to move out beyond your party to bring in members of other parties to form a coalition that has enough to get over the threshold. So that forces more of a consensual form of governing where you have coalitions of parties rather than just Tories win on 30 some odd percent and they form the government. They don't have to really care about the Liberal Democrats or Labour or any of the other parties.
3.23: Now, of course, they have to care a certain degree. If they hope to beat Labour, they, to some degree, have to appeal to voters who are thinking of whether to go to Labour or the Conservatives. To some degree, they have to adapt to the preferences of a larger share of the electorate. It's not that they can be super narrow and ignore the preferences of a larger share of the electorate, but they only need a certain proportion. If you have a society like Britain or the US, where the distribution of votes, let's say for the Republicans or the Conservatives in this country, is more even, with the left-wing parties piling up votes in the cities, most of those votes are wasted in terms of the outcome. Where you have a party that has a very efficient distribution of the votes, it can get in on a relatively low percentage and still win overall. Then you might say there's a representation problem.
3.24: There's a group called the Electoral Reform Society, which has some useful resources in Britain , which I've drawn on here to talk about a number of different options for electoral systems. Within the more majoritarian camp and within the more representational consensual camp, there are some sub-varieties here, which I'll just talk through. There's a few dimensions here to this. When designing one's electoral system, you have to think about how well does it represent the population? To what extent does it offer you a local politician who can hear local concerns , minister to local concerns, and reflect the needs of constituents? Which is an important element of designing a system, is that it's locally responsive.
3.25: Then you also have this question of, to what extent does it leadto more choice for voters that reflects a wider degree of the interests and motivations of voters? If you have just two parties, that doesn't give the voters much choice. You just have a choice between A and B, and maybe neither of them is really what you're really looking for. Whereas if you had a choice of 10 parties, then you're more likely to find a flavor that you like. This is this idea of electoral systems that produce party systems which produce more choice for voters. A menu with more options compared to a menu with two options is arguably better.
3.26: We'll just assess these electoral systems. The first is the first-past-the-post system, otherwise known as single-member plurality. Plurality refers to something less than a majority. You just have to have more votes than the other parties. In this system, you have, say, one MP per constituency or one representative of Congress in a congressional district. You divide the country up into these constituencies. Usually, they are apportioned to be of equal size. Now, sometimes there's population growth more in certain areas than others. In the US case, for example, for a long time, the rural constituencies actually had more representation than their population.
3.27: But there is this process of redistricting where the districts, the lines between the districts, are sometimes redrawn, or there are new districts created in a way to reflect the shifts in the population. Maybe you need to create more city districts if the cities are growing. That is a way in which the system should be responding. Now, it is true that historically, sometimes there's foot-dragging on that, depending on which party is more advantaged. In the US case, for example, the Republican Party was disadvantaged by the growth of urban constituencies which tended to vote Democrats. So there was a delay in the 1920s and '30s. Or sorry, in the '60s, there was a delay in terms of redistricting, but that eventually occurred.
3.28: So the winning candidate then only needs to achieve a plurality. That's the first-past- the-post. It's very much an adversarial system that's created winner-take-all. The cabinet is only Tories . There's no Labour members of cabinet, for example. So it's very much the adversarial winner-take-all majoritarian system. You then have another system which is also majoritarian in a way, which is that you have a second ballot, like in France, where there's the first round, a bunch of candidates run , and they split the vote up. Nobody has over 50%. In a second ballot system, there's only one run-off. So all but the two parties go into that second round, and then whoever wins on that second round becomes the president. So that is a second ballot system.
3.29: Notice that that's doing a couple of things compared to thefirst-past-the-post system where you win 35%, but you've got an efficiently distributed vote and you can become Prime Minister, for example, or President. Although it's unlikely you'd be President on 35%, but just sticking with me for a minute here, on the second ballot system, it forces people who voted for somebody else to decide, "OK, who do I think is my second preference, the least worst ? Maybe I preferred the Socialists in my—and I voted for the Socialists in the first round. Second round between Le Pen and Macron, OK, maybe the lesser of two evils is Macron. I'll vote for Macron." And so it builds in a wider range of choices into the final winner.
3.30: So you could say it's more representative because at least somebody feels like, "OK, I contributed in the second round to who got elected." So you're representing at least 50% of the population, whereas under the first-past-the-post, you may only be representing 30 something percent of the population. OK, so in first-past-the-post, then, you just cross out one party on your ballot, and it just goes straight to—and this is at the constituency level. You have to win more constituencies. So it's not just who has the most popular votes. We saw in the US case that Hillary Clinton had more of the vote than Donald Trump in 2016. But taking account of how that vote is spread over constituencies, the Republicans win more constituencies and constituencies within states , so they win more states, so they win the election.
3.31: And that's first-past-the-post system. In terms of its rating, according to the Electoral Reform Society, their argument is that it does a good job in terms of local representation. You have an MP. The country is broken up into many different constituencies, so you have somebody to go to if you have a problem. Reasonable local representation, but in terms of voter choice and in terms of representation, not very good because you may only get two parties, two reasonable parties, to choose from. In terms of the share of the population that sees themselves reflected in government, it may actually be a minority of the country.
3.32: In terms of proportional representation, now moving more to —so we talked about first-past-the-post and a two-round ballot system. Those are both, to some degree, majoritarian. And if we move to the party list system, this is much more about representativeness mirroring the population. And what that is, is the percentage of the vote translates into percentage of seats. So it does a very good job on proportionality, representing the population in proportion to the vote. In terms of voter choice, it also does a reasonably good job because you get a proliferation of parties, and you can see that in the continental European proportional representation systems where you have lots of different parties. And so, many people in the electorate can say, "Aha, I'm being represented here in government."
3.33: Now, there are different subtypes. One of the conditions is typically a threshold. You can't get seats in the legislature until you are over 5%, let's say, in Germany. These very small fringe parties are excluded from representation. It's not fully proportional, not fully representative, because the fringe parties are excluded. Is it good to exclude the fringe parties? That's a debate. If these fringe parties are extremist, and you include them, do you not sully your electoral system? That's one argument, that you can't have them involved in coalitions because they're beyond the pale. The other argument is that if you exclude these people, they're more likely to make trouble and they're more likely to be anti-system in orientation.
3.34: And that's also an issue for peace agreements and civil wars, where if you try to exclude the most radical faction—if we take Iraq and you're going to exclude the extreme Shia or the extreme Sunni in the coalition, let's say, maybe their incentive is then to try and torpedo the system and try and engage in insurrectionary activity. The argument can be made both ways.
3.35: So just sticking with the party list system, which is a version of proportional representation, which is that you have a list of parties and you simply choose which one represents you. You're putting a mark on just one of the parties or candidates. That translates directly into the legislature. So proportion of votes equals proportion of seats . We have a picture here of the Israeli Knesset and the balance of power between the different political parties. So that's the party list system. Very good in terms of representing people. You have a wide range of parties to choose from. You see yourself represented. Now , how that translates locally, as I mentioned, it may be you've just got one national list, so you don't have local representation. There are no constituencies. You don't have conservative and left-wing constituencies. You just have the national.
3.36: Or you can sometimes get, as in Bulgaria, and there's a map here, where you take the proportional breakdown in the national level and you have a fractal or microcosm of that reflected in these constituencies. You don't have a single member who's conservative representing a conservative area. You have representatives of all the parties in proportion to their vote represented in each of these constituencies. The argument there is it at least gives people some local representation. But of course, you've got multiple members there locally. It's not one individual who's responsible for their constituency.
3.37: And so the local responsiveness is not as good in this PR system. So its rating is, if we were to compare the first-past-the-post and the PR system, the PR system does worse on local representativeness and responsiveness than thefirst-past-the-post system, where you have your local MP you can go to. And here you've just got a bunch of MPs, none of which have direct responsibility for their constituency.
3.38: We also have a number of systems that are in between the extremefirst-past-the-post and the party list PR, fully representative party list PR, in proportion to the population or first-past-the-post system, the two alternatives. You have the alternative vote, the AV. Actually, in this country, some of you may or may not remember , there was a referendum on whether to adopt this system for the country . There may indeed, by the way, looking ahead, especially if the Liberal Democrats go into government in coalition with Labour. If that's who forms the next government in this country, then the Liberal Democrats are going to be pushing for one of these alternative systems, because if you are a third party, if you're not one of the major parties, you are going to do better, obviously, under a proportional representation system or some system that allows minor parties to have more legislative representation.
3.39: One of the questions in this country, anyway, is to what extent the Liberal Democrats would make it a condition of joining with Labour in a coalition government . But one of their conditions would be to change the electoral system in a way that would benefit the small parties like the Liberal Democrats more in the future. With the AV system, which there was a referendum on, is a hybrid. We have, on the one hand, single member, a constituency, so good local responsiveness. There is a ranked system of voting, so you don't just pick one party . You actually have a ranking of all the parties, one to five, let's say, of the parties. You're ranking the different parties under the AV system. So one for your first preference, second for your second, and so on.
3.40: And winning candidates must gain 50%. So there's a requirement to meet a 50% threshold in order to form the government. So if no one party reaches 50%, then you have to—what you do is you eliminate from the bottom and transfer votes until you get up to 50, until one candidate has a majority. There's a slight variation of the system under the single transferable vote, where all candidates drop out except the top two. What this is, is it's a more majoritarian system than the list proportional representation. There are still people who are not represented under the AV. All you need is 50% plus to get into government. So that still means you can have almost 50% of the electorate not represented in the legislature.
3.41: Whereas under the PR list system, everybody, pretty much, except for the fringe parties that don't meet the threshold , everybody's represented in the legislature. And so this system is better thanfirst-past-the-post , where you could be in, as I say, on 35%. Here you've got to be at least 50%, but it doesn't necessarily mean you have to have much over 50. So it's not as representative as the PR list system. So it's a bit more perhaps likefirst-past-the-post . There's still a majoritarian element rather than a consensual represent-everybody philosophy behind the system.
3.42: Single transferable vote is operating on a similar principle, where you rank the parties, and then if the party that you voted for, number one, doesn't come through, your second preference votes get transferred into a particular party, and eventually, whoever reaches 50 % forms the government. One place we see that is Northern Ireland, where it's a proportional representation. You vote. The electoral system is designed to translate votes into seats, but there's also this second preference, third, fourth preference, votes which get transferred in as well . There is, it's PR with single transferable vote is the system in Northern Ireland .
3.43: Now, of course, in Northern Ireland, this is a society which is divided between Protestant and Catholic , where people tend to vote on their ethnic lines. So Protestants vote for unionist parties, whether the the DUP or the UUP, and the Catholics would tend to vote for Sinn Féin or SDLP, the Catholic parties. So one of the reasons why Northern Ireland has a proportional representation system is to try and make sure that what happened between 1922 and 1972, where Catholics had no representation in the assembly, that that situation, or they lose every time and they're outvoted every time, that that doesn't happen.
3.44: You can have what you want in a system, particularly in a divided society where there's a risk of civil war like Northern Ireland, part of the peace agreement is that you set up a political system that includes everybody, and therefore the government is more consensual and less adversarial than in mainland Britain. That was deliberate because they really worried about groups who felt they were outside of the system, engaging in insurrection and civil war-type activity.
3.45: The PR system is more appropriate to designing electoral systems in societies that are post-conflict or have strong ethnic and religious divisions. One of the arguments is that you can't have a first-past-the-post, winner-take-all system system in a deeply divided society. It's just going to lead to more conflict and greater risk of civil war. There are other options which blend features of both systems. I'm not going to go into too much detail on them, other than to say there are different options to try and balance out representativeness with effectiveness as well, and local representation. You have also mixed electoral systems. I mentioned the PR, proportional representation, first-past- the-post. Those are the two key ones to bear in mind, and they have different advantages, different pluses and minuses.
3.46: You also have mixed systems that blend elements of PR and elements offirst-past-the- post . In Germany, for example, you have a proportion of seats filled through the first- past-the-post system, and then the remaining is filled through the party list proportional representation system. You can also blend elements of the two electoral systems as well. I guess this gets us towards a question of, what is going on with elections in terms of voters' heads, and what do elections mean? I just have two charts here which show the results of two 2019 elections in Britain. The first is based upon the European elections. We're going to have European Union elections occurring soon. European Union elections are on a proportional representation basis. That is , the percentage of the vote that you get is the percentage of seats that you get in the European Parliament. So that's the PR system, whereas in Westminster, the national elections are based on first-past-the-post.
3.47: Now, the other difference is that the European elections, many people think they don't matter very much because Europe doesn't have much power. It spends only 1% of the total GDP of the European Union . So you could argue it's not that meaningful. People don't see it having a big presence in their everyday life. So they can take a risk and vote more expressively. They can say, "Well, this is who I am. I'm going to vote for the Brexit Party, and I don't have to worry about if I vote for the Brexit Party, that'll help Labour get in instead of the Tories." That tactical voting consideration is not an issue. It's just pure, "I can express my own preference." Whereas in a Westminster national election scenario, you have to take account of, "Well, if I vote for this minor party, that might help the party I don't like get into office." That's called tactical voting.
3.48: Just comparing these two charts here, roughly around the same time, you can see in the European elections that the Brexit Party is coming out tops here. 29 seats, the Conservatives only 4, Labour 10. Two things are happening. First of all, in terms of vote share, people are voting expressively for minor parties much more in the European elections, like the Liberal Democrats or the Brexit Party. The major parties are getting a very small share of the vote, 14% for Labour , 9% for the Conservatives.
3.49: However, if we look at the Westminster elections, it's the exact opposite. The minor parties are getting very little, and the two main parties are getting almost all of the vote. We have two totally different results, the same country, roughly the same time. This raises the question, can we say that a particular election result is an accurate representation of a population and how it feels about the policies offered by the parties that are running in the election? You would draw a very different conclusion if you looked at these two sets, these two sets of electoral results.
3.50: I think that gets then to this question of the meaning of elections. What does it mean when you have a certain pattern of votes in an election? There are different theories about this. There are those who say, well, we can't necessarily look at a set of results and say that is really representing the way people feel about issues. It may not be. It may reflect a whole range of considerations, including tactical, including local confidence in your local MP, leaders, and so on. So this idea that the people have spoken is not necessarily the case with a certain set of election results . There isn't necessarily a general will here.
3.51: There's a whole range of factors that govern how people vote. And you could see that in the examples that we just looked at with different systems, you can get totally different results. And so you have to be very careful in interpreting results. You have to know which kind of electoral system exists in order to understand what the vote actually means at a deep level. What are voters expressing with their particular pattern of vote? Maybe no system can really perfectly translate the wishes of the people into power. Maybe there's no perfect system, but arguably , we can actually arrive at the least worst system.
3.52: I'm going to step out of the Western context a little bit to look at much of the developing world where many countries use a form of proportional representation. Why would countries opt for this proportional representation system? We've already suggested that a PR system where you have to form a coalition between a bunch of parties to get into power means you have to satisfy a whole range of different interests and parties, and you have to constantly broker between the leaders of these different parties. And that truly means that it's a more unwieldy, difficult process of legislating. I mean, yes, it is more representative. More people feel that they are represented in government. But on the other hand, decision-making is cumbersome because you have to deal with a bunch of different coalition partners. You're worried that they will threaten to leave your government.
3.53: And of course, if enough parties in your coalition leave and you drop below the threshold, then you're out of power . And so there's always that threat. And sometimes very small parties can be kingmakers. So sometimes in Israel, the ultra-Orthodox parties have been kingmakers, and they can switch between coalitions. Even a small share of the vote, they can say, "We're taking our 2, 3, 4, 5 percent, and we're taking it out of your coalition , making you fall, and giving it to this coalition, putting them above the threshold, making them go into government." So small parties can sometimes hold the balance of power and, therefore, achieve undue influence out of all proportion to their actual vote. So there are different risks in the PR system, but yet that is the system that seems to be adopted in many developing countries.
3.54: Now, one of the reasons is because many developing countries are ethnically divided or voting occurs on ethnic lines. On the chart here, we have Lebanon and showing geographically where the different ethnic and religious groups in the country live. We could take a case like Ethiopia as well, which has different ethno-regions as well. It's just very difficult to imagine forming a government in a society like Lebanon or Ethiopia, where you have a history of violent conflict between groups that are often divided on ethnic and religious lines, and imagine that you can do a Westminster-style first-past-the-post or an American style first-past-the-post system. You have to try and get more buy-in. You want to avoid people feeling they've been excluded from the system because that then gives them an incentive to undermine the system, perhaps through violence.
3.55: There's another map here showing the degree of ethnic diversity, the number of ethnic groups in a country, but also weighted by their proportion—something called ethnic fractionalization. What is the chance that two random individuals drawn from the country are of the same ethnic group? If you take an extremely fractionalized country like Tanzania, the chance that you would have two individuals from the same ethnic group is extremely low. If you take a country with very low fractionalization , very high homogeneity, like Japan, two random citizens, there's a very good chance they'll be of the same ethnic background. That has implications for how you design your electoral system.
3.56: In this map, what you can see is that a large part of the Global South, particularly sub- Saharan Africa, Southeast Asia, parts of West Asia, have high ethnic fractionalization . To some degree, that is associated with more civil conflict. In designing your electoral systems, you don't want to design an electoral system where certain ethnic groups are always out of power, and they never see themselves in power. This gets to this group rights point versus individual rights. Yes, we have to have one person, one vote, but also the recognition that the society is made up of groups that matter a lot to people, and that shapes politics a lot, means you have to make some accommodation to the idea of representing all of the groups, or most of the groups, within government at least some of the time.
3.57: You can't really do that in a first-past-the-post system. I used the example of Northern Ireland, where the Unionist Protestant parties won. They were in office every election for 50 years , and the Catholics were out of power. That can be associated with greater risk of civil war. It's also worth saying that, in terms of political philosophy or political theory, which is another branch of politics, a lot of the political philosophy was developed in places like Britain, France, to some degree the US, which were more ethnically homogenous. There was some diversity there, but by and large, you could almost imagine that you didn't have to take group into account very much in designing a political system.
3.58: Whereas in a highly ethnically diverse, fractionalized society like Nigeria or Kenya or Indonesia, it's not as easy to assume that you have this homogenous population . What you have is, yes, you've got a population, but they also have strong group attachments, particularly in the post-colonial countries that were created after decolonization. There are varying degrees of emphasis on so-called group rights or collective rights. So a proportional representation system, which allows a large share of the population to see itself reflected in the legislature, is very important in a society where those group rights are very important. So if people are voting for ethnic parties, they want to see that they get some representation in the legislature . And if they don't get that representation, election after election, you can have problems.
3.59: And so this question of how you design an electoral system in a divided society versus a society that is more homogenous, like the US or England. Now, the US, even though it did have different sects of Protestants, it didn't really have these deep ethnic divisions at quite the same level as we're seeing in some of the countries I just talked about. And so there is a tendency then, in these more ethnically divided societies, to move to a PR system rather than a first-past-the-post system . And that's recognizing the group rights principle being somewhat important. That is, it's not enough just to represent one person, one vote. We have to try and get to some representation of groups as well.
3.60: The legislature in a first-past-the-post system, as in Northern Ireland, is going to be a pretty good reflection of the share of the population that are members of the unionist and the nationalist community . Or similarly in Lebanon, you're going to get a reasonable representation of Shia, Sunni, Christian, etc. Whereas if it was winner-take- all, you wouldn't get that. So the group rights principle is part of democracy and crafting democracy in divided societies.
3.61: The other part of it, by the way, is the executive, the cabinet. The cabinet under a power-sharing system. And when I say power-sharing, I probably have to explain this. You have a principle called federalism, which is a way of recognizing group rights. So in the US case, you have the federal government in Washington, and then you have the states, which you can think of as groups. I mentioned the Senate, two senators per state is a group rights principle. Now, in a society like Lebanon or Northern Ireland, the group rights principle is that a group will have its share reflected in the legislature and in cabinet. The cabinet is not going to function the way it does in the US or British case, where it's all members of the same party. The cabinet will actually have a mix, which is reasonably representative of the parties that the people vote for. So all ethnic groups see themselves in that cabinet, which has power.
3.62: Something similar in Northern Ireland as well, where you tend to have a first minister from one community and the deputy from another community. And in Lebanon, where you have the prime minister from one group in the Constitution stipulated that the prime minister is from this group, the president is from that group. And so you have this built-in group rights principle in democracy. Now, some say that's a bad idea, and it entrenches groups, and it entrenches people thinking and voting as members of ethnic groups. That is a risk of this system. But if you go the other direction and you go for a majoritarian system, the risk is groups get frozen out of the system , and therefore, they're more likely to rebel.
3.63: You have to think about which is the greater risk in designing your system. Maybe the way to do it is to start out with a system that has high proportionality, like Northern Ireland or Lebanon , and then maybe evolve towards a slightly more majoritarian system with adopting, perhaps, the alternative vote, where you have to have a certain proportion of votes from all groups, but it's not perfectly proportional to all groups. That's kind of like an in-between version of an electoral system. So part one has been about electoral systems, PR versus first-past-the-post, and the conditions under which it's better to use one system or use another system. The strengths and weaknesses of the major forms of electoral system.
3.64: Part two, I'm going to talk about parties. Now, there's a relationship because there's a relationship between the electoral system and the party system. If you have a proportional representation electoral system, then you are more likely to have a multi- party party system with many different parties. If you have a first-past-the-post electoral system, you're more likely to have a single or two major parties dominating the system. So what is a party? What is a political party ? A party is a group of people organized for the purpose of winning government power. Now, a party is not the same as an interest group, and it is not the same as an ethnic group.
3.65: Now, it can be similar, in the sense that if people are voting completely on ethnic lines and all members of an ethnic group are voting for one ethnic party, then yes, the political party is a perfect reflection of the ethnic morphology of a country. It's more often the case, I would say, that you get, as in Northern Ireland, you get multiple parties within an ethnic block. You get the DUP and the UUP, two Protestant Unionist parties representing the Protestant community. There's still some competition, but it's within-bloc competition. Generally, however, and particularly as we move to societies like Britain or the US that are not divided in this way, in the same way as Lebanon, and particularly in a first-past-the-post system, the parties tend to be coalitions of different factions and interest groups. Uneasy coalitions, perhaps, and that's why you get actually divisions within parties.
3.66: If we take the Republican Party, or the Conservative Party here, there is a divide between the more free market, what are known as Liberal Conservatives, and the more populist National Conservatives. So that is a division within the parties because the parties are coalitions of different interests. Now, sometimes parties are also coalitions of different ethnic groups. The Democrats in the US for a long time were a coalition of southern white Protestants and northern white Catholics and Jews. That was the groups that made up the Republican party coalition. You can sometimes have parties that are bringing together a coalition of different ethnic groups, as well as a coalition of different ideological factions.
3.67: You have political parties, you have ethnic groups, but you also have other kinds of interest groups that are not based on ethnicity or religion. They may just be based on the miners, the unions, the teachers, the gun owners. You have these different interest groups. Sometimes those interest groups form lobby groups, and those lobby groups are trying to influence the government, especially in between elections, or even during elections, force all of the party, force the party to sign up to my 10 pledges. The National Rifle Association will rate all the candidates by how good they are, their voting record on gun rights, and then send that to the constituents. That's the activity of one interest group. They're trying to influence the direction of policy, typically within one party.
3.68: Sometimes you have lobby groups like business interests, which might try and lobby both parties and shape the direction of policy, no matter who's in power. Unions would have less power over the Conservatives, the business interests less power over the left- wing parties like Labour. Now, with a certain degree of convergence, at least on economic policy, businesses are going to be lobbying both parties, and both parties are probably going to be listening as well . Parties, at least in first-past-the-post systems, tend to be coalitions of different factional interests, and perhaps, sometimes different ethnic groups and interest groups.
3.69: What are the functions of parties in a liberal democracy? If you go back to the federalist papers in the US, initially, they wanted to avoid parties forming altogether. They were very much against the formation of parties, but others have said this is very integral to the functioning and smooth working of a liberal democratic system. Parties are needed to provide political elites, policy leadership, to offer alternative policy directions to the electorate. They tend to aggregate interests into larger groups, so aggregating multiple different factions into one group that has to get along. People can't get everything they want. They have to accept that they have to make deals with other factions within the party to prioritize certain policies.
3.70: It may be that, in Canada, the Conservative Party, there may be people who will want to see access to abortion restricted, but they will accept that that's not something that's feasible in the Canadian system. That policy preference is not something they're going to be able to insist on, but they may still feel more comfortable with the Conservatives rather than the Liberal party. Parties will amalgamate different interest groups and prioritize which policies they're going to focus on in their administration . They also help to organize government as well.
3.71: We have different party systems then arising. I mentioned there was this link to electoral systems, where you have a proportional representation electoral system. You're more likely to get a larger menu of parties because even small parties can get representation. It makes sense for you to vote for those small parties. Then in the next stage, perhaps the party that has the largest votes can try to form a coalition by putting together and negotiating with a bunch of smaller parties. So this process of negotiation and consensus amongst various stripes of opinion.
3.72: Again, I wanted to emphasize that, even in a first-past-the-post system, the governing party has to manage differences between factions, and there's negotiation between factions. So it's not true that the first-past-the-post system is resulting in no consensus. There has to be some negotiation between factions, but it's not as much as in a PR system where you really have to negotiate between parties that form over 50% typically of the electorate. So you have to be broader and you really have to scale back the purity of your demands. You have to actually negotiate and scale those back. And so there's more of an emphasis on compromise.
3.73: You can, of course, also get an attempt by a series of less large parties to exclude other parties. And this typically happens with the populist right, which there's an attempt in certain European countries to prevent the populist right from getting into government. That gets harder and harder to do when the populist right gets a larger and larger share of votes . Here we've got the 2023 Dutch election where Geert Wilders' PVV came out tops by far with 37 seats, compared to the next share is the PVDA with 25 and the VVD with 24. But there's an attempt by some of the other parties to keep them out of power.
3.74: But that will mean you might get an economically left party representing unions with an economically right party representing business. Those parties trying to form a government means that it's going to be very fractious to do anything in terms of policy, when you have such a range of views on the economy within one coalition. Yes, they are both wanting to keep the populists right out, but they don't agree on that much in policy terms. And so, again, we can get the rise of populism and the attempt to exclude them can lead to a more difficult governing .
3.75: Now, you compare the results from the PR electoral system in the Netherlands on this left chart, where you've got many different parties, and then the American results where it's two main parties, two parties heavily , heavily dominating the vote, a very different party system. So contrasting party systems, we have a multi-party system with a two-party system in the US case . And there is a whole debate about which is better, which is worse. It's worth saying also, and I'll come to this in a minute, there are certain tendencies, socially, politically, that will tend to lead party systems to splinter more or aggregate more. We may be in a time, we may be in a period in which there's more fragmentation and splintering . That's one of the questions we want to ask, is what are the forces that tend to lead party systems to move in different directions?
3.76: What is a party system? It's a relatively stable network of relationships between parties , and it involves the number and size and ideological orientation of parties. I just use that contrast between the Dutch 2023 election results and the US results to see the difference. In terms of the different party systems that may exist, you can sometimes have a one-party system. Japan was like that for a long time, where it was one party that basically dominated and won every election. It's such a dominant party. There are also systems where there is a so-called natural party of government , the party that tends to form the government. The Conservative party in Britain has been one of the most successful parties in its history in forming the government, and I think it's around two-thirds of the time it's been in power. In Canada, the Liberal Party has been the so- called natural party of government.
3.77: I think these things can also shift. You can move from a system. Britain is a two-party system, but with a natural party of government. Canada is roughly a two-party system, similarly with a natural party of government. But those systems can evolve to a system where there is no longer a natural party of government, and it's a more even, finely balanced electorate . That may be what's happening in both Britain and Canada right now. That natural party of government, that's referred to as a dominant party system. Japan has now had an alternative party come into power, but for a long time, it was just one party.
3.78: Now, of course, you have autocracies like China, where clearly the Chinese Communist Party is going to be the only party, or Iran , for example. Those are one-party systems. But you could have a one-party system even in a liberal democracy. It's just that people tend naturally to vote for the establishment. So that could exist, as existed arguably in Japan for many decades. OK. And also the electoral system, as mentioned, is associated with the party system. If you have a more proportional representation electoral system, you're more likely to get a multi-party party system. And likewise, first-past-the-post is associated more with a two-party system .
3.79: There are a number of other distinctions we can make here between types of parties that political scientists draw. One is the distinction between cadre parties and mass parties. The cadre parties typically have an elite which tends to guide policy and control the party much more. Perhaps to some degree, the SNP in Scotland might be an example of this, where there is a guiding elite which determines the direction of the party. On the other hand, you might have a mass party movement like Beppe Grillo's Five Star in Italy, which is very much based on bottom-up participation in determining policy to construct a wide electoral base.
3.80: So one of the issues here is, how much of the direction of the party and its policy is under the sway of a set of leaders and elites, or how much is the party genuinely a reflection of grassroots behavior? There are also shifts, by the way, over time in the US system, a move away from anointing and appointing who is going to be the candidate for the party. That decision used to be made by party elites in smoke-filled rooms, behind closed doors at party conventions. But increasingly with the primary system, candidates had to compete with each other to win the backing of members of the party in a competition. And that's arguably a more democratic system .
3.81: Now, some people would say that's a bad thing because it leads to an emphasis on extremism, that candidates have to appeal to their base, so they have to go extreme in the primaries to win support amongst—soif you're going to become, if you want to lead the Democrats, you want to lead the Republicans, you have to play to your base, and that might take you in an extreme direction. Whereas maybe if the party was deciding on the candidates behind closed doors, they might pick someone who they think can win electorally. So the decision is not, "Who do I like emotionally?" It is, "Who, practically, is likely to fall more in middle?"
3.82: And so maybe the less democratic system led to more moderation, and maybe the more democratic system leads to more extremism. But then people would say, yeah, but the more democratic system is more representative, and it represents people better than the elites in smoke-filled rooms deciding on the candidates, which might be a system that actually reflects elite interests rather than popular interests. So the case for the more democratic grassroots mass party is that this is a better reflection of a wider range of interests, not just the interests of an elite.
3.83: There are also, it's worth mentioning, parties whose avowed aim is to overthrow the system . And so the Islamists in Iran, the communists in Iran, prior to the Iranian Revolution, their view was that, "Yeah, we're going to take over, and that's the end of democracy ." So you can get these parties that are anti-system and anti-liberal democracy, but they can still run, arguably, in elections, and get a certain amount of the vote. Most parties , of course, are constitutional parties that accept the existing system and would accept defeat and wouldn't just cling on to power after they get in.
3.84: I mentioned this distinction between mass and cadre parties, between parties being more democratic and grassroots, and allowing the membership to have more of a say in the direction of policy, and cadre parties where it's more of an elite that tends to determine policy . One of the critiques of the elite system—this is going back. Now we tend to see more critiques of the popular and the risks of a more populist system. But in the past , you had more critiques of the elitist system. And one of the critiques of elite systems is that there is a tendency for political parties to create oligarchies, which tend to determine the direction of policies, and they can very much determine policies that favor, particularly a donor class or particularly the economic military political elite that tends to be getting its way.
3.85: A lot of political science, a number of political science studies, show that elites are more likely to get their policy preferences enacted than, particularly, the working class or sectors of society that are less well represented within the elite. And so earlier in the century, a number of writers like Ostrogorsky or Michels talk about this idea of party machines, and Michels' term "the iron law of oligarchy." This comes from the early part of the 20th century, this iron law of oligarchy, which is about the concentration of power within political parties in the hands of an elite. So the fear in this case is lack of representativeness, lack of responsiveness, to the mass of the population leading to these party oligarchies.
3.86: And so there were attempts, I've mentioned the US case, to reform what was seen as previously an oligarchic system of backroom deals and compromises between party bigwigs to determine who was going to run to the primary system, which is more open and more popular. Now we're seeing more criticism of that kind of a system, for introducing extremism into the polity . There's a debate. Again, this is a debate over populism as well. Is populism bringing in voices that have been excluded? Or is it emotionalizing politics , leading to less rational, less moderate, less effective politics?
3.87: And so moving forward in the last few slides here and thinking about what's happening in different parts of the world, but let's say the West, to party politics. Is there a crisis of party politics, a withdrawal of trust, withdrawal of legitimacy from the system? On the one hand, populist right parties in Europe have been expanding, and it looks like they are going to do better than ever in the coming European elections. We have an increase in support for populist right parties like the Alternative for Germany, the Rassemblement National in France, the Freedom Party in Austria, Wilders in the Netherlands, and so on. Even in Britain now, we're seeing somewhat higher share of the vote for a third party-like reform than we would have even a couple of years ago.
3.88: What's going on in party politics in the West? Is it in crisis? When they say a crisis of party politics, of course, what they mean is that the main parties are losing support. The Christian Democrats and Social Democrats across Europe are losing support. And parties at the fringes, it could be the left fringe, Greens, or far left, or it could be the right fringe with populist right, are gaining greater and greater support. And the mainstream establishment is losing support. So what is causing this shift , this fragmentation? More and more parties, and voters are moving between parties more and more. There's more floating in the proportional representation continental European system. There's a lot more movement now, and certain Farmers' Party in the Netherlands expands, then disappears. Votes move wildly from one election to the other.
3.89: How can this be explained? One argument is that, really, the parties, the cadre-type elite parties, were not responsive to the mass of the population, didn't reflect their interests. And so it's healthy and natural that they actually are taught a lesson and people move to other parties and other options that better represent who they are. It could be that those parties were dominated by an oligarchy of political insiders and had become complacent. And this is a natural renewal of democracy. And once the big parties get the message, they can adapt and be more representative of the population, and they'll get their votes back. You can see this to some degree, where in Britain, for example, the conservative Party did adopt some of the views of people who voted UKIP and were able to get their vote in the 2019 election.
3.90: We've seen this in Nordic countries as well, where the Social Democrats adopted some of the positions of the populist right in countries like Norway and Denmark and have done better as a result. Maybe this is just about the system, the system correcting itself in a way and adapting to change. OK, and so just to conclude, we had really two parts to this lecture. The first was about electoral systems, where we talked about majoritarian on the one hand, first-past-the-post, in particular , and then more consensual or representative systems like proportional representation . We looked a little bit more at proportional representation as applied to deeply divided societies in the developing world, in large measure, not only in the developing world, but ethnically , religiously divided societies, that in some of these societies, the PR system is more appropriate because it is able to deal with problems of groups that feel that they're excluded from the system , and that in those societies, we may even see executive power shared within a power-sharing cabinet .
3.91: How you design your system, therefore, can be related to a whole series of factors, including how ethnically homogenous, politically homogenous, the society is, how much of a history of violent conflict it has had over time. Looking at the mainstream Western societies, you can see that, particularly in first-past-the-post systems like Britain or the US, parties serve to aggregate different interests into larger holes . So they have to deal with different factions, they have to form a government, and they have to negotiate between those factions. But in the proportional representation system, there is a broader range of representation and broader range of groups that you have to negotiate between to form a government. And so there are plus and minuses . Again, it seems like there's a tension between better representation and more efficiency, and the first-past-the-post is arguably more efficient. PR is arguably more representative.
3.92: We've seen that these party systems can shift and change over time . Moving from electoral systems to party systems, you can see that party systems can move from one party to two parties to multi-party. That seems to be the direction of travel in the West, in the PR systems of Western Europe. We're seeing moves towards the flanks. What is going on? Is this—some would say it's a good thing. It's democracy-adapting. It's allowing more voices into the system. Others would claim that this is actually caused by a crisis in the system where people are withdrawing trust in the establishment and that that is a dangerous or, perhaps, portends instability.
3.93: There's a debate that we can have about that, but just to say that it's always important to bear in mind that the design of an electoral system tends to influence the party system. When thinking about the design of an electoral system, one must bear in mind what the history is of a particular country and what the morphology of different groups is in a particular country. Thank you. Lecture 4: Electoral Studies At a glance — Electoral studies.
4.1: In this lecture, what I'm going to be addressing is electoral studies and voting. The first three topics that we've considered are largely either about theories of politics or about comparative political institutions. We looked at presidential and parliamentary systems. We looked at first-past-the-post versus proportional representation electoral systems. We looked at two-party versus multi-party party systems. These are very much about the institutions of government. What I'm going to be now moving into is looking at political behavior, the behavior of individuals and groups in politics, and trying to explain that behavior.
4.2: All of these lectures that we've heard so far are within the empirical side, the political science side. They're not about how the world ought to be. They're trying to explain the world as it is, but just different dimensions of that political world. In terms of voting, we're trying to account for the behavior of individual voters and groups of voters in the electorate over time . We have different theories of why people vote the way they do, why elections go the way they do, and why certain coalitions form and other coalitions decline over time. So these are some of the questions that we'll be looking into in this lecture.
4.3: There is a venerable science of voting, and the term psephology, or psephologist, you may or may not be familiar with that term, which is really characterizing an individual who's interested in the study of elections and electoral behavior, a psephologist. So this is really going to be a lecture on psephology, the science of electoral behavior. And there's a well developed literature on electoral studies , and it has its own journals and its own sections at political science conferences.
4.4: I'm going to begin with a simple model, perhaps the building block, which is the social model of voting, sometimes known as the Columbia model, which comes from Columbia University, 1940s , original in American political science. Political science, really, has an older history in the US as a formal discipline. I think the American Political Science Association, I think it goes back to the beginning of the 20th century. There's a long history there. But focusing on the Columbia model, really, this was saying, if we want to explain election results and voting and how people vote , we have to understand which groups they belong to. Older voters, younger voters, female /male, white/black, Protestant/Catholic, which region, southern US versus the West versus the Midwest, urban/rural, income, again, socioeconomic class —these sorts of variables.
4.5: These are characteristics of an individual. And so the theory here is, if we know an individual , older, wealthier, let's say, Protestant, white, rural , southern, we might be able to say they're a Republican voter. That would be the way this model would work. It's based on group memberships predicting vote. And one of the questions we would ask as a political scientist who studies elections is, how accurate is that model based on these group characteristics in predicting a vote? If I were a betting man and I had to bet money, what is the chance that, if I knew these characteristics, I'd be able to predict precisely how someone would vote?
4.6: Now, if it was just a coin toss, it would be 50%. I'd get it right half the time. Maybe if I know age and race and religion and gender and region and occupation, do I get up to 80%, 90% or just 55%? These are questions about how good a model is the social group model, the Columbia model, in predicting elections. As we'll see, it's not as good as you might imagine, actually. Although it can be stronger in certain periods than in other periods and in certain societies than in other societies. I don't want to blanket say that it isn't a good model.
4.7: I'm mainly going to be looking at electoral politics in the US, Britain, and to some extent, other Western democracies here. But we can apply many of these insights to other countries as well. I want to say something also about the coalitions of voters, the coalitions of groups that make up the voting for a party. When we talk about the Democratic coalition or the Republican coalition, usually what that is, is it's a mixture of the different groups that have aggregated together to support the party. It might be in the case of the New Deal Democrats under Franklin Delano Roosevelt in 1932 to 1945. But extending the New Deal coalition arguably extends into the late 1960s , was a coalition of southern white Protestants, northern so-called white ethnics who were Catholic and Jewish. That was the coalition of groups that came together to support the Democrats , and they all voted heavily Democrats. So that was who largely supported the Democratic Party.
4.8: The term alignment, if we say the democratic alignment of 1932 to 1968, or perhaps the conservative alignment in Britain between 1979 and 1995—these are long stretches of time where one party is in office, and that puts the party in a majority position. So if you are able to tap into a magical alignment where you get the southern white Protestants and the northern white Catholics and Jews to be voting for you, election after election, at a high rate, then that is an alignment between certain groups of voters and a certain party. Southern white Protestants align to the Democrats, northern white Catholics and Jews align to the Democrats. That is stable, and it was enough to put the party in office over a significant proportion of this period.
4.9: In the UK case, it would have been the wealthier part of the population, but also certain parts of the working class that supported the Conservative party under Thatcher, for the most part. Between 1979 and 1995, more recently, New Labour was a coalition of well-educated, high-income, progressive voters and working-class voters. That was the New Labour Coalition. One of the things that we're going to look into is whether these coalitions last, what causes them to break up? What caused, to some degree, the white working class to drift away from the Labour Party, ending the New Labour Coalition? What led white southern Protestants and northern white Catholics to leave the Democratic Party, causing a collapse of the New Deal coalition, which was the New Deal alignment of that period?
4.10: So these alignments can be very important when certain groups are oriented to vote for certain parties for a significant stretch of time. Then those parties can dominate in power for much of these periods. But there are periods in which things change, and there are two charts here. The one on the left shows what happened to white Catholics in America between 1952 and 2019. In 1960, approximately 85% of white Catholics voted for the Democrats, voted for John F. Kennedy in 1960. So Kennedy wins like 86% of the white Catholic vote. Now, Kennedy is the first Catholic President of the United States. That's clearly going to be important as well. But it's not, by all means, it's not the main part of the story.
4.11: And what this graph shows, if you look at the blue line, as it drops from 86% down to, by the time we get to 2019, that 86 has turned into less than 30%. Meanwhile , the white Catholic share of the vote captured by the Republicans, which is only around 20% or thereabouts, right into about 1980, and then after 1980, Ronald Reagan starts to win the so-called Reagan Democrats, white Catholic Democrats. By the time we get to 2019, the Republican number is pushing 55% up from 20%, even as late as 1980. There's been a real shift. White Catholics have defected from the Democratic Party, and they've moved into the Republican column . That's obviously going to have a big impact on any alignment. So the New Deal coalition falls apart. And now I could have done southern white Protestants. It's even more dramatic. Shift away from the Democrats to the Republicans over time.
4.12: We can ask if a similar process is occurring now. The graph on the right is the party identification of non-white Americans —Hispanic, Asian, black Americans—between 1980 and 2019. What that shows is that when Barack Obama was elected in 2008, first black President, so it's similar perhaps to Kennedy, first Catholic President, Obama now had and seems to have had an impact. So 75% of non-white Americans who are a growing share of the US population are identifying as Democrats in 2008. If you look at that blue line, by 2019, that's fallen to just 51%, from 75 to 51. It seems to be falling every election.
4.13: Now, the Republican share of the minority vote is relatively flat. It's not rising, but the independent, the share of people who say, "I'm not Republican or Democrat," amongst non-white Americans, has been going up. What that means, however, is that, come election time, the Democrats cannot be as—they are not able to rely as much on the minority vote to keep them in power.
