One of the worries for the Democrats is that if this trend continues, that shift in the minority vote will cost them a number of key swing states in the coming election.
4.14: But this is an example of what we call dealignment. The links between white Catholics and the Democratic Party get weaker over time. That's a dealigning process. Where those links are strong, that's an aligning process. And actually, a shift in loyalties, moving the white Catholics, moving away from the Democrats to the Republicans, is what's called a realignment . In this country, one of the arguments is that the white working class have been in a process of realignment away from the Labour party. And this is true also in continental Europe, that the white working class has moved away from the social democratic and, to some degree, communist parties towards the populist right in particular.
4.15: Why groups of voters decide to move away from the parties their group has traditionally voted for towards other parties is a question that many electoral studies scholars ask themselves. What's driving this realignment? But seemingly, at the same time, what you've had is well-educated, wealthy voters aligning away from conservative parties towards left-wing parties. And so now in Britain, for example, the Conservative vote in 2019 was slightly more working-class than the Labour vote. That would have been unthinkable , even as late as 1997. What's causing this realignment ? Highly educated, well-off voters moving to the left and relativelyless well-off working- class voters moving to the right.
4.16: That's a lot about social groups and the Columbia model of how social groups fit into election results. Which type of person tends to vote for which type of party based on their social group. There's a lot of discussion about minorities or Catholics or other social groups, young people, rich people, educated people. What the Michigan model, which emerges in 1960, does is, it says, well, actually, these models based on group identity and membership, they may give us reasonable predictive power, but they can only get the answer right maybe 60% of the time, which is better than 50%, which is chance , but it's not that good. That we can do better than that by understanding a person's party identification.
4.17: Which party do you identify with? Now, that's distinct from, which party do you vote for? You can be a Democrat in your party identification, but maybe because you don't like Joe Biden, for whatever reason, you're not going to vote Democrat this time. You might even vote for Donald Trump or the reverse. Maybe you're a Republican, but you're maybe a free-market Republican, and you don't like Trump, so you might vote for Biden. The Michigan model, it says that, yes, your group membership does influence your party identification. If you're African-American, you're very likely to be a Democrat. But there are other influences. Your family, who they've tended to vote for, can also influence who you vote for.
4.18: The point about your party identification is their view—the view has developed in this famous book called The American Voter, came out in 1960. Angus Campbell , Philip Converse, Warren Miller, and Donald Stokes. This is a classic in the electoral studies field that everybody has to study. It puts out this model of party identification as being central to explaining vote choice. Your party identification will tend to mean that, if your party takes a particular view on a particular issue, you will shift your attitudes on particular issues to line up with the attitudes that you're supposed to take as a member of this party. That's a pretty radical claim.
4.19: The claim is that you don't have issue preferences on your own about tax and abortion and immigration. You're going to follow the lead of the party that you identify with. If they say you should support high immigration, low tax, whatever, you will move with whatever the party cues you to believe in. Their argument as party identification is very important, and it comes from identities that are acquired in early adulthood. Just as you would identify with a religion or an ethnic group, you identify with a party. It becomes part of your personal identity of who you are. The argument is that these party identities, once acquired, are relatively fixed throughout the life course.
4.20: They are not the same thing as ideology. In 1960, the median American voter was conservative. When you asked them, "Where are you on a 7-point or 5-point scale, between very liberal and very conservative?", they would tend to fall on the conservative side. But on party identification, they would tend to be Democrats. So how strongly are you Democrat versus a Republican? They would fall on the Democrat side. So the median voter would be a conservative Democrat. Now, you might say, well, aren't the Democrats supposed to be the Liberals and the Republicans, the conservatives? It doesn't make sense from that level of analysis, from a sort of alignment between what the party elite stand for.
4.21: So the elite Democrats and the elite Republicans wouldn't get this wrong. But most voters, they were quite comfortable to say, "I'm a conservative, I'm a Democrat," or "I'm a liberal and I'm a Republican." These two things weren't as fixed as they have become. It's another story which I'm going to get to. And so this shows you the independence of party identity from ideology. So you can be a conservative, but you're a Democrat, because Democrat is almost like an ethnic or religious identification. It's part of your identity, and it's separate from your views on issues and ideology.
4.22: There have been a number of studies in political science. A lot of political science takes place in articles rather than books. There have been a number of studies that will ask people about their views on a particular issue, and they'll ask half the people their views on an issue, and then the other half, they'll say, "Well , this is what the leader of the Democrats believes. What is your view on the issue?" You can see that half of the people are seeing that the party is endorsing a particular belief, and the other half are only just seeing, "What's your view on this particular belief?" Those studies consistently find that, when you indicate that that's the view of the party that a person is identifying with, they are more likely to endorse that particular issue belief.
4.23: So that is proof of this idea that people will follow the party line on particular issues. If Donald Trump says, "Yeah, Russia is our friend," then Republicans who would have thought of Russia as the enemy, now a significant number of them will switch and think of Russia as a friendly country . I'm not saying that that's Trump's view, or free trade. There's been a shift on free trade, let's say, between Reagan, perhaps, and between Trump. That's called party cueing. So this idea is that the party which you identify with prompts you, tells you that, on this issue, you should have this position. And so you take that position. That is suggesting that party comes first and issue comes second .
4.24: The opposite view is that, no, you can't. If Trump came up and said, "We should have open borders," no, actually, he would lose support because people have deeply held policy beliefs, and you can't just manipulate those. Whereas the Michigan model, which tends to prioritize party identity, would give more leeway to political leaders and opinion-formers to shape public opinion, rather than just reflecting public opinion. Now, there are others who say, well, a leader can affect issues that don't matter to people as much, like free trade or foreign policy. But they can't really move issues that really matter to people, like maybe on abortion, low tax, immigration. They have more sway to move people's beliefs that are lightly held than the deeply held beliefs.
4.25: But in any case, the view that says party identity is central, that Michigan model view, and that parties can essentially manipulate public opinion and prime people to take their view on a particular issue, that is contested by the rational voter model, which is a rational choice theory model, which says, no, people have very clear interests. They have very clear ideas and preferences, and parties have to minister to those ideas and preferences. So the individual comes prepackaged with a set of policy beliefs and interests. And party identification is not something you get with your mother's milk, or it's not something that you're deeply attached to from early adulthood. It's not an identity. It is actually just a running tally of how well parties are catering to your particular mix of attitudes and interests.
4.26: So this is the so-called running tally idea of Morris Fiorina, and that goes very counter to the Michigan model. And this is the idea that people are quite fluid. They can shift their party identification based on how well the party is satisfying their needs and addressing their interests. This is also buffeted by events such as inflation or a poor economy, and that can shift people from one party to the other. If we look at this chart, however, you can see there is some movement. There is a certain range to which party identification goes up and down, but within reasonably narrow bounds. Other studies show that people's party identifications are actually reasonably sticky throughout the lifetime. But there's a debate. Fiorina's claim is that they're not as durable and sticky as those who hold to the Michigan model claim.
4.27: There are also other considerations like tactical voting, which might mean that you may really like the libertarians, but when it comes down to it, you'd probably dislike the Republicans less than the Democrats. So you'll tactically vote Republican to keep the Democrats out of office. There's tactical voting, which is another rational way to behave. You're calculating your interests, looking at which party best satisfies your basket of interests. The party identity doesn't really determine where you go, and it's not particularly derived from identity. The party identification is just a tally of how well the parties are ministering to your interests and beliefs.
4.28: I'm going to go through a whole set, and this is really only going to be an overview, a whole set of debates within electoral studies, to just give you a flavor of the kinds of debates that are taking place in political science journals and some books, trying to explain why people vote the way they do. So one question is, how important is the economy? To what extent is it the case that, when the economy is doing badly, people vote against the party in office? That's one theory.
4.29: This is a chart that's here looking at gas prices, or in this country, petroleum, petrol prices, and the popularity of a president between 1977 and 2022. You can see there is some relationship there, that when gas prices are high, presidential approval falls. We could look at inflation as well. When inflation is high, perhaps approval of the government tends to fall. How much is this about individuals feeling the pinch and the pain, their money not going as far, and personally thinking, "Oh, I'm hurting, and therefore, I'm no longer a believer in whoever's running the government"? That's called egotropic voting. You're voting based on your own self-interest. Or how much are you worried, not about yourself, you're doing fine, but you're worried about other people? They're not doing as well, or relatives, or friends, or so on. So you're actually more concerned about the economy as a whole and how it's affecting society. That's called sociotropic. It's more altruistic.
4.30: We can actually apply this egotropic, sociotropic divide to non-economic issues as well as economic issues. I'm just using an example here of an economic issue. To what extent are people voting on the basis of themselves personally and their personal success or the pain they're feeling? Or to what extent are they voting based on how they think the government is affecting society as a whole? Another debate is between prospective versus retrospective voting. That means, are people voting against the current government because of how they've performed in the past, punishing them? It's a retrospective vote if you're talking about the performance of a party in the past. A vote is an evaluation of how a party performed during its period in office. That's Fiorina's argument. That is a retrospective voting model.
4.31: Another argument, however, is that people know that people are thinking about how a party will govern in the future. They vote for, rather than voting against. So they really are inspired to vote for a particular party because of its vision and because they think they will do well. You have these two theories, one that it's about, you're voting against a party in power for how they've performed, or that you vote for a party in power. I've got some poll results here from the UK which show evaluations of leaders. You can see that actually both Rishi Sunak, Boris Johnson, and Liz Truss, these are conservative leaders. Their popularity declines over time . This goes from 2020 through to January of '24.
4.32: But even the Labour leader Kier Starmer's popularity declines over time in this series. You might say, in the case of Britain in 2024, that the reason that the conservatives are 20 points back in the polls is not necessarily going to be because people are fired up about Kier Starmer and think that he's going to do an excellent job. So this much more looks like a vote against the conservatives . And so that would tend to back the retrospective model of voting more than the prospective model of voting. But maybe the vote for Tony Blair, perhaps, might have been more of a prospective vote for people who are maybe excited, to some degree, about New Labour, something fresh and new, possibly.
4.33: Again, these things have to be studied through survey analysis. Surveys are the main method that is used in electoral studies, by the way. We've talked about egotropic, sociotropic voting. We've talked now about prospective versus retrospective voting. There is also a distinction between what's called positional and valence issues. Positional issues are issues where people disagree strongly . It's more connected to ideology, whereas valence issues are issues everybody agrees about. If you think about a strong economy, short waiting times for the health service, low unemployment, there's very few people that want high unemployment and long health care waiting times to see their doctor or to get an operation . Those are issues that pretty much everybody agrees on. So they're competence issues.
4.34: And it's just about parties competing over who's going to be more competent in managing these issues. But then you have other issues—Brexit, abortion, immigration, affirmative action—that are much more ideological. These are positional issues. And the positional issues, here it very much divides people by politics. One of the questions is, which of these issues is more important? Is it more important how a party is seen to be performing on the valence and competency issues, essentially, or is it more important whether a party is representing the issues, stances that you care about, on immigration, affirmative action, Brexit, etc.?
4.35: It seems like, if we were to go back 10 years , 15 years, it seems that the talk was more around, oh, politics is becoming more managerial. It's about how well parties are seen to be managing the economy. It was a time when socialism was increasingly off the agenda and pure free market was off the agenda, and it seemed like there was a mushy middle on the economy. A lot of the parties were coming together, at least in their economic outlook. They were becoming more similar. Labour wasn't the party of trade unions and socialism, and the Conservatives, the free market and business. Actually, Labour under Blair was more business-friendly and less union-friendly and didn't look as different. And the Tories, to some degree, have moved to the left on some economic issues.
4.36: And so, in that situation, a lot of the discussion was around managerialism and the importance of valence issues for voting. People vote on competency grounds. Now, certainly post-Brexit, but even slightly before Brexit in this country, the view started to shift to say, well, actually, there are these positional issues which are starting to matter, and particularly post-2014 , the rise of the populist right across Europe, and with the rise of Trump in the US, there's more of a focus now on positional issues helping to explain how people vote.
4.37: There are also, by the way, certain issues like illegal immigration, which some people argue are competency issues, others argue are positional issues. Another set of debates revolves around how important economic considerations are versus, broadly speaking, cultural considerations. Do people vote—are they pocketbook voters, voting based on whether they think they're doing well economically or whether they think the country is doing well economically? Are they voting on economic issues or are they voting on more cultural issues? I mentioned immigration, but also culture wars issues around freedom of speech, for example, or around the treatment of history, so critical race approaches to history, for example, or gender. To what extent are these cultural issues important? Religion and abortion are arguably more cultural as well.
4.38: One of the arguments is that we are shifting from a post-war Western electorate that was more economic in its voting, where the economic left versus right, free market versus tax-and-spend, that that was the dominant dimension after the war for many decades. But we're now moving into a situation where the cultural divide between the so-called globalist and nationalist, or multiculturalist versus nationalist, or open-closed , which is another, perhaps, way of characterizing this dimension , that this cultural dimension is becoming more important.
4.39: One of the more important theorists of this shift is Ronald Ingelhart, who passed away a few years ago, and his co-author, Pippa Norris, of Harvard University. They have written a lot about this cultural revolution and the realignment, that the cultural issues are being mentioned more and more and more in party manifestos, and the economic issues are not being mentioned as much, or at least they're not being mentioned more. The cultural issues seem to be having more and more prominence. Immigration is one example of a kind of issue that has gained, seems to have gained, prominence in election contests.
4.40: There's a graph on here that just shows the way this has played out in terms of people's income. You would expect if economic divides were important, that the richer part of the population would vote for the conservative parties and the poorer part of the population for the more left-wing parties. That is how it looked. If we start in the post- war period, you can see in all of these graphs going from the 1940s through to 2020, or as we move towards 2019, that the graphs go upward at the end. The richer people are voting more for the parties of the right, and the poorer people, parties of the left.
4.41: That seems to hold all the way until we reach the 2010s . Then in the 2010s, you can see those lines flattening out and even reversing themselves. So the richer people are actually voting more for the left than the poorer people. There seems to be something that's going on with Western electorates. Now, that graph is from the US case, but we can see something similar in other Western countries. The realignment away from the left-right cleavage , and this term cleavage is used in political science. What is the main cleavage in the electorate? Is it economic or is it cultural? And which kind of cultural cleavage? Is it religious, religious conservatism versus secularism? Or is it this multiculturalism, globalism versus nationalism , the more national populist dimension? That one seems to be the most important right now.

4.44: There's also a question about how group identities—I want to return to these group identities which the Columbia model talked about. How do those group identities affect issues? We have identities, we have issue positions, we have party identification and voting. They're separate things, but they are related in certain ways. Here in Britain, we can look at how different ethnic groups in the population think about the immigration issue. 4.46: You can see there are differences between groups. So Bangladeshis are less anti- immigration than Indians. If we were to have Afro-Caribbeans, they're even more pro- immigration than the Asian groups. There are differences between groups in their issue positions. Groups can have different positions on issues. Also, some groups are just wealthier or poorer. That might affect who they're going to vote for. Some are more religious, some are more secular. You have these different ways in which group identities influence issue positions.
4.47: There's also another concept which is important in intellectual studies called salience, and that refers to the priority of an issue to you as an individual . So you may say, "Yeah, I'd like immigration reduced." If I say to you, "What are the most important issues facing Britain? Give me your top three," and you say, "The economy, health care, and green issues ." Oh, no, not green issues. That's probably not a good one. Let's say foreign policy. So economy , health care, and foreign policy are your top three issues. But if I ask you your attitude to immigration, you say , "Yeah, I want it reduced." But it's clearly not that important an issue to you if it doesn't make your top three.
4.48: If, however, immigration is your top issue, or your top-two issue, then it has high salience for you. One of the things that we notice, certainly in the last 10 years, is that with larger inflows of immigration, you tend to get a rise in the salience of immigration —the proportion of people saying immigration is one of the leading issues facing Britain or the US or the European Union. And so this chart, for example, from the Eurobarometer survey, if you look at that black line from 2010, immigration goes from about 10 % of people saying it's one of the top three issues facing the European Union to almost 60 % by 2015 during the migrant crisis. It comes down a little bit. It's recently come back up again.
4.49: Now, what that is, is that people who say, "I want immigration reduced, but immigration is my number 5, 6 issue," it's now risen from 5, 6 up to 2 or 3, or even 1 . That rising salience changes the electoral calculation. It's heavily linked to populist right voting. It's not so much that people's attitudes shift from wanting immigration increased to wanting it decreased. That shift is much less. There's very little movement there. It's more tied to ideology. But the priority of immigration for people rises from a low-priority issue to a high-priority issue. This is now a high-priority issue for right-wing voters across the West in Britain, in the United States, in Europe. This is an example of rising salience from which we should probably expect improved support for the populist right. It's not an iron law, but that's what we would expect.
4.50: I want to turn now to ideology. That is liberal and conservative or, in this country, left and right ideology. What is the relationship between ideology and voting? Ideologies are packages of issue positions. Maybe the conservative ideology might involve you in the US being pro-gun, anti-abortion, low-tax, maybe being in favor of not being as involved in foreign conflicts. That might be the package that has been created. We can ask the question of why those issue attitudes are bundled together. Is there something philosophically that naturally means that those positions should be bundled together?
4.51: Some would argue, actually, it's pretty accidental and not necessarily based on a consistent philosophy. For example, a consistent liberal individualist philosophy might be low-tax, weak state, don't tell us what to do in the bedroom. That libertarian attitude would actually be against the government legislating on abortion, for example. There are a number of different contradictions. We can see, for example, free trade could be seen as part of a consistent package with low tax. Free market, free trade. Why is it that an opposition to free trade is now part of conservative ideology in the US, although not in Britain, but in the US it is?
4.52: The first point to make is, it is not necessarily the case that ideologies are consistent, philosophically. Also, most people may not necessarily know what fits in with the conservative ideology or the right-wing ideology in the left. If you were to give them a quiz, "Is taking this position on free trade a right-wing or a left-wing position?", many people wouldn't necessarily know . At least that was certainly more the case in the past. It's partly the case that people don't think ideologically as much as elites and pundits might think they do. They have preferences on issues, but that may not be consistent with an ideology.
4.53: It's partly about how issues are packaged in different countries. In Eastern Europe, for example, there tends to be a connection between being very redistributionist on economics and being culturally very conservative, so almost being a socialist or a communist on economics and being culturally very conservative. That package goes together in Eastern Europe, whereas in the West, actually, if you're on the left, you tend to be very culturally liberal and socialist on economics, whereas in Eastern Europe, it's a different relationship. So that speaks to the fact that parties and history have led different issues to be packaged in different ways in different countries. So ideologies are not this iron-consistent thing. They are political parties and intellectuals put together to allow people to simplify reality.
4.54: There are two issues here. One is the degree to which people package issues into ideologies. As a voter, if I have a certain view on abortion and a certain view on taxation, am I able to correctly match that to a particular ideology and identify the right way I should be identifying? That's called issue constraint. To what extent are people constrained by an ideology, such as being a liberal or a conservative, constrained to having the "right", the right views on the issues that match their ideology? There's constraint, which is one issue, and the second issue is the alignment or the sorting. There's constraint versus sorting.
4.55: Sorting is, to what extent are conservatives voting for the Republicans and Liberals voting for the Democrats? I mentioned, in the Michigan model, 1960, the average American voter was a conservative Democrat. So you had weak sorting in 1960 . The chart here, if you look at the left, there are two scatterplots out of Alan Abramowitz's book, The Great Alignment, which is about explaining polarization in America. And what he's doing here is, he's plotting the average ideology in a state along the bottom. That is the share that is liberal minus the share that is conservative. Then up the top is party identification, the share that is Democrat minus the share that is Republican.
4.56: In the period 1974 to 1982, you can see there's no statistical relationship. There's no relationship, no pattern in those dots. It's just a spread of dots . So even if your state is really conservative, like Mississippi, it may not be particularly Republican. It doesn't seem to be related. And likewise with the more liberal states, they're not necessarily more democratic in this period, 1974 to '82. But if we go ahead to 2012, all of a sudden, you can see those dots are clustered around this line that's sloping upwards. And that's showing you that what's occurred between the '70s and '80s and the 2010s is a sorting of the electorate by ideology into the right party.
4.57: Now the conservative states like Idaho and Mississippi are heavily Republican, and the liberal states like Massachusetts and Vermont and New York are heavily Democrat as of 2012. Why do we see this shift? Why is it that all the liberals started voting for the Democrats and all the Conservatives started voting for the Republicans between the 1970s and the 2010s? Why this sorting of the electorate? And that is one of the issues in the study of polarization. Now, one explanation could be , well, the education level is rising. More people with university degrees. Higher education means more people are able to understand that being conservative goes with being a Republican and being liberal goes with being a Democrat. People got better educated. They were better able to pin the tail of ideology on the donkey of party, and that's what explains this.
4.58: But of course, we don't see this in every country. It seems to be really particularly acute in the US. It can't just be a story of rising education. There are also some other wrinkles. This has happened, especially amongst white Americans, much less amongst non- white, and especially much less amongst Black Americans, who remain—their sorting of ideology into party remains much less acute than in the white population. So there's something going on with this polarization.
4.59: Studies of voting are also increasingly focusing on two dimensions, two cleavages, within the electorate. One is the economic left-right, tax-and-spend versus free market. The other is the cultural, open-closed or liberal-conservative dimension between, for example, views on immigration, abortion . That distinction, the cultural distinction, in some ways, cross-cuts the economic one. A lot of white working-class voters in the West, economically, they want more tax-and-spend, better public services, more taxation of the rich. There are two dimensions to Western electorates now.
4.60: Combined with the Norris-Ingelhart argument about the rising importance, the realignment away from the economy towards the cultural cleavage, that helps to explain results like the one that I've put up here, which shows this two-dimensional space and dots for each voter. 4.62: So if we're thinking about, again, we're getting back to that idea of, we want to improve on the coin toss in terms of predicting who's going to win an election, we need to take into account not just party identification, but we also have to take into account leader evaluations. There are other factors as well in predicting elections. One is the importance of incumbency, which is somebody who is in office running for election again. Biden is an incumbent. 4.64: Just stepping back and thinking about this theoretically, this term "funnel of causality" has been used by scholars, essentially by intellectual studies, as a way of thinking about all of these factors that we've talked about—group memberships, socio-demographics like race, religion, education, age, party identification , issues, your position on different issues, and leader evaluations, how much you like particular leaders. The way this funnel is constructed in this model is we have the longer term, more stable dimensions at the top, funneling down to the more short-term and variable dimensions as we get closer to the vote.
4.65: Also, the argument here is that your leader evaluation is going to be a much better predictor. They may only improve us from 50% coin toss accuracy to 60%. The more we go towards issues, and particularly candidate images, leader evaluations, if we know what people think of the party leaders, that's probably going to get us above 70% predictive power, 80% thereabouts.
4.66: The other thing is that the more you go down this funnel of causality, the more there is a flexibility and short-term variability in the particular characteristic. Whereas your socio-demographics, that's pretty fixed. Your education, your income, OK, it can move around a little bit. Your ethnicity or religion is generally relatively fixed. So one of the questions is, how much are the relatively fixed conditioning factors going to be important in elections versus the shorter-term factors, issues, events, and leadership evaluations?
