So literacy spreads, and there is, with the novel, you get a spread, at least you take the position of the main character. The argument here is that those novels can help to spread empathy with those who are different from you, and that enlarges the circle of empathy. And that means you're perhaps a little more reluctant to engage in dehumanization of the other, including perhaps criminals, so you may not engage in very cruel punishment of criminals either.
5.24: In terms of the master trend, just looking over time, this graph here just shows Western and Eastern Europe, and it plots the number of wars each year between 1400 and 2000. What you can see is a gradual decline from about one and a half or two conflicts a year in 1400 to what looks like roughly 0.2 or 0.3 by 2000. Very low decline. Now, it's up and down. There's a lot of blips, and clearly, 1939 to '45, there was a spike in Europe. But the general trend, if you look at the graph, seems to be, in both Western and Eastern Europe, a decline. That would fit in with some of the theories that Pinker is propounding, such as the civilizing process , followed by commerce and the Enlightenment, these things bringing the level of violence down in the world.
5.25: Now, we can argue, some people, the rational choice people would say, this is all about, it's all about calculation and the fact that people could get wealthier by trading than going to war, and all the Enlightenment stuff doesn't matter at all. Other people would say, no, the ideas, the civilizing process, and the humanitarian ideas are very important, and the reading publics and all this cultural stuff is important. There's a debate between the rational choice, who focus a lot on self-interest and material motivations, and those who focus more on the cultural motivations around ideology, for example.
5.26: Moving more into the more recent period, it's worth saying that war tends to come in waves, and it tends to be linked to shifts in the number of states. So whenever you see the expansion of empires, there are wars of conquest. The breakup of empires , we see secessionist wars. And whenever you have instability, you have more violence . That's a lesson that Pinker draws from his long historical tour, is that anarchy is really the breeding ground for violence. And that's also one reason why, in the UN and in international law, there's such an emphasis on state sovereignty. Even if a state is abusing its own citizens, very reluctant to allow others to intervene in a state, and very reluctant to allow secessions, too.
5.27: How difficult it is to recognize, for example, the Kurds, Taiwan, Somaliland, and these other places, Kosovo, a lot of resistance to recognizing new states. And this is because of, one reason is because of the fear of anarchy . I mean, another reason is that most states don't want to have secessionist challenges within their borders. So you have these waves then of war. One wave occurred with a breakup of the Ottoman Empire and the Austro-Hungarian Empire after World War I. Another wave was with decolonization . And decolonization leads to the emergence of these independent postcolonial states. But those postcolonial states, instead of fighting against the colonizer, you now have fighting within, between ethnic groups for control of the states.
5.28: Anytime you have a change in the state order and a breakup of empire, there's a risk of more violence. And that's one of the reasons there's emphasis on state stability. Stability in the international system. There's a concept within international relations called the democratic peace theory, which is the idea that democracies have not gone to war against each other. Again, not fully true. Obviously, democracies go to war against non-democracies . If you just think of the Iraq war, it's one example of that. But there is an argument that says that, in democracies, because the act of war has to be supported by the population, there's more deliberation and there's more thinking that goes into whether you go to war. The idea of somebody just saying, "We're going to go off to war because I want to make myself great," that's harder to achieve in a democracy.
5.29: Now, there are others who say democracy actually increases the chances of war. So there are skeptics of this position. There are some who say, well, in a democracy, the public can sometimes clamor for war, and you can get whipped up by the press. And so there are also risks with democratization that might increase the chances of war. But in general, this democratic peace theory has some currency and some popularity in international relations.
5.30: Now, in terms of some of the empirical analysis, some comparativists contend that, actually, the greatest risk of war is not in an authoritarian regime or in a democracy, but actually in a semi-democracy , what are known as anocracies. And those are the least stable and the most likely to be associated with war. Now, most of that war, by the way, today, those semi-democracies, the war is civil war, not war between states.
5.31: I now want to shift gears to talk about the post-1945 period and some of the trends that have taken place in the world since then in terms of war. And the first is that interstate war, war between states, which is one of the major subjects in international relations, has declined dramatically so that there have arguably only been several, perhaps two only since 1945 , or maybe three. The separation of Bangladesh from Pakistan could be counted as a war, but also the invasion of Kuwait by Saddam, and more recently , of course, the invasion of Ukraine. But almost all of the wars in the world today are civil wars, are intra-state wars.
5.32: One of the questions we might ask is, what's the trend then in civil wars between 1945 and the present? So what this chart actually shows is the trend in total war and the breakdown of the different types of wars. The blue bars, the blue is the interstate, and that is extremely low. You can see throughout this period, barely any of it going on. Almost everything else is war within states.
5.33: Now, it could be that it's a situation like Syria, where you have a war within Syria, but you have international players involved. Iran and Russia, on the Assad, behind the Assad regime, for example, would be an example of that. You can have internationalized intra-state war, and that's quite prominent today. If you look at Yemen, Iran and Saudi Arabia are on different sides in that conflict. You have an international dimension, but the war is still fought by groups within a country. So it is still basically a civil war conflict.
5.34: The other trend that we see here is, you can see the increase in war between 1945 and 1989, which was when the Berlin Wall came down. So the proxy wars during the Cold War seem to have contributed to greater civil war and violence in the world. After 1989, we see a drop in the number of civil wars until about 2006-07. 2006-07, and then we start to see more conflict, particularly in the Middle East, after the Arab Spring. In places like Libya, we have some conflict. Yemen also, we see a rise starting in about 2007. Back up to the level it was in 1989. So all of the decline in civil war between 1989 and 2006 had been reversed already by about 2012.
5.35: Now, what does that mean? Does that mean that the world is becoming less stable and more violent? And we can ask why that might or might not be the case. One factor seems to be the aftermath of the Arab Spring, the growing conflict between Shia and Sunni in the Middle East, seems to be one factor behind some of these wars. But of course, that's not going to explain what's happening in Ethiopia, for example, or what's certainly not what's happening in Russia , Ukraine. That is the trend in terms of total number of conflicts.
5.36: In terms of number of deaths, we see somewhat of a similar pattern. Since 1989, you see a drop in the number of people dying in armed conflicts until the 2010s , and then an increase, a little bit of a drop, and then a rise again in 2022. It seems like the world got more peaceful for a long time, and certainly after 1989 , there was a drop in civil wars. But we've seen an increase more recently. Just to look in this next slide at falling violence around the end of the Cold War, the number of wars ongoing dropped from about 40 in 1989 to around just above 20 by 2000, 2002.
5.37: So why do we see that drop in the number of wars? And there are a number of reasons why we see that drop. One is that one side wins a war. So, the Sri Lankan regime won the war against the Tamils. Now, you could say that that conflict will burst into flames sometime in the future because the grievances haven't been addressed. And that, I think, is a reasonable supposition. But one example could be that, or in Syria, where the Assad regime has defeated the largely Sunni opposition. So when you have a kind of, one side winning, that's one major way that wars end, that violence drops. Another, however, possibility is that peace agreements and international interventions have played a part as well in reducing the level of violence in the world and the number of civil wars.
5.38: There was also a lot of optimism because we saw a rise in the number of democracies after 1989, the end of communism, clearly the breakup of the Soviet Union, former Yugoslavia, the rise of new democracies. That was quite exciting and may or may not be related to the decline of violence. Here's another chart just showing different types of war. After 1989, we saw a drop in the number of ethnic wars and the number of revolutionary wars, which are more class-based. If you think about Latin America, the Zapatistas and groups like FARC in Colombia, they're not really ethnic. I mean, they may have an indigenous element to them in some cases, but basically, they are revolutionary rather than ethnic.
5.39: We also have religious wars, which you could argue, in the Middle East, in a place like Syria, I mean, yes, it's partly ethnic, but it's also partly religious between, say , Shia and Sunni, or between Islamists and essentially Arab nationalists . But there's been a drop since 1989 in this graph, but then a flattening out and then subsequently a rise. If we look in the different regions of the world in this graph , we can see that Africa is a very important site for civil war. In many years, it dominates. It's a majority of civil wars are taking place on the African continent. But Latin America, where it's more to do with gang violence and drug violence, that's also significant.
5.40: So I want to look now spatially at some patterns. And there's almost a conflict zone in the world, which is we sometimes call the Global South. It's between the tropics. And this is a fine-grained map of grid-level violence from the Peace Institute, PRIO. And this shows you that almost all of the violent conflict is taking place in that tropical belt. With the exception of Ukraine, almost everything that's going on is happening within that belt. And there are many regions, Myanmar, Yemen, Ethiopia, Congo , but also in Central America and the Golden Triangle, we're seeing drug-related or regime-related violence there.
5.41: This is a map of global wars. Again, it's almost all the violence is concentrated pretty much in that tropical belt, with the exception of Ukraine, Russia. The picture looked very similar about five years ago. There aren't really—it may be that certain countries are lighting up. It might have been Yemen was violent. Well, that's come to an end, again, because of stalemates or defeats , but now Ethiopia. It just seems that this is the zone where we're seeing a lot of violence.
5.42: One of the questions we might ask is, why is so much of the violence occurring in that zone? And this is where comparative politics comes in. And what comparative politics would do is, it would say, OK, we're going to look at all of the countries in the world. What are all their characteristics? And what are the characteristics of a country that predicts whether it will experience civil war within its borders? So what is it that predicts civil war? That's an important topic. So I will go through a number of potential causes, and we'll then look at a paper , which is one of the most highly cited papers in political science, which tries to explain the causes of civil war.
5.43: So one argument could be that this is about democracy, the democratic peace theory. Now, democratic peace theory is about war between states, no two democracies going to war with each other. But you could make the argument that also a democracy might lead to less violence within a state. And we can see, from this map, that there are a lot of authoritarian regimes in that Global South tropical region, but not all of them are authoritarian, actually . You've also got authoritarianism outside that tropical belt in places like China, North Korea, and Russia.
5.44: What about poverty and low income? This seems to be perhaps a better bet. You can see that most of this region is poor in the orange and brown tones. So could it be that poverty, poor countries are more likely to engage in civil war? Why is that? One reason could be that you have less to lose by joining an insurrection because you are going to be in poverty anyway, and at least joining in an insurrection means you have a chance at something better, gaining resources . You also have fewer alternatives in terms of well-paying jobs, and so your opportunity cost of engaging in a violent insurrection is lower.
5.45: Also, we can look at the availability of lootable resources, that is, gems, gold, and also oil resources, and the location of those resources. So you might say, well, a country that has more precious stones and oil reserves is more likely to experience civil war as people try and fight to control those resources. This is a map of gemstone resources. You can see East Africa, for example. Southeast Africa is one place that has a lot of resources. Myanmar, which is also very conflict-ridden, is another place where you find gemstone resources . In terms of oil, this map perhaps would suggest that oil on its own is not really likely to be the explanation. However, there are certain countries in Africa, like Nigeria, that have more oil resources. And is it the case that countries with more oil resources are more prone to violent conflict?
5.46: Another possible explanation is the topography of a country, since almost all civil wars are fought in the countryside. Almost all civil wars are fought in the countryside, so it's going to be very difficult to fight as an insurgent if you have nowhere to hide. This is something very practical. So a more mountainous country, or a country with more forests or inaccessible terrain, is going to be more friendly for insurgents to operate and organize. This map shows you that, in terms of mountainous territory, there are certain regions, such as Eastern Africa, for example, or much of Southeast Asia, that might be friendly to rebel movements. The location of forests here, in particularly the tropical belt of Africa, that also might make it easier for rebel movements to hide, places like the Eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, where we see a lot of violence.
5.47: Another possible factor is ethnic fractionalization, the number of ethnic groups in a country and their relative share of the population. The way this is calculated is the likelihood that two random citizens of a country will be of the same ethnic group. If that likelihood is very low, you have high ethnic fractionalization. So the likelihood is, if you take two individuals from Nigeria or Congo, there's a very high likelihood they're going to be members of different ethnic groups. In much of sub-Saharan Africa, you have very high ethnic fractionalization. And is ethnic fracture—and you see that in Southeast Asia.
5.48: So a lot of this tropical belt is more ethnically diverse than the wealthier parts of the world. If you look at Europe, for example, if you look at East Asia, and even though there is diversity in North America, it's mainly immigrant diversity in urban areas. So the question of ethnic diversity, particularly indigenous ethnic diversity, is an important consideration as well. So do more fractionalized countries have a greater risk of civil war?
5.49: Another factor we could look at is the age structure of a population. Almost all violence is committed by young men between about 15 and 30 in most societies, and that holds for crime, that holds for a whole series of different forms of violence . So you would think that, on average, a younger population means you'll have a greater risk of conflict and war. There are a whole bunch of other factors that play into this. If you have a big youth bulge, what's called a youth bulge, a large number of people between 15 and 30 in your population entering the labor force, usually the labor force is designed for a smaller population. And so there's a greater chance those young men will be unemployed, and therefore, the insurrectionary activity becomes more attractive and less costly.
5.50: So the calculation is, well, I don't have much to gain in the labor market, and I have very little to lose by joining one of these insurrectionary movements, plus younger men, testosterone, and all of that. They are involved in more violence. So if we look at this map of the world, we can see that much of sub-Saharan Africa, the average age is below 20, and much of Southeast Asia, it's below 30. So is that very young age structure then going to be conducive to more violence?
5.51: What are the other factors we might look at? One of them is religiosity, perhaps. Is that going to be a contributing factor? The share of people who say religion is very important to them is higher in some countries. But again, that doesn't seem to a perfect correlation either. So we see it quite high in sub-Saharan Africa and Southeast Asia. Islam, some have argued that a lot of the conflicts have taken place recently in Muslim parts of the world, and that's mainly North Africa, Middle East, Arabia, into Turkey. But again, it's not a perfect match . We can see a lot of the conflict has actually occurred in sub-Saharan African countries that are not Muslim. And so, how well does that explain? It explains for Syria, perhaps for Yemen. It doesn't explain as well for Ethiopia, for Congo, and so forth .
5.52: Another factor that comparative politics scholars might look at is state penetration. How well established is a state in terms of having control over peripheral areas? Because that state penetration and control and monopoly of violence is very important, according to Hobbes and according to Pinker. You need that state authority to be able to tamp down private violence. But in states that were founded more recently, authority, particularly in the peripheral areas of a country, how much does the writ of the Iraqi government run in the Kurdish regions, or of the Syrian government run in the Kurdish regions of Syria? Perhaps not as much, especially if those regions are mountainous or in some way, if the terrain is inhospitable.
5.53: The founding date of the state, we can see that most of the states in this tropical belt , sorry, in the tropical belt outside of Latin America, but Africa into Asia, those are post- colonial states with recent founding dates. And in some cases, these are weak, in some cases, failed states like Somalia, you could argue, or Afghanistan, relatively weak state authority . Where you have weak state authority, you're more likely to have civil wars. Now, it's a bit of a chicken and an egg because civil wars weaken state authority. But in general, if you have a weak dysfunctional state, arguably you're going to get more groups trying to break away or rebel or engage in civil war.
5.54: And that then brings me to this article by David Laitin and James Fearon, which is one of the most cited. It looks at the determinants of civil war onset. That is—what we're trying to explain, the outcome variable, is the likelihood that a country will experience a civil war onset , so the start of a civil war. That is what we're trying to explain. The factors that we're looking at here are a whole range of factors . This is, again, that modeling exercise. Similar to the one that we did when we looked at voting behavior, where we've got 200 countries over a span of about 50 years, and we've got a whole series of characteristics of these countries—how large they are, how mountainous they are, how rich they are, are they democracies or not , how ethnically and religiously diverse are they?
5.55: And so those are thrown into this model, and we can see a couple of factors are jumping out as predictors of civil war. Anything with three stars on this chart is a more important predictor. So one of those is per capita income. Poorer countries are more likely to experience a civil war. So that seems to be the most important factor, along with the proportion of a country that is mountainous. So that gets to this idea that the more mountainous a country, the more rebels are able to hide in places that the national army can't get at them. So you need to have a territorial-based amount, an effective military rebellion. So a mountainous country with low per capita income is more likely to experience a civil war onset.
5.56: There are a couple of other important factors. Being an oil exporter makes you more prone to civil war, and that gets to greed-based explanations for civil war, this idea that wars are fought to control lootable resources. But also we see some evidence for this new state hypothesis, that the more recently the state was founded, which is perhaps correlated with weaker state authority, the greater the risk of civil war. Now, in terms of democracy versus authoritarianism , democracies are actually not less likely to experience a civil war onset, but anocracies, which are the semi-democracies, are more likely to experience a civil war onset. Again, that perhaps speaks to instability, anarchy, that whole equation. Where you have instability of the regime, that seems to be associated with more violence as well .
5.57: Now, in terms of ethnic and religious fractionalization, Fearon and Laitin didn't find the ethnic fractionalization to be a significant predictor, but they did find the number of religious groups and the spread of religious groups, the more such groups, the more violence. Now, other papers have, instead of testing ethnic fractionalization , total diversity, they have tested for ethnic polarization, which is where you have two groups that are relatively large. And Sri Lanka would be an example of that. If you have two groups that are relatively large, then that, in many papers, a number of papers have found that to be a risk also of civil war. Whereas Tanzania, with its hundreds of small groups , presents actually a lower risk of civil war.
5.58: The other finding some papers show is, when the regime, like in Syria, is controlled by an ethnic minority, or Iraq, before under Saddam Hussein, by an ethnic or religious minority, that is also an elevated risk of civil conflict. Just stepping back for a minute to return to Pinker, Pinker's argument was an optimistic one, that the level of violence in the world is declining over time. War is declining. That optimistic view of the world was also held by people like Francis Fukuyama and Matt Ridley. So Fukuyama's argument is that a lot of violence was being sublimated into capitalism. So instead of showing your manhood through war, you're showing it through accumulation of resources, and there was this pacification.
5.59: This was occurring in the '90s. When Fukuyama was writing in the '90s, this was post-1989 . We're seeing a rise in the number of democracies, decline in the number of civil wars. A very optimistic view of the world. It's been criticized a lot, but still remains a very valuable book to read and an important argument to understand. So the idea of The End of History, by Francis Fukuyama. Against that optimistic view that violence is declining, war is declining, yes, there'll be a few blips. Yes, there may be a Russia- Ukraine, there may be an Ethiopia, but basically the trend is downward.
5.60: There are those who say, well, actually we're entering into a more dangerous phase in the world, partly perhaps due to population pressure, the increase in population in the developing world, coupled with global warming and climate change and pressure on resources, these Malthusian arguments by people such as Robert Kaplan or Thomas Homer-Dixon. Their argument is actually you might see large-scale migrations as a result of climate change and population pressure, as well as disease and other factors such as Ebola. So that is a more pessimistic outlook, that we are entering a more dangerous phase in the world.
5.61: Then there are writers such as John Gray in the pessimistic tradition who would say, actually, those who talk about the end of history are implying that humans are making moral progress . So Pinker's book is also a book about humanity making moral progress over time. And John Gray is very much a skeptic of that. He would argue that there's only a cyclicality, and there is no linear moral progress. And those who believe in that are essentially believing in a religion, that they believe history has a direction. And this idea of history having a direction is wrong-headed, according to John Gray.
5.62: So if we take the recent period, no doubt we see there has been an increase in violence in the world since about 2006, and that would be perhaps evidence for the John Grays of this world. On the other hand, if you take the very long view, going back to hunter- gatherer days, you could say, well, this is just really a drop in the ocean compared to the number of people that were killed in those hunter-gatherer societies . So who has it right, the optimists or the pessimists? Pinker and Fukuyama seeing a decline of violence in human history. Their argument would be, yes, there can be temporary reversals and blips, but that should not be used as evidence that the theory is incorrect.
5.63: And Pinker argues there are a number of structural features that are embedded in human history that are inclining in the direction of greater pacification, most notably perhaps commerce, but also value change. Commerce and value change playing a role in pacification. So greater interdependency, meaning less likelihood of countries going to war against each other.
5.64: So that leaves us with the question, really, to end this lecture—which way do we think things are going to go? Obviously, there's views about the long term, and then there's views about our lifetime. Maybe we have a different conclusion depending on the time horizon . But one of the big questions is whether there are these structural features that are driving human societies towards lower levels of violence. Just as a last coda, because it's one of my areas of specialty, another argument is that because the population of the world is getting older, even in the developing world, we're seeing a drop in fertility rates. Because of the older nature of the population, the risk of violence is going to be lower, as we have fewer people in that 18 to 30 age range. Lecture 6: Designing Democracy At a glance — Designing democracy.
6.1: OK, so today we're going to be speaking about the design of democracy in ethnically divided or heterogeneous societies. If you recall, going back to the first couple of lectures when we talked about different democratic systems and electoral systems, a lot of the political philosophy around democracy and liberal democracy came from relatively ethnically homogenous Western societies that could, at least in theory, make the assumption that there were not significant group differences within a society. You could talk about individual citizens as being somewhat homogenous.
6.2: But most of the world actually isn't like that. The question is, as you expand democracy from the core countries of Western Europe and North America to other societies, how can you actually adapt it to work in those societies? Some people argue that democracy will never work in such societies, but others are more hopeful. They just would argue that you need to have a certain kind of democracy to work. In terms of the questions that we'll be addressing today, one of the questions is to do with the, if you like, quote- unquote, "imperfect overlap" between ethnicity and politics. That's really what drives nationalism, this idea that there are either multiple ethnic groups within one political roof or one ethnic group is divided into many different political units, as is the case with the Arabs today or what was the case with the Germans and Italians in the 19th century.
6.3: How do we manage ethnic diversity in a particular society? I mean, this is partly about not having ethnic violence and civil war, and it's also partly about having a legitimate state and a democracy in an ethnically diverse or divided-type of society. These ethnic questions are tricky because maybe where you have rich or poor, you can agree to have a certain level of taxation and welfare spending. Perhaps those economic issues are easier to resolve than zero-sum issues such as, who gets this territory? Is Western Sahara part of Morocco or not, for example? Is Kosovo part of Serbia in any way or not? These are symbolic questions, and they raise more zero-sum type issues where people tend to think, "No, symbolically, this is ours, not theirs." Israel, Palestine, another example. Non-tradable issues, it's harder to arise at those sorts of accommodations.
6.4: There are two major approaches to managing ethnic difference in a society. One is to eliminate ethnic difference, and the other is to manage difference. It might sound just from those words that eliminate is morally awful and manage is very good. But as we'll see, in fact, there are good and bad forms of both elimination and management. It's not as simple as that. There are both democratic and non-democratic forms also of elimination and management.
6.5: In terms of, and this is using some of the work of Brendan O'Leary and John McGarry in terms of enumerating these different methods. In terms of elimination of difference, you obviously have violent non-democratic methods like genocide that clearly eliminates ethnic difference within a society. Ethnic cleansing, or what's called forced mass population transfer—and those of you who are old enough to remember the war in former Yugoslavia, this was a technique that was being used there. But it has been used by many countries and civilizations, over many millennia, to create a more homogenous population.
6.6: Now we move to the more democratic forms of elimination, and these would include partition or self-determination or secession. So, allowing Scotland, Quebec, to secede, there's nothing undemocratic about that. If Scotland and Wales left, and you just had England, that would be a less diverse society. It wouldn't necessarily be an undemocratic thing if it was voted for by the Scots or—the Welsh, it's unlikely, but the Scots. Then we last get to integration or assimilation of groups, which can be coercive, but it can also be voluntary and therefore perfectly compatible with democracy. Those are also methods of elimination.
6.7: The second group of methods are to do with managing existing difference. And we also have non-democratic and democratic forms of managing ethnic difference, rather than trying to eliminate it. One method could be hegemonic control. If you think about the Sunni dominance under Saddam in Iraq, or the Assad regime, which is Alawi, their dominance over Syria—these are examples of one group largely controlling a society. Another extreme example might be the Americo-Liberians. These are Liberians that are descended from American slaves who emigrated and formed the elite of Liberia, and they controlled Liberia for many, many years.
6.8: So this idea of hegemonic control, or this question of ethnic democracy in places like Israel, Estonia, Malaysia, where you may have a democracy and everybody has participation, but one ethnic group is clearly privileged, perhaps in the constitution of the state. Arbitration as a means of managing ethnic differences, which is a way in which sometimes outside countries or agencies, sometimes internal, seek to manage conflict between groups.
6.9: Option three under management is federalism, which is that you give different groups their own federal territory or federal unit or canton, and that's a way in which you manage difference. So some powers are given to the federal units, some powers are maintained at the center. And there's also a non-territorial form of federalism, which is used in Lebanon and Northern Ireland, called consociationalism. It's where the groups are not spatially delineated, and so it's very difficult to use federal units. We'll get into more detail on all of these next.
6.10: In terms of methods of regulating conflict and hopefully implementing democracy, these are ideal types. And very often, what you see is that a mixture of those—we had eight types there, eight or nine types. You often get a mixture of those used. In the case of Tito in the former Yugoslavia, there was a mix of control. Clearly, the Serbs were a dominant group in a way. Tito's regime kept very tight control on the expression of group difference, but there were also elements of power-sharing within the regime. Over American history, we've seen some genocide, some control, some integration.
6.11: In terms of methods for eliminating differences, this is where countries try and reduce ethnic difference within their territory. So this is a way of eliminating ethnic difference within the territory. And the methods listed on this slide, genocide, forced mass population transfer, partition or secession, integration and assimilation. I've already gone over broadly what those are. Just deal with some of these. The first is ethnic cleansing. I'm going to leave genocide aside because genocide is genocide. There's not much to say it, other than it's awful.
6.12: But in terms of some of these other means of eliminating difference, if you take forced mass population transfer or ethnic cleansing—for example, the Serbs in Bosnia in the war in the former Yugoslavia—as a way of changing facts on the ground to make a territory seem like it is controlled by your ethnic group and give you territorial claims, make your territorial claims more easy. Whereas if you have another ethnic group there that claims that it is, essentially that that land is its ethnic homeland, it is difficult. Particularly if they have buried their dead in the territory for many years and have a certain emotional attachment to the land, it's harder to make a territorial claim to that land. So ethnic cleansing is a strategy that was used by the Serbs, for example.
6.13: That can be distinguished from agreed population exchanges, which are not the same as ethnic cleansing, which are forced mass population transfers. So the Greek-Turk, Greek-Turkey population exchange after World War I is an example of this agreed mass population transfer. It's not the same as people being forced out. It's worth also noting that ethnic cleansing often does not terminate an ethnic conflict. The Chechens in USSR were deported in large numbers, but that didn't prevent the Chechen wars from occurring. Ethnic cleansing has been used by empires. So for example, the Russian Empire in the Caucasus tried to ethnically cleanse Muslim populations from its territories.
6.14: There's also a fuzzy line between mass population transfer and legitimate deportation and immigration control. There's a slide here about 1.7 million undocumented Afghans being ordered to leave Pakistan recently. We've seen in the past large numbers of Mexicans being deported from the US in the 1950s. And so there's a difference, perhaps, between legitimate enforcement of borders and deportation of illegal immigrants versus actual ethnic cleansing. So if you take what's going on amongst the Rohingya, Rohingya in Myanmar being forced out, that would be an example of ethnic cleansing because they actually have been living in the area for many generations. And then you have situations that are in between. So there is this question about legitimate residents versus illegitimate residents. And depending on whether a resident is legitimate or illegitimate, the deportation is a violation of human rights or not a violation of human rights.
6.15: Option C, in terms of elimination, is partition or secession. Here's a picture of Israel- Palestine. Partition, the so-called two-state solution, would be an example of partition, where you would have a territory for the Palestinians and a territory for the Jews, or at least for Israel, which Israel does include 20% Israeli-Arab population, which doesn't live in the territories. Partition is an example of where, if you took Israel-Palestine as one unit, clearly with the Palestinians, it's maybe 50-50. I don't have the exact number between Arab and Jew. If you did a two-state solution, it would be more like 80-20 in Israel, 80% Jewish. And in the territories, it would be something like 100% Arab or thereabouts. So, partition is one way in which you could imagine the degree of ethnic difference being reduced within Israel-Palestine.
6.16: Another method, of course, could be secession. I mean, you could imagine secession and partition being somewhat similar. So if, let's say, the territories, the Palestinian territories, seceded and formed their own state, then that would be equivalent functionally to partition. Another example of partition is Czechoslovakia being partitioned into Czech Republic and Slovakia, so-called Velvet Divorce. Sometimes these are peaceful, like Czechs and Slovaks. Other times, they involve a lot of bloodletting, like Pakistan, India. It's a very difficult question as to, people say, well, the partition of India was a terrible thing because it led to millions of people dying. I guess the question is always one of, what is the counterfactual? If you tried to keep Pakistan in India, would you have had less violence?
6.17: Northern Ireland, Ireland, that's another similar question. Clearly, there's been civil war, an attempt to acquire the northern six counties for the Republic of Ireland. That's what the IRA was all about and the troubles in Northern Ireland was all about. Now, you might say, well, it would have been better not to partition Ireland, but then you might have had different kinds of violence emerging, which could have been worse. These are the kinds of questions that one has to think about when we think about managing ethnic conflict. Sometimes partition is the least worst. It can be done in bad ways, in good ways. Sometimes holding plebiscites at a detailed level might be a way of drawing the lines between—so, a key question is where you draw the lines.
6.18: As in Israel, where is that border wall? Where should it go? Should it, perhaps, include some parts of the territories, but then parts of Israel go to Palestine, and so there's perhaps an exchange based on where Arabs and Jews are living? These are questions that are always raised in the peace agreements. Does Scotland have the right to self- determination and to leave Britain? But then would the Highland Scots have a right to leave Scotland? Who determines which peoples have this right of self-determination? What is the relevant unit also in which they should exercise self-determination? Should the parts of Scotland that perhaps don't identify as Scottish or are not separatist, should they be included, like the borders region of Scotland? Should they be included in the unit that secedes? Should the English-speaking parts of Quebec be included in the part? If Quebec were to secede, should the English-speaking parts go with it, or should they stay with Canada, is an important question. And what constitutes a majority? What is the number that you require in a referendum for independence?
6.19: There is a question also around anarchy in the world because we saw that when empires break up and new states are created and when there's anarchy, that's when we see a large increase in violence and instability. And does secession produce copycat secessions and a domino effect? Generally, the UN is opposed to secession; most countries don't want secession within their own borders. It's worth saying also that over 90% of the world's countries have at least some ethnic minorities, so there are almost no ethnically homogenous countries. However, about 70% of the world has an ethnic majority of at least 50%, and 80% of the world has an ethnic majority or plurality of at least 40%. So most countries have an ethnic majority and some minorities.
6.20: And most of those minorities are not immigrant minorities. They're mostly native minorities. And native minorities are actually the groups that are involved in violent rebel movements. This is a question then that the international lawyers and international system thinks about very carefully. They allowed East Timor to become a country in the United Nations. They're not going to allow Taiwan or Somaliland or Kosovo easily to become a country because they don't really want to encourage—the international norms are such that they want to discourage the creation of new countries.
6.21: That brings us along to option D, which is assimilation and integration. This is a picture of Ellis Island in the US. It's famous for immigrants coming to the US. The policy at the time was very much one of Americanization or assimilation. There's a difference between integration and assimilation, in that integration is seen as just, as long as you are working and are loyal to the state, participate politically, what you do in private is your own business, and you can have your own ethnic identity, and you don't actually have to become part of the ethnic us. You can be ethnically separate, but as long as you are integrated politically and economically.
6.22: Assimilation, however, usually carries a meaning of something deeper, which is that you are also culturally and probably, in your identity, becoming the same as the ethnic majority population. Now, there are different levels and degrees of assimilation. It could be that you speak the language, but you maintain your religion and your separate ethnic identity, or it could be that you change, ultimately, your children change their ethnic identity and become like the host society. It's also a question of what are you integrating into? Do you integrate into a very civic, political-style national identity that is less thick? It's kind of a thinner national identity based perhaps around some common values, maybe certain bits of history, versus do you assimilate to a more ethnic national identity?
6.23: Hungary is a country where there actually was a lot of melting and assimilation between the late 1700s and the 20th century of different groups into the Hungarian nation, similarly with Turkey. But the national identity they were expected to assimilate into was actually one that had a very ethnic cast. When I say ethnic, I mean based on myths of genealogical descent and origin. Whereas perhaps in Britain or the US, there's maybe a set of values, a constitution, a certain version of history, but it's a thinner and lighter, more civic identity.
6.24: Now, you can have one-way or two-way assimilation, where the immigrants are expected to completely conform to the host society, or you have two-way assimilation, which is favored more by liberal progressives, which is that both are adapting to each other. The immigrants adapt to the host. The host changes a bit to the immigrants. That's the so-called two-way assimilation. There are state-led high-pressure forms of assimilation, like the Russification in the Tsarist Empire, the Turkification in the Turkish Republic under Atatürk, and even Americanization in the early 20th century, which was arguably more high-pressure.
6.25: There's different theories of assimilation. Milton Gordon's book, Assimilation in American Life, it offers a seven-step process where you go from getting a job assimilating to the economy to then politically, culturally, speaking the language, but eventually, marrying in, changing identity. That is the deepest layer of assimilation that takes place. It's worth saying assimilation theory is no longer talked about very much in academia, with a few exceptions. But there are a few writers, such Richard Alba, Rogers Brubaker, who do talk about it, but it is something that has largely been avoided by academia more recently.
6.26: There can be liberal and illiberal forms of assimilation. In many countries, let's say, in the interwar period, the countries that were on the winning side in World War I, Romania, for example, which because they were on the winning side, they got more territory and they got ethnic minorities as part of that territory. So, Hungarians, Hungary was on the losing side and lost two-thirds of its territory. So a lot of Hungarians wound up in other countries. And the Germans lost as well. So Germans wound up in other countries as well, German minorities. And some of these countries tried to high-pressure assimilate the members of these losing ethnic groups like Germans and Hungarian by preventing them from speaking their language in school, for example.
6.27: So you have a high-pressure assimilation of groups that are, in many ways, native or indigenous to the territories they're living in. This isn't immigrants we're talking about. These are long-settled groups that consider themselves native to the territory. And that generates a lot of resistance. Arguably was a factor, perhaps, in causing World War II, but not the main factor, but it arguably was an irritant. There's a whole debate around assimilation versus multiculturalism, that this idea of whether you can have unity and diversity, is it possible to have unity with diversity, or does it have to tip one way? The diversity is either going to lead to disunity, or the unity is going to lead to less diversity. It's very difficult to have both at the same time.
6.28: Also, the question is, can you actually pursue, let's say, integration, without that eventually becoming assimilation? If people are integrated in the labor market and they're participating politically, do they not then take the next step after learning the language and also move closer to the host population through intermarriage and identity change?
6.29: In terms of means of integration and assimilation, both coercive and non-coercive. We have voluntary assimilation, people choosing to assimilate, or you have state-led coercive assimilation as well. What are the means that are adopted by states? Could be integrated schooling, language instruction, civics and history lessons, forced integration, or integration of workplace and public facilities. In terms of assimilation, and particularly high-pressure means of assimilation, for example, in Bulgaria, in the 1990s, there was a law that forced all of the Turkish-origin Muslim Bulgarians to adopt a Christian surname. That would be an example of forced assimilation or banning the use of other languages. Now, of course, if you go back in history, this is what a lot of countries did. France banned the speaking of Catalan and Provençal and all these dialects as it was building its nation.
6.30: So assimilation has been a common theme in nation-building through the 18th, 19th centuries. The aim is to create a single history, a single language, single school system. Going back to the 19th century, this was to make sure that people paid tax and served in the military and were loyal to the country. OK, so I've talked a lot about the elimination of differences through secession, partition, assimilation, integration. We're now going to move to regimes that manage differences, where rulers accept this is a diverse country, and we've got to manage that and work with the grain of that diversity somehow. There are different ways to do it. So there are undemocratic ways to do it.
6.31: Most empires in the world, like the Ottomans, the Habsburgs, they were essentially hegemonic control systems, what O'Leary and McGarry would call hegemonic control systems, where you had a dominant ethnic group, the Austro-Germans in the Austro- Hungarian Empire, the Ottoman Turks in the Ottoman Empire. This was the dominant group in the Empire, and they controlled other groups. They weren't trying to assimilate everybody necessarily into being, let's say, speaking German, although there were phases of assimilation, but generally, they weren't trying to build a nation. They accepted, "We're an empire, we have many different groups, but we want to control these groups."
6.32: And so this is a hegemonic control approach. Within countries, you also tend to have dominant ethnic groups in many cases. And sometimes those groups are minorities, like in Syria with the Assad regime, the Alawi sect, which is semi-Shia, is dominant in Syria, and they are controlling the Sunni Arab majority of Syria.
6.33: In terms of other methods, we have arbitration, which is where you have often an external, not always, but often an external auditor imposing a settlement on groups within a country. Federalism, which involves devolving power to federal units which approximate to the different ethnic groups in your society. Sometimes that can involve very small units, cantons, as in Switzerland, where you devolve power to the cantonal level. Switzerland, you actually have power at the communal, the cantonal level, and the federal level.
6.34: Option four is a non-territorial form of devolution of power, known as consociationalism, which is a way of sharing power between ethnic groups that are not territorialized, like Northern Ireland. The groups are mixed together, like Lebanon. They're somewhat separate, but they're also somewhat mixed. And so you can't create federal units easily in Lebanon without having a lot of people stuck in the wrong unit for their ethnic group. Just working through these different methods, we start with hegemonic control, which has been very common through world history and in those great multi-ethnic empires, such as the Tsarist-Ottoman Empire, but also the Soviet Union, if we can think of the Soviet Union as an empire.
6.35: Now, some states, you can look at Indonesia and say, "Is that an empire in some way?" Well, it's not an empire, but it's a state where you have a Javanese majority, and then you have all these minorities in the islands that are—now, to what extent are they under the control of the Javanese majority? But anyway, this idea of hegemonic control where you're managing groups and group differences. So you have to deal with, you have to recognize, to some degree, group rights, but you want to manage that.
6.36: There's also this term ethnic democracy or Herrenvolk democracy. Some people would argue that certain countries, yes, they offer democratic rights to minorities, but only certain groups can occupy top positions in the state. So, places like Israel, Northern Ireland under the Stormont regime, Estonia, Malaysia, et cetera. Countries where there are rights for minorities, but perhaps a titular ethnic group dominates the power structure. Arbitration is the second means of managing ethnic differences. Here we see a picture of Tony Blair, Bertie Ahern, and George W. Bush, who were all involved in the Northern Ireland peace process as arbiters. What arbitration means is that these arbiters—the Irish government, the American government, and the British government —were trying to push the unionists and nationalists to a solution in Northern Ireland. So it wasn't just saying, "We're not just going to be a go-between." That's mediation, where you're not imposing any solution.
6.37: The idea of an arbitration is the arbiter imposes, in some way, some kind of a solution or tries to get the parties using various carrots and sticks to the table. And maybe if we think of Israel-Palestine, maybe that's going to be a combination of also arbitration from the Americans. Typically, one side, so the Catholic side in Northern Ireland would see Bertie Ahern and the Irish government as, to some degree, their friends or looking out for their interests. The Protestant side, it was trickier because it wasn't obvious who was going to look out for their interests. Perhaps Tony Blair and the British government would be closer to that position, although I would say the unionists didn't have as much trust in Britain as the nationalists did in Bertie Ahern.
6.38: And similarly, if we were to take Israel-Palestine, the question is, so who's going to look out for the interest of the Palestinians? It would probably be a Sunni Arab state. And who is going to look out for the interests of the Jews and of Israel? That's probably the Americans. And so the Americans and one of the major, or a group of the major Arab states would be the arbiters if they were trying to get those parties to agree to some a solution.
6.39: There are different kinds of arbiters. You can have an internal, actually a member, somebody within the country who is trusted by both sides, or you have external arbiters. Sometimes you have a so-called father of the nation, like Julius Nyerere in Tanzania or Mahatma Gandhi in India. Gandhi may have been trusted by both the Muslims and the Hindus. In Canada, it might be that the native peoples trust the Canadian federal government more than the provincial governments. Provincial governments might be looking out for resource interests. So maybe there's more trust in the federal government than in the provinces. So there's a way in which the federal government can be seen as arbitrating between the interests of the provincial governments and the natives.
6.40: You then have external forms of arbitration, which could be, as we saw in Northern Ireland, there could be states that the parties trust. So maybe the Israelis trust the Americans, and the Palestinians trust the Egyptians or the Saudis or the Turks. So you maybe have external states, but you can also have supranational bodies like the United Nations, European Union, NATO, which can be the external arbiters and can be involved in peace agreements. And so we saw that. We see different combinations. Very often you see, so in the case of South Tyrol, which is part of Italy, which is an ethnically German part of Italy, there was negotiation between the Austrian and Italian governments, a condominium between the two.
6.41: The whole point of arbitration is to arrive at some kind of final arrangement to resolve the territorial conflicts. That arrangement is going to have to involve something more than the arbitration, because arbitration is kind of, like, just a process. It's not actually a constitutional way of dealing with powers between groups. In addition to arbitration, you need another method, which is typically going to be federalism, sometimes dominant control, but either federalism or consociationalism. In this last section, I'm going to talk a bit about federalism and consociationalism. So federalism really is about devolving power to federal units. In Britain, we have this term devolution. It's not full federalism because the devolved parliaments in Wales and Scotland have some powers, but there's a lot of power still at Westminster. Whereas in Germany, the Länder have a lot more power, and they're seen as more co-equal.
6.42: US states, Canadian provinces, all have power, so the Canadian provinces have power over education and resources. Often, the federal center has power over foreign policy. There's sometimes a splitting of tax-raising powers. The Canadian provinces have provincial sales tax revenues, but your income tax goes to the federal government. Cantonization differs from federalism in a number of ways, as in Switzerland. Cantons are often smaller. They can involve asymmetrical powers where certain cantons have more powers than other cantons, and that's allowed within the system. To some degree in Spain, there are different sets of powers allocated to different regions. Quebec, for example, has certain special powers that the other provinces don't have within the Canadian federal system, powers over language and culture.
6.43: There's also a difference between systems where the power resides mainly at the federal center. Britain, of course, power is mainly at the federal center. There's some power to the Scottish and Welsh and Northern Irish assemblies, but it's more power at the center. Other systems are more devolved. They're called confederations. The power is more down with the federal units.
6.44: Assessing federalism, how well has it dealt with ethnic tensions and conflicts in the world? In so many of these cases, it's very difficult to provide a definitive answer. So federalism has a mixed record of success. It seems to have worked to some degree to resolve conflict in certain countries. You can look at Canada, the federal system there. You can look at the federal system in India. Has that reduced ethnic tensions, religious tensions? One argument, if you take this country, one argument is that devolution has helped to deal with some of the grievances of the Welsh and the Scots. But the other argument would be that, while creating those parliaments gave political entrepreneurs, the regional nationalists, a power base and an institutional framework and a whole set of concretized, say, Scottish nationalism, and therefore, it made it more for the country to break up.
6.45: Others would say, actually, it's drawn the sting. If you didn't allow for the devolution of power to Scotland and Wales, we'd have a bigger problem with Scottish and Welsh nationalism. In Canada, it's worth saying, by the way, that the Quebec nationalist movement, they came very close in the 1995 referendum. I think it was 49.5% vote. So it came very close. But since then, separatist sentiment has declined to the low 30s. You could argue perhaps that the devolution of powers, that the federal system in Canada was able to adapt and allow Quebec to have most of what it wanted without seceding. So maybe that's a success.
6.46: In other cases, however, it would appear that federalism hasn't solved the problem in a place like Nigeria, where the devolution of power to the federal units is fine, but the problem is that you're never going to get ethnically homogenous federal units, and where there are minorities who find themselves suddenly in a federal unit where it's mostly the other group, you then get discontent. You might have a country like Nigeria, this is very multi-ethnic at the national level, but when you break it down to the federal units, there may be two groups, not 15. When there's two groups, the chance of conflict is greater than when there's a whole bunch of groups and there are shifting coalitions that are possible.
6.47: OK, I want to finally talk about a non-territorial form of federalism called consociationalism. It's a big word. This is the system, the democracy that you need to craft in a society where the ethnic groups are not neatly delineated. In Canada, most of the French are in Quebec. In India, you have different states where the groups are collected territorially. But in Northern Ireland or Lebanon, you don't have that. You have the groups mixed together very much. If group rights and group identities are really important in those societies, which they are, and people vote on ethnic lines for ethnic parties, then you need to have a different design. This is where this idea of non- territorial federalism, or consociationalism, comes about.
6.48: It has four features, and we could do a whole lecture on this, so this is going to be very quick. But one of the features is a proportional representation system, rather than a first-past-the-post. So, all the groups are represented in the legislature and feel that they're being listened to. The second is the executive or the cabinet is not based on just one party, like in Britain or the US; the party that wins forms the cabinet. No, in the consensual system, it's made up of all the different parties. And so the type of democracy is not meant to be adversarial but consensual. In addition, there are certain powers that are devolved to the ethnic groups. Instead of devolving power to federal units, you're devolving power to groups. Rights to language, perhaps, would be one.
6.49: Then you have an emphasis on proportional employment. Northern Ireland has the 50/50 policing, Catholic-Protestant recruitment. Similarly, in other countries, it might be the civil service must reflect the population, or government spending must be proportional to the groups in the population. There's a lot of attention to fairness between groups in a consociational system. Sometimes you have the idea that you have a veto. Minorities can veto legislation; and in the Northern Ireland assembly, there's a threshold amount. No legislation can pass just on the votes of one community. There has to be a certain proportion of both communities that accept legislation for it to go forward. And that provides a check against legislation that can be seen as discriminating against one of the groups. Of course, the whole point of this is to prevent groups that feel discriminated against from losing trust in the system than trying to overthrow the system through civil war.
6.50: In terms of the success rate of consociationalism, again, it's tricky to know what would have happened if Lebanon decided to do first-past-the-post. We can't be sure what the result would be, so it's not a perfect science. We can look at the history of certain countries. We can say, well, Lebanon's had civil war from 1975 to the early '90s, and then there was a flare-up in 2006, and now we've got problems still there in Lebanon. Same with Syria. Now, is that because of the consociational system? The question is, what is the alternative? Is it for the Christians to control the country, which was sort of how it was? Is it for the Shia or the Sunni to control the country? That would arguably be worse. It's not easy to do a partition, either. In societies where you have these intermingled ethnic groups, and group identities are really important for people in the way they vote, then this may be the only option.
6.51: But there are strong criticisms as well. People who say, well, this is entrenched in ethnic identity and ethnic politics in Lebanon. One of the problems you now have is you've got these ethnic elites who are making deals amongst themselves, but neglecting the poor and the working class within each of the ethnic groups. So they get left out. And we have a dysfunctional, corrupt elite. Even though it's multi-ethnic, it's a multi-ethnic corrupt elite in Lebanon because there's no real competition. Because one of the virtues of the first-past-the-post system is you have competition between parties on policies, whereas in a consensual system, it's smoke-filled rooms and deals stitched up. That is a criticism. But the other side of the equation is, well, what's the alternative? If you were to go for first-past-the-post in an adversarial system in Lebanon, you might be inviting violence.
6.52: Just getting to the last few slides here then, in terms of which constitutional and political design to adopt for democracies in a divided society—I mean, part of this is based on the pattern of ethnic groups in your society and how important ethnicity is for people's voting patterns. In terms of, for example, if you have mainly immigrant groups, then assimilation and integration becomes more of a possibility. If the society is mainly made up of indigenous, what are called primary ethnic groups, and that's most of the world—if it's mainly primary ethnic groups, then assimilation is much more difficult and will be resisted and contested. Almost every rebel movement, civil war, is driven in some way by a primary ethnic group, rather than a secondary or immigrant diaspora. Partly it depends on whether groups are indigenous or immigrant, but also partly depends on whether groups are territorially clustered, perhaps in India, perhaps in Nigeria, or whether they are intermingled, like in Lebanon and Northern Ireland.
6.53: We'll just look at a few cases here. Britain, where the groups are territorially located, at least the indigenous groups are territorially located, Scotland is over 80% ethnically Scottish, for example. Wales is not as homogeneously Welsh, but still, because of the territorial concentration, secession or partition is a possibility. Whereas Northern Ireland, that's not the case; the groups are too intermingled. Canada, again, is an interesting case where the English are in most of the country, east and west. Quebec, where the French are located, is compact territorially. You can imagine a secession in Quebec coming off all right and being democratic.
6.54: But on the other hand, that northern two-thirds of Quebec are indigenous-speaking or English-speaking. The immediate question that is raised with a Quebec secession is whether that northern two-thirds, which was only granted in 1912, should have the right to secede from Quebec. And that, again, leads to potential prospect of multiple secessions, or recurrent secessions, as groups secede from groups that have seceded and so on and so forth. So again, it depends. You can use federalism where groups are territorially concentrated, but not where they're intermingled.
6.55: Another example we can look at is Sudan. There was a secession. South Sudan was created as a new country and accepted into the United Nations as a recognized country. But within South Sudan, we have a range of different ethnic groups, and that has meant, well, has been the basis for a lot of civil war within South Sudan, which has a lot of the risk factors associated with civil war, such as very low income and challenging topography. What is the solution? A partition doesn't necessarily solve the problem. Having said that, there's no question there was a lot of repression from the Sudanese regime against the South Sudanese. Maybe it solved one problem, but then there is another, perhaps a vacuum of authority that is created in South Sudan, and that's behind a lot of the conflict going on there.
6.56: Iraq, a tricky case. We've got certain parts of Iraq, where the ethnic groups are territorially compact. Much of the Kurdish region, but not all of it. So you have places like Kirkuk, which are ethnically mixed. So it's difficult to easily impose a federal solution in Iraq. So there was some attempt, really, there to have a combination of certain federal powers with certain non-territorial federal elements, or consociational elements, in the Iraqi peace plan as well. And again, that's determined by whether ethnic groups are regionally concentrated or whether they're intermingled.
6.57: There's also other factors, of course, that will come into play, such as the location of oil resources. There's always a tension between drawing the borders around where your ethnic group is located and wanting to take more land, even if you don't have co- ethnics on it. So in both the case of Northern Ireland and Lebanon, Lebanon, the dominant, the ethnic majority, used to be Christian, and their view was, "Well, what is the maximum amount of territory that we can hold?" And similarly in Northern Ireland. Now, of course, there's been ethnic shifting in both of those societies since, which makes it more complicated. Nigeria, a case where groups are territorially located, but once you created those federal units, there are always cut-off minorities within the federal units, and that can create antagonism as well.
6.58: Just in terms of the condition for the success of democracy in deeply divided multi- ethnic societies, one is, to what extent are the groups territorially compact and separate so that you can create federal units? To what extent is there an ethnic majority that is demographically dominant enough that it could be a little bit flexible and a little bit more generous and not insisting on completely the same privileges as the other groups?
6.59: Demographic stability. If the groups are not shifting in composition, then it's easier to maintain a system. The problem in Lebanon is that you had a decrease in the Christian share from two-thirds down to something like 20 or 30%. And the Sunni population first increased because of Palestinian refugees, and then the Shia population increased due to higher birth rates. And so you had a change in the proportion. So the Shia were saying, "Well, we don't have as much representation as our numbers warrant because we're now a larger group than we were when Lebanon was founded." Northern Ireland, too, the shift from about two-thirds Protestant to about 50-50 has also been part of the reason for instability in Northern Ireland.
6.60: There are also other factors that can make it easier to make a society work, such as a history of political cooperation between groups and also cross-cutting cleavages. So Switzerland, for example, is very multi-ethnic. It's got Italian speakers, German speakers, French speakers, Romansh speakers, but there are other cross-cutting dimensions. So the Protestant-Catholic divide cut through both the German and the French areas. So you had French Protestants and German Protestants, and French Catholics and German Catholics. And so this cross-cutting cleavage effect tends to weaken the separatism of the different ethnic groups.
6.61: Or it could be an ideological divide between, say, socialists and liberals. So if you have these kinds of cross-cutting cleavages, that can make it easier. And so if we think of even a contemporary situation like the US and people say, "well, this is a very divided society," and it is very divided ideologically, but there's also an ethnic or racial cleavage, which to some degree cross-cuts the ideological divide. That means that the US is not as at risk of conflict as it would be if there was just one cleavage. So if all the Democrats were non-white and all of the Republicans were white, then you'd have a riskier situation, for example. But because you've got Democrats and Republicans in both groups, for the most part, then you have that cross-cut, which reduces the instability. Thank you very much.
6.62: Integration and assimilation seem to be a pertinent issue in the West. So especially even in Russia, actually, we saw something like the forced assimilation of Russian- speaking natives, for example. And you said it's not something that's researched at the moment. I was wondering, that's also something that's not spoken about in the media very much. Is that because of career-ending possibilities or emotional reasons? Or what was exactly going on there?
