Lecture 7: Evolution of the Nation-State At a glance — Evolution of the nation-state.
7.1: In this lecture I want to speak about the rise of the modern state. The world is now subdivided into almost 200 sovereign nation-states , and those states have certain properties. They have very delineated borders. They are often centralized in terms of tax collecting and public spending. And very often, they'll have a currency, common currency, common laws, that apply across the territory. One of the questions that I want to ask today is to look historically and to say, how did we get to this particular setup we have now? Another feature of today's nation-states is that they are nations that appeal to patriotism, and that the entire citizenry is involved in the nation-state, not just a small elite.
7.2: There are a number of different features of today's nation-states, and we want to ask, first of all, how did we get here? Second part of the question is whether the nation- state form can be superseded in the future, because if it's contingent on a certain accident of history, on a certain confluence of factors, then it's also possible that if that confluence of factors changes, maybe the nation-state will go out of fashion in favor of empires or city-states or something else.
7.3: We want to look at the broad sweep of history. This is a more historical topic, the rise of the modern state. We're going to go way back to those hunter-gatherer bands we talked about when we were talking about Steven Pinker's work on war and how we've seen a decline of violence from the hunter-gatherer band through the Middle Ages and into the modern period. Similarly, what we're talking about here is political evolution, and it's similar to biological evolution in a way. We can use an analogy, a move from a single-celled organism, which are our ancient ancestors, and eventually we move to complex organisms such as ourselves, where each organ has a specialized function, liver, heart, et cetera, and it's multicellular , much more complex and therefore can do a lot more things.
7.4: Similarly, you could argue with the state moving from the hunter-gatherer band through to empires and city-states and nation-states. These get more complex. Societies and politics become more complex with specialization, not just everybody hunting and gathering, but you have people who are blacksmiths, people who are rulers, religious specialists, military specialists. By specializing, you're able to create more resources and wealth in a society, and also military power. So the more complex states are able to defeat the simpler states. An empire can defeat hunter-gatherer bands quite easily.
7.5: Looking at political evolution, we want to look at various arguments for why the political organization of human societies has moved in the direction that it has. There are a number of features here. One is that the scale, moving from a small hunter- gatherer band to something very big, like an empire. Centralization of power, not just many different clans, but a central ruler, central state. The participation of the population, not just a tiny elite with slaves or peasants, but actually everybody participating in politics as a voter, for example, being able to read, not just a small number of people being able to read, but everybody.
7.6: And one of the questions is, what is it that's driving this evolution? Is it, as Marxists would claim, changes in the mode of economic production, from hunting and gathering to agriculture to industrial capitalism? Is it changes in culture ? The so-called Axial Age, when we see around 0 AD, we see the rise of Christianity and rise of Buddhism and the rise of other religions, roughly within several hundred years of this, or the Reformation, Protestant Reformation, or the Enlightenment. These sorts of cultural shifts, are they really the key to explaining the evolution of political organization? Or is it about military hard power and technology, weapons that can shoot straighter, faster, with greater impact, the efficiency of killing, going up with new military technology?
7.7: Or is it political institutions? So the rise of, for example, abureaucracy that is picked not because they are related to you, but because they actually have skills that they demonstrate in an exam, perhaps. So a more meritocratic bureaucracy . What is it that's driving the evolution of the political organization to get us to the modern state? We'll also, along the way, look at a number of other factors, including this question of national identity and patriotism, which actually wasn't always there, but is there in certain kinds of forms of political organization and not in others.
7.8: In terms of some of the critical forces that are at work in this process of evolution, one is that, in this evolutionary battle, let's just say, if it's the case that a bigger unit defeats a smaller unit because it can marshal more resources or it can specialize and create more advanced technologies, you're going to see an evolution of the system towards bigger and bigger political units. That would lead to the decline of hunter-gatherer bands and the emergence of these bigger entities. But sometimes, maybe, the big entity is like an empire; it's too big and it's unwieldy, so then decompose into smaller states . There are all kinds of evolutionary pressures that could lead us towards the size of unit that we have today, which is generally smaller than an empire, bigger than acity- state , and certainly bigger than a hunter-gatherer band.
7.9: We also have very economic and status dynamics within these societies between ruler and ruled. How much of a division and how much specialization between, say, the rulers and different groups of producers within a society? And related to this first question of warfare, to some degree, warfare is what leads to evolution . So whichever size and organization of unit is more militarily successful is likely to evolve and become the norm. And then what that can mean is that, functionally, that is in terms of what makes sense to survive in this evolutionary battle, which is really much of human history, is a kind of anarchic battle between these different entities since there wasn't international law. Largely, this was about "might makes right," in a way.
7.10: And maybe certain visionaries were able to say, actually, if we unite the tribes here in Arabia or in Switzerland or Ireland, if we unite these tribes, we're going to have better luck against the empire that's trying to crush us. And so maybe somebody got people together and said, "We've got to unite to resist the threat from Rome, from the Habsburgs , or whatever." So that could be a functionalist argument that it simply makes sense to expand the scale of political cooperation.
7.11: I also want to talk about a number of theories of political evolution. One theory is that of the mid-20th-century American sociologist , Talcott Parsons. We've already encountered briefly when talking about functionalism and where politics fits in amongst biology, chemistry, on the one hand, and sociology, economics, and other factors on the other. But what I want to look at is this evolutionary theory of Talcott Parsons to explain that shift from very simple societies to complex societies. Parsons took the analogy of the organism evolving , becoming increasingly specialized and interdependent. And he foresaw a general pattern of cultural and political evolution, a shift from ascribed identities to more achieved and meritocratic identities, from particularity to universality, and from the group to the individual.
7.12: Now, that's been criticized for essentially embodying certain kinds of American liberal capitalist biases. We can have that debate, but is that influencing this theory or not? But the argument is, therefore, there is a general movement of history, almost in a way, through this process of evolution. Parsons had 6 evolutionary universals he argued that societies went through as they became more complex and developed. These are social stratification , cultural legitimation, bureaucratic administration, money and markets, generalized legal system, and democracy. So I'll just talk through these six steps. Now, other writers had their own evolutionary steps. So Marxism has primitive, slave, feudal, capitalist, socialist. Again, seen in evolutionary terms, society is moving through these steps and that they must go through these steps as they evolve.
7.13: To talk a bit about Parsons' evolutionary steps, so the first step is social stratification . That's moving from a hunter-gatherer society where everyone's totally equal. They all hunt or gather. Typically, the women are more likely to gather, the men more likely to hunt , to a system of social stratification, where you have a group of people who don't hunt and gather. Maybe they're thinking about how to make war, improve technology. Maybe they're religious specialists. Parsons would argue that that social stratification is very important because you can't get a more advanced society without some kind of hierarchy. You need hierarchy, actually, in order to advance. And so the perfectly equal hunter-gatherer stage is not particularly conducive to evolution and advancement in political terms.
7.14: So social stratification occurs first with certain more stratified, still hunter-gatherer, but more stratified tribes, and then ultimately, agricultural civilizations, where you have the accumulation of surpluses, maybe through storing of grain resources. And that accumulation of wealth means the accumulation of a kind of capital, which then allows for investment. Rulers who can then think , "OK, if we get everybody to cooperate in an irrigation system, we can increase the agricultural yield. We need policing. We need eventually law codes." All of this generation comes out of having a group of people that aren't required to constantly be hunting and gathering, or farming. They can pay attention to forms of innovation that can improve the society.
7.15: Cultural legitimation, again, is another step in Parsons' evolutionary schema , and that really refers to religious legitimation of the existing political order. Why do these aristocrats and kings or queens get to rule? Why are there religious specialists and scribes who don't have to work in the fields like the rest of us? Well, if there's a religious explanation, then that will be accepted by the population more easily. And so that will help to legitimate the social order and the political order. Now, of course, it may legitimate a very unequal order, which can include slavery, but the argument is that this is necessary in some ways for societies to be stable and develop new technologies and advance down that evolutionary track.
7.16: Bureaucratic administration, step three, which is really referring to the kind of meritocratic recruitment into the bureaucracy that really is invented in China with the Chinese civil service examination. That is a Chinese innovation, which is subsequently taken up by Western countries as we enter into the 18th century. And so a shift from nepotism and clientelism and loyalties that are based on family ties and relatedness to the most talented people being promoted in the bureaucracies, and bureaucratization of the societies, a standardized set of rules within the bureaucracy.
7.17: Step four is money and markets, the development of money and markets. The Roman Empire , and a number of these civilizations, developed coinage . And money, that's a medium of exchange that smooths commerce. It's a store of value. It really allows the market to develop, and trade to develop more easily, as compared to a barter system. So the money and markets stage is very important for societies to gain wealth and complexity .
7.18: Then step five is having a common legal system. There was Roman law. There are different legal systems that develop as well that are standardized based on certain general principles. There's a difference between those that are universalist, principle- based legal systems coming out of that Roman law tradition, which has influenced continental European law more. Then there's the English common law tradition, which is more based on precedent and particularity . That's a different, a different trajectory of legal development.
7.19: Then the last stage was democracy, and that's, again, been criticized to some degree. Is this necessarily an evolutionary step, or is this, again, influenced by an American liberal democratic capitalist view of the world? Maybe, maybe not, but that's certainly not a stage that would be in the Marxist schema, for example. Marx has a different schema. It starts with primitive, which equates to hunter-gatherer stages, moving to feudal, capitalist, and then socialist. But the difference in Marx is that Marxism very much posits the economy, the mode of production, as the key. So changes in the techno- economic, what they would call, the Marxists would call, the base of society, that always comes first. So, culture doesn't really matter that much. Culture is kind of a second-order byproduct of the system. It's not something that changes the system.
7.20: And also Marxism isn't really about military technology and war driving the system either. That's not really central to the Marxist schema. The Marxist schema argues that everything derives from the economic changes. So the shift from hunting and gathering to agriculture to industrial capitalism is central to their understanding of political evolution . They're very focused on conflicts between different social strata in the society, which are associated with occupations. So the working-class industrial laborers , the capitalists who are the owners of capital, the conflict between those two driving forth—through the contradictions between these, we then see the emergence of a new higher-level society coming out of that conflict.
7.21: The view is that ideologies are largely there to justify the privileges of the dominant class. Now, there are then, so we've talked about the Parsonian model, the Marxist model. 7.22: It's a conquest and defense model. Smaller units are simply not able to survive in this evolutionary race. They're not adaptive , initially. Very small units like bands are not adaptive. 7.23: Charles Tilly, his theories very much are based on this idea of warfare as very important. 7.24: It also involved neutralizing divisions within the territory, within your polity, so you would have to have policing plus a military. There are then authors such as Michael Mann who says , "Well, we can't reduce everything to economics the way the Marxists do." It's not necessarily only about military evolution of technology. 7.25: So there are four potential sources of social power, and they interact, and it's impossible to reduce the story just to one of these forces. 7.26: And so there's a question as we move from lower levels of complexity to higher levels of complexity, from the tribe to the state, how that happens. 7.31: One of the arguments is that, prior to mass literacy and mass communications, this sense of patriotism didn't exist. 7.32: The argument is that, in the premodern era, the mass of the population were producers, but they were not, for example, in the military, because militaries were typically made up of mercenaries hired from elsewhere and not made up of citizens. So you had foreign mercenaries , partly because you didn't want to give your peasants guns, or not guns, but depending on which era we're talking about, you didn't want to arm them, or they might turn those weapons on you and overthrow you. 7.33: OK, I just want to talk through then some of the evolutionary stages in terms of political organization. 7.34: Very cosmopolitan in most cases. And what I mean by that is that you had many different groups of people living in the empire, and often, in many cases, even running the empire. 7.35: Moving in Europe into the feudal period, in the period from the fall of Rome up until the rise of absolutist states in the 1600s, we have this period marked by a decentralization of power. 7.36: You had city walls, typically, to protect particular principalities. And in between these small states, if you like, these cities, in between them, it was very hazardous. 7.37: Does it occur because we get the beginnings of capitalism and industrial capitalism? 7.38: Industrial capitalism requires a larger market that requires common weights and measures, common currencies, common property rights and laws. 7.39: We move to a more patrimonial, centralized situation in which states become—you get a centralization of power into larger units. Prior to the age of the modern nation-state, you may have had radically different dialects as you move from place to place. That's pushing us towards a setup in which we have a standardized coinage, laws, language, and that means more something like the nation-state.
7.40: Maybe the nation-state is more efficient because it provides a lot of things that a modern industrial economy needs. Now, we have other forms of political organization. I've talked about the industrial nation-state, but there's also the agricultural empires . Then we have city-states which occupy a distinct niche. 7.41: And so city-states occupy a new niche in the system as we get into the Middle Ages. And they are led not by a king, typically , but by some kind of a patrician elite who run the city. Now, one of the interesting things about the city-states is they do have this concept of patriotism, the idea of patria. That comes out of the city-state, not out of the empire. 7.42: Those city-states occur also in the trading cities of the Middle Ages, the Ständestaat. These are city league like the Hanseatic League in the Baltic . Germany, up near the Baltic. 7.43: You have a number of different actors in these systems that determine how they develop . In England, for example, you had the king, the nobility, and the mass of the population . 7.45: Maybe a compromised position is to say that the elites in England and France had a competition , had national identity, but maybe the mass of the population in the countryside didn't really understand that they were part of this thing called England or part of this thing called France. It's very hard to know because no one can conduct surveys and anthropological studies of the French peasantry in 1600 to know what they thought. They were illiterate. They didn't write things down. The only people who wrote things down were elites, and so we only know what elites thought. Now, elites could sometimes talk about the feelings of the peasants, but they didn't tend to do that too much. We don't have a very good idea of how the typical peasant thought about themselves and their political identification .
7.46: There are just a number of slides here showing the court of Louis XIV at Versailles, circa the year 1700, a classic example of an absolutist state that was very much engaged in competition with other states in Europe, such as England or such as Spain at the time. The notion of who had power in absolutist France, it was very clear that everything centered on the Sun King, Louis XIV. That meant that, what was the basis of the legitimacy of that regime was that Louis XIV claimed the right to rule from God. So the divine right of the king to rule came from God. It didn't come from being a representative of the people. There was no popular sovereignty, nothing like what comes with the French Revolution, nearly 100 years later.
7.47: Sovereignty accrues to the monarch as a representative of God on Earth, and that is the basis of legitimation. It's a religious legitimacy for power rather than a nationalist legitimacy for power, and it doesn't really invoke the nation-state. Now, that's not to say that there wasn't a narrative about France, and the history of France, and France against its enemies. There arguably still was a sense of national identity, even though the masses were not allowed to participate in running politics in France. This gets to a debate between two schools of thought. One school of thought that says there was a sense of national identification in the pre-modern period, and the other school of thought that says there was no such identity.
7.48: This second group, one of those in that second group, would be a sociologist by the name of Ernest Gellner, or Anthony Giddens would be another name in this group of scholars. What they would argue is that what you tended to see prior to the French Revolution was strata of elites. This would have been the nobility, the clerics within the Catholic hierarchy , for example, nobility and warriors. They identified with a religion like Christianity , which was universal, or they identified with Islam. So that's not restricted to a particular piece of territory. It's centered on a holy city like Rome, for example, or perhaps like Constantinople, sorry, Istanbul.
7.49: So you would have this imperial city with this universal religion. And these cosmopolitan elites were quite happy to marry across language lines. They didn't care so much what your language was and whether you were of this ethnic background or that ethnic background. What mattered for them was the status of being elite. So that's all they cared about. If you were elite and you had the same religion, then you were OK in a way in this system. So they had these kind of broad, very cosmopolitan —when I say cosmopolitan, I mean identities that are not particularistic, but are based on universal faiths, like Islam or Christianity that are very big. They're identifying with all of Christendom, all of the Dar al-Islam , the very large entities.
7.50: Then you have the peasants who are living in their villages who speak dialects that are maybe hard to understand , even several hundred miles away. And they never leave their village or wander very far from it. And they have no conception of the nation, in any way. That is the social structure and the identity structure of the premodern period, according to what are known as modernist theorists of nationalism. Against that are those who say, well, actually, we can see in the writings of a lot of the elites of this time a very pronounced national consciousness. And so the only question is how far down the social scale that national consciousness went. And in fact, the word nation derives from Latin and was used in Rome. The word ethnos for ethnicity comes from ancient Greek, which was used. So these have long lineages, and there's a lot of mention of nations and peoples in the Bible and by elites.
7.51: So clearly, there is evidence then for some sense of premodern national identity, but there are some evidence of people who've gone into these local villages and found that the locals really knew nothing about the history of France, let's say. People in a Breton village, when asked, "When was the French Revolution?", they would say, "Oh, yes, a long time ago." There is evidence that, in fact, these villagers and these provincials really didn't have a sense of national identity. So there's merit to both of these arguments .
7.52: And finally, we then, we've talked through the patrimonial empires , the city-states. We entered into a decentralized feudal period, recentralizing into the absolutist state. And then finally, we get to the modern nation-state, which has a number of characteristics. It has the same centralization that you got in the early empires like Rome, but it has a number of features that you find in the city-states, such as a sense of patriotism and citizen participation. It's a combination of features that you find in empires and city- states. But in terms of scale, most modern nation-states are smaller than those large, sprawling empires . They're also more culturally homogenous than the older empires.
7.53: One of the questions we might ask is, is this the final, is this the end of history, the final form of human political organization? Or are we likely to be moving towards either something larger, so regional blocs like the European Union, for example, or ASEAN, if we take Asia, or are we going to be moving to something smaller, like a modern version of city-states? And that's a question that we can talk about more when we talk about globalization in the next lecture. Thank you. Lecture 8: Navigating Globalization At a glance — Navigating globalization.
8.1: Welcome. So last time we talked about the evolution of human political organization, from the hunter-gatherer band through to large agricultural empires like Rome, through feudalism, to the absolutist state, and then the modern nation-state, along the way detouring and talking about city-states as well. And just at the end, we touched upon the possibility of superseding the nation-state to perhaps moving towards something bigger or smaller as a new form of human political organization. So today, what I want to address is this whole question of globalization. Is globalization really spelling the end of the contemporary nation-state? And are we going to be moving into a global world, or at least something that is larger than the nation-state?
8.2: Let's just talk about globalization. Globalization is a very new word. The term globalism and globalization only date from 1960, though the word global is 400 years old, but the word cosmopolitanism is much, much older. And there are cosmopolitan philosophers from ancient Greece, for example, and so the Cynics and Stoics, for example. The idea of cosmopolitanism means "the world is my city." And that's kind of a political philosophy that is really about identifying with the world as your political and cultural entity. So that's got a longer history. So I kind of want to look a little bit at both of these, but I'll focus mainly on the, on the globalization angle.
8.3: This discourse really gets a shot in the arm with the Canadian media theorist Marshall McLuhan's work on the global village. He has this term, "global village", coined in 1962, and this was the emergence of television and seeing the potential for television to unite people across borders. Now we might say, you know, 1962, television was, you know, maybe one or two channels in certain countries, so it was hardly the Internet. And of course, since, we've seen much more global forms of communication. But even in 1962, there were prophets who foresaw this idea of a global consciousness, which McLuhan described as being synchronized, simultaneous, and global. So everybody living in the same moment anywhere on the planet and tied in with that kind of more liberal individualism, that idea of being detached from groups like nations and becoming part, just an individual floating in a global consciousness.
8.4: Is this a utopian dream connected to that older cosmopolitanism, or is it actually a reality driven by technology? And the argument of McLuhan was no, technology is inevitably moving us towards this more globalized consciousness. So we want to assess the globalization argument on several dimensions. One cultural, the other economic, the other political. And so we have this debate which emerges and becomes really strong in the 1990s in the wake of the end of the Cold War. There was a certain optimism around, we've superseded the Cold War division and we're moving towards a more globalized world.
8.5: Globalization is defined by the sociologist, British sociologist Anthony Giddens, as, quote, "the intensification of worldwide social relations which link distant localities." David Held defines it as "the extent, intensity, velocity, and impact of worldwide interconnectedness." So there's two kind of concepts there. One is extent, so going beyond the nation-state, across national borders, globally, so moving the scale of human existence to a global level, and then intensity, quicker, faster, and more intense communications along those more globalized networks. Within the globalization debate, you have two camps, in a way. You've got the globalists and, yes, that is a term that is used thousands and thousands of times in academia. It is not a conspiracy term. You have the globalists and you have the skeptics.
8.6: And within the globalists, you have some subfields. You have the more neoliberal capitalist globalists, such as Kenichi Ohmae, who had formerly worked for McKinsey, and you have the more social democratic or third-way globalists, such as David Held, Anthony Giddens, Ulrich Beck, or Daniele Archibugi, just to take a number of examples. These would be social democrats, but who envision social democracy operating at a global scale. And then you have a series of skeptics. I've listed a few here. Michael Mann, who we encountered last lecture; Paul Hirst, who actually taught at the university I used to work at, Birkbeck; Grahame Thompson; Anthony Smith. These are only some of the skeptics of globalization.
8.7: So in terms of the globalization hypothesis, we have three major vectors of globalization. One is the economy or the material sector. The second is the political, and the third is the cultural. And I'll talk about these in more detail in what follows. First, material or economic globalization. And this is technology and the economy. So in terms of technology—the Internet, satellite television, mobile phone connectivity, to some degree, air travel. I know the speed of air travel has not increased for a long time, but on the other hand, there's cheaper flights in many parts of the world. So air travel is part of the equation. All of these then produce, and we can also add remittances, for example, and other forms of global connectedness that are reliant on cheaper satellite TV and Internet. So that then enables an expansion in communication networks and an intensification of the messages flowing on those communication networks around the world.
8.8: Economically, there is rising trade in goods. And I'm going to come on to the trends in the last decade and how they've been affected by things like the pandemic and populism. But international trade as a share of GDP in the world has risen a lot since certainly 1945, let's say. There's the rise of global financial markets and trading of financial assets, stocks and derivatives, and other financial assets from many different countries traded in many different markets. And then you have global economic institutions, and this is more a political economy topic. Institutions like the World Trade Organization, International Monetary Fund, and World Bank that were founded after World War II at Bretton Woods, a conference at Bretton Woods.
8.9: And then you have a number of supranational organizations. The European Union, which grew out of the European Economic Community that was founded just after the war, particularly in the 1950s, but then expanding into become the European Union of 27 states. So that's, the European Union is both expanding and it's intensifying in a way by deepening the number of functions that the EU actually handles. You have the free trade agreements such as north, NAFTA, the North American Free Trade Agreement covering Mexico, the US, and Canada, and a number of other supranational institutions. So there's kind of an economic architecture of institutions, as well as economic flows such as international trade and financial flows. And then you have new technologies knitting together many parts of the globe. So African fishermen using mobile phones to trade. So maybe we're in the realm now of material globalization due to these new technologies.
8.10: In terms of the theory of why globalization should emerge economically, we can go back to the neoclassical economics of Adam Smith and the principle of comparative advantage. So if England and Portugal both try to produce their own milk and wine through economic autarchy and self-sufficiency, both England and Portugal can consume less milk and wine than if they specialized, and Portugal just did wine and England just did milk, and then they traded their surplus. Everybody would be better off than in a situation where each party was trying to be self-sufficient .
8.11: And there's some of this debate now over reshoring of industry from, reshoring the production of chips and various other products, this idea that countries should be more self-sufficient in energy. These are debates that are ongoing now. To what extent do you go with economic self-sufficiency and nationalism, or do you go with free trade, which is more kind of globalization? But the idea of the comparative advantage is that you're better off if you specialize in trade than if you try and aim for self-sufficiency.
8.12: The neoclassical economic theory also would argue that factors of production—labor, capital, and resources—in a perfect free market system, they should flow to where they are most productively used. So if labor is really productive in India and is only being paid a small amount, then there's a big incentive for places with a lot of capital, like the West, to move production to India in order to use that high-productivity, low- cost labor. So the system will tend to continue to move capital into India until the wage levels of Indians rise to an equivalent level of their Western counterparts.
8.13: Now that could also be labor flowing from India into Britain or in other countries. Productivity equaling price, that would be the equilibrium. So in a way, the neoclassical economic model really would argue that globalization naturally emerges because of asymmetries in the price and productivity of these different factors of production in different parts of the world. So in order to achieve equilibrium, you have global flows of labor, of capital, and so forth. And that's why, if you read a neoclassical economics text, you will often see criticism of economic nationalism, that any attempts at self- sufficiency result, which are described as autarchic, impede the efficiency of the market and reduce global GDP.
8.14: And so, there are barriers to the flow, for example, of capital. So restrictions on foreign ownership, licenses, taxes, perhaps corruption that prevents places with a lot of capital, let's say in the West, from moving some of those, that financial capital, and investing in places with cheaper labor where they could make higher profits, which would raise wage levels in the developing countries they move to. But that might be impeded by a whole series of these sets of regulations that would make it difficult for foreigners to own factories, to own land and other factors of production in overseas jurisdictions. Then there could also be other kinds of unofficial barriers, such as language barriers, customs barriers, or nationalist hostility from locals.
8.15: So there's this kind of tension between the innate global cosmopolitanism of the neoclassical economic model, which really favors frictionless free trade and free movement of labor and capital around the world, and as a means of maximizing GDP, and economic nationalists who want to retain a degree of independence for a country, independence from depending on foreigners for their resources and labor and capital. And so nationalism, for example, would block the flow of labor through immigration restrictions. It may block the flow of resources by preventing foreign companies from mining or logging, or removing resources from a country and exporting those resources. It might block capital flows by insisting on capital controls or taxes and making investment risky, raising transaction costs. So there is a tension then between economic nationalism and the neoclassical globalization model.
8.16: And resistance to foreign ownership, foreign land ownership, foreign goods and culture, is going to limit the ability of that global marketplace to operate. So there's a strong kind of liberal capitalist, neoliberal, neoclassical imperative toward globalization. And of course, once you have a global marketplace, you also need a series of legal and political mechanisms to ensure the harmonious functioning of that global marketplace. So enforcement of property rights—if you have, if you aren't paid, you need to be able to go to a court to enforce a contract. And that necessitates some kind of legal order as well, some kind of political order. And maybe the answer, therefore, is that you have a global government or a global polity.
8.17: Now, for some of the globalists, this is unrealistic. So what they see as a sort of intermediate step is the emergence of supranational regions like the European Union as a prototype. So the EU becomes a prototype for other supranational regions to emerge. Maybe those supranational organizations are flimsier, like the North American Free Trade Association or the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. There's very few domains in which those organizations have much power. There's simply free trade deals that have been struck between a set of countries, a certain arrangement between a specified number of countries, but with limited powers.
8.18: But maybe they are the beginning of a world of supranational regions. And a number of different authors have talked about the emergence of these global regions that maybe, in order to resist, in order to be able to compete globally, you need to amalgamate your resources into something larger. It's a bit like when I talked about political evolution. The smaller tribes had to amalgamate into larger confederations to resist the other larger confederations and empires. So maybe in a world of behemoths, you've got to throw your lot in with another behemoth and go for these global regions. So there may be a foreign policy justification, as well as an economic justification to creating these supranational regions.
8.19: So I mentioned that neoclassical economists are very much in favor of frictionless movement of the factors of production—goods, capital, labor—across national boundaries. Kenichi Ohmae, his work, The Borderless World, is a good example of this kind of globalist thinking, which argues that the nation-state is obsolete and is being rendered obsolete by the rise of multinational corporations which have operations in many different countries. And that the optimal economic units, if we're just talking about maximizing global GDP, the optimal economic units are maybe regions that cross borders, like Ontario in Canada, Michigan in the US, or at the time, Hong Kong wasn't part of China, but Hong Kong, Canton is another transnational region. Also, that you can have entities like Singapore which import virtually everything. And yet because they have free trade, they've got cheaper food than places like Japan, which subsidize their farmers and try and maintain agricultural self-sufficiency. So maybe the best way is to do a Singapore and to embrace, fully embrace free trade and that will maximize your welfare and your income.
8.20: For Ohmae, then nation-states were becoming obsolete because of the rise of globalization, the movement of capital information, and the multinational corporations were able to source labor anywhere in the world, capital anywhere in the world, put this all together, and not have a national identity. So he talks about a firm sourcing its capital in London, locating its plant in Malaysia, tapping information from a database in Tokyo, and hiring people in California to design the factory layouts. And so you're sourcing factors of production anywhere in the world, in this frictionless world. And that's really the most efficient way of maximizing global welfare.
8.21: And that's enabled by new technologies, the Internet and satellite. So these are the technologies that are allowing for these more extensive and intense global networks. And these very productive transnational corporations do not, are not tied to a particular home country. Of course the counterargument to that is, in fact, these transnational corporations do tend to have a national identity —that Sony is, in some ways, Japanese, and Nokia is, in some ways, Finnish and so on. So you tend to have, the counterargument is that actually there is a big invest, a big stake that nation-states and transnational corporations have in each other. But Ohmae is arguing the converse, that in fact they are fully global and don't have a national orientation. And so they're really agnostic as to who they hire, what the national backgrounds are; they're just meritocratic and they're concerned only with profit. And they'll buy and sell anything, anywhere.
8.22: As a result then of the rise of the transnational corporation and these global networks that are facilitated by the Internet and other technologies, you're getting a more global economy and that's then going to necessitate a global polity. And so there is a theory called neofunctionalism, which is sometimes known as spillover theory, where one thing functionally necessitates another. So the globalization of the economy makes it necessary to have a global polity, makes it necessary to have a global culture, and that all of these things follow one from the other. So because we're getting this global economy, we're going to need more of a global polity. We can't just have the nation- state, we need something bigger.
8.23: And there are a number of reasons why we need something bigger. One is to regulate transactions across borders, enforce contracts across borders, prosecute criminals who go across borders, deal with macro-economic policy for the world. So if there are financial risks caused by the bursting of a property bubble in Asia or a technology stock bubble in Asia, that could affect the West. And so you actually have to have some kind of coordination and policy regulation that operates across borders. And there are the social democrat globalists who would say, well, in addition, yes, you can have a global capitalist economy, but we have to be able to deal with the inequality that may flow from that. And so we also need some kind of global redistribution of wealth between countries, between wealthy people who may be concentrated more in East Asia or Western countries to the global poor in the developing world.
8.24: Labor standards, environmental standards, these are the kinds of things that a kind of global social democracy needs to address. So that's kind of suggesting that this supranational body should also take on properties of the welfare state and ensure a certain degree of redistribution of wealth. Now, to some degree, that also requires a global identity, because if people don't identify with other people, they're not going to be willing to pay tax to support those other people. And we've seen in the European Union, for example, that the richer countries in the north of the EU, like Germany, have been reluctant to subsidize some of the struggling countries, such as Greece, in the southern part of the EU.
8.25: So even in the European Union, which has very limited tax-raising and spending powers, even there, where you have no shared identity, say Germany and Greece are separate countries, yes, there is a thing called the EU, but maybe the bonds between Germans and Greeks are just not strong enough to support the Germans subsidizing the Greeks. Whereas in the US, people in a wealthy state like California might be, or Massachusetts, might be more willing to see their tax money spent on welfare programs that might benefit people in poorer states, such as Alabama, for example. And so, maybe then because there's that shared American national identity, people are more willing to pool their wealth and subsidize people who are less fortunate. Whereas in a polity like the European Union, where there isn't a shared national identity, Germans will be very upset if a large amount of their wealth, or if a significant proportion of their wealth, is sent to other countries. That's still very difficult.
8.26: But for the social democratic globalists, that's going to be important, when thinking about this new supranational entity that will replace the nation-state, that must replace the nation-state, as a result of that economic globalization necessitating political globalization. And so when we talk about political globalization, there are a number of entities which globalist theorists will look to. So, for example, there is international law and international norms embodied in some of the international institutions, like the United Nations and, to some degree, in regional institutions like the European Union. There is a European Court of Justice which engages in the interpretation of law. And some of the decisions of the European courts influence, even in a country like Britain, which is not in the EU, but certainly when it comes to EU member states, the decisions of the ECJ will supersede those of the national courts. And so here we see that a supranational institution is having power over national institutions.
8.27: There is, however, a debate, one could say. If you take the United Nations, is the United Nations really transcending nation-states or is it reinforcingnation-states ? So are the globalists perhaps too quick to say the UN is an example of globalism and overriding the nation-state? What separatists are yearning for, what Somaliland and Kosovo would love, is a seat at the UN. The UN is almost the final stamp of approval, like you are a nation-state. And so maybe the UN actually reinforces the nation-state norm and it doesn't undercut the nation-state norm.
8.28: Now, the EU is more clearly an institution that arguably undercuts the idea of national sovereignty more because certain functions are allocated to the European level, and there is qualified majority voting. So certain nation-states can oppose an EU policy and be outvoted. They don't have a veto in all parts of EU legislation. They do it in some parts of EU legislation, but not all. So there is an extent to which, when you join the EU, you accept that your national sovereignty will be overridden in certain policy areas. Now, there's a secondary question as to how much a country like Hungary would abide by EU regulations regarding accepting refugees or perhaps regarding relationships with Russia and so on. So in the breach, maybe the member states don't always observe what they signed up to. But at least in theory, these organizations are, in some ways, taking power from the nation-state—the EU, certainly, UN is more arguable.
8.29: We also then have other entities that are transnational, like nongovernmental organizations, such as the World Wildlife Fund, Friends of the Earth, Oxfam. These operate within, they lobby UN agencies. They also lobby nation-states. So that international civil society is kind of like an international or globalized, globalized political lobbyists in a way we can think of them. And so there too we have evidence of something that looks global in nature. So political globalization seems to be proceeding, at least to some degree, through the growth of these regional organizations and through global NGOs and civil society. Globalizers also make a case, a normative case. So I've talked mainly about the "is" rather than the "ought", globalization as an empirical phenomenon, rather than what we ought to be doing.
8.30: A lot of those who see the rise of globalization are also advocates of globalization and would argue the case for a more global approach to human problems. So climate change, for example, and in the past, the question of the ozone hole. But these sorts of challenges are not really specific to any one country. They affect people all over the world. Health challenges like AIDS, or more and more recently, the pandemic, for example—these would be health challenges that are potentially global. Global organized crime, new scientific questions such as biotech, labor laws, corporate regulation. These are all global problems that necessitate in some ways global solutions. So we should have a layer of government that is global, that can really take a sort of global view and get people from different countries on the same page and working to solve these problems. So that is the normative case for global government.
8.31: Now there's the term government and governance. Government suggests a global superstate, which many of these theorists do not advocate, actually. Rather a lot of them would argue for a global layer of governance alongside regional and national. So that is the outlook, for example, of David Held, this multi-tiered political unit where you have some powers at the global level, some at the regional, some at the national, some of the local. However, it is the case there seems to be a push, generally, amongst a lot of these offices for more power to be devolved upwards to global institutions.
8.32: So the view tends to be that there's too much power at the nation-state level and not enough at these global levels. And that there needs to be some, sometimes a certain degree of enforcement coming from the global level. Because in a way, if certain countries aren't cooperating in solving a global problem, then there needs to be some carrot, some stick. So there has to be some sovereignty at the global level. That would be the argument, that the global problems require global solutions. A global market requires some kind of global market regulation, which entails globalized politics to some degree.
8.33: So David Held's notion of cosmopolitan democracy, it takes that term cosmopolitan, which comes from ancient Greece, and it applies it into the modern era of globalization. And so Held is arguing for this multi-tiered polity, where some powers are held at the global level. And the argument is this is already happening. There's this kind of inevitability. We've already got the EU; we've already got global NGOs like Friends of the Earth. And we need to rethink governance. It shouldn't all be concentrated at the nation-state level.
8.34: OK, so I've talked a lot about the globalists. We've talked about economic, political, and, to some degree, cultural globalization. I'll say more about that later. I now want to introduce the writings of a number of skeptics. Michael Mann, sociologist, long based at the University of California, Los Angeles, he talks, he says, well, there's been a lot of obfuscation in the globalization debate, that actually there are, we must make a distinction between local, national, international, transnational, and global. So, trade between Ontario and Michigan is not globalization, according to Michael Mann; that is a transnational flow of goods across one border. And yes, it's the case that you have got certain parts of the world where you have very strong transnational flows between two countries very locally. So that's not, you cannot call that globalization.
8.35: What Mann would argue is that the power of the local has certainly diminished over time, but the power of all of the other networks, the national, the international, transnational, and global, have all strengthened. So the global has not strengthened at the expense of the national, but rather the global has strengthened and the national has strengthened. The only loser, in a way, is the local. And that you can actually see the expansion of nation-state, national networks, and international networks. So for example, the spread of railways within countries in the 19th century, like India and the US, and the spread of railways across countries. So that's an increase in the national network and an increase in the transnational network at the same time.
8.36: The state has lost some power, but it had already lost power, for example, over religion. The link between religion and the state religion had become less powerful as a force. So the Anglican Church in Britain, a less powerful actor in the 19th century than it was prior. So already there was a loss, to some degree, of power in certain domains. The state having less power over religion, but it gains power elsewhere. So for example, the expansion of the welfare state, the state is spending more money, more of a country's GDP, than ever before. So in that sense the nation-state is gaining power. It's not losing power. It just depends; it's ebbing in certain areas, so less power over religion, but more power over income and spending.
8.37: Much of what is talked up, talked up as globalization, is in fact well-established cross- border transnational trade flows between developed countries. So Canada is the US's largest trading partner and vice versa. And this has been largely unchanged despite talk of global trade flows. So a lot of these trade flows across borders are well established and there's not necessarily been much change in who the trading partners are of major countries.
8.38: Most of the world's global production is still for the domestic market. Transnational corporations are heavily intertwined with the home state, which take pride in—Japan takes pride in Sony, Finland takes pride in Nokia, and so forth. So that is —they're seen as national champions and they have certain political influence. And there was a certain intertwining of the nation-state with these global companies. So they are not fully— Microsoft and Apple and Google, these are not fully global companies. They are in fact, in many ways, national; and even international finance is constrained in certain ways in terms of which companies raise money from which stock exchanges.
8.39: In terms of global migration, this is very highly restricted and limited. And it's inconceivable that the working class in the wealthy parts of the world would be willing to accept a wage similar to that of the developing world proletariat. That's politically unacceptable to most citizens in the developed world. So these are just a number of different reasons to be skeptical of the argument that we are entering a global world and that globalization is sweeping all before it and transforming the main unit of political organization from the nation-state to some kind of a supranational or even global state. That's unlikely to be the case.
8.40: Mann also argues that in terms of the real economy rather than the virtual economy, in terms of manufacturing, for example, in terms of spending of GDP, this is largely again taking place within nation-states.
